Rapoport v. Rapoport, 2011 ONSC 4456

COURT FILE NO.:

HEARD:
April 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 18, 19, 20, 21, May 2, 3,
9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 16, 17, 18, 2011

WHALEN J.:

I.

Introduction

A.  Nature of the Claim and Approach

[
1
]

This is an application for change of a Divorce
Order granted April 16, 2009, in particular with respect to: custody of the two
children of the marriage; the amount of child support; arrears of child
support; the amount of spousal support; and, arrears of spousal support.  In
addition, the Applicant (who will be referred to as “the husband”) sought an
order for contempt against the Respondent for her alleged failure to deliver
certain household contents that he said were to be his under the Divorce
Order.  The Respondent (who will be referred to as “the wife”) opposes the
changes sought and asks for changes of her own in connection with custody and
access.  She also asks for confirmation of the arrears of child and spousal
support without changes in the amounts originally ordered.

[
2
]

After giving some general background
information, describing the Order underlying the case, and detailing the relief
sought on each side, I will deal with the custody and access issue in greater
detail, outlining the applicable law then reviewing the evidence with factual
and legal analysis.  Following the same format, I will then deal with the issues
of child and spousal support.  Finally, I will deal with the contempt issue.

B.  General Background

[
3
]

The husband (born October 1, 1947) and the wife
(born September 10, 1970) were married on July 16, 2001.  They have two
children: Jacob, born October 15, 2001; and, Levi, born July 8, 2004.  They lived
in Whitby, Ontario throughout the marriage and since.

[
4
]

The couple separated on October 16, 2006,
although they continued to live in the matrimonial home under circumstances of
high conflict.  On February 2, 2007, Czutrin J. granted a consent Order giving
the wife interim sole custody of the children and interim exclusive possession
of the home and contents.  The husband was granted access to the children from
Friday through Sunday of the first, second and fourth weekends of each month,
plus one evening a week. This Order was modified on June 26, 2007, to require
the delivery and return of the children through an intermediary as a result of
the couple’s on-going and escalating conflict.

[
5
]

Because the husband is a senior member of the
family law bar in the District of Durham, the action was launched in Toronto, where both parties retained
prominent experienced counsel.  The dispute was so intense that the couple exhausted
virtually all of their resources by the time of the Divorce Order in 2009.  They
advised me that between them they had paid over $700,000 to their lawyers.  Indeed,
the wife testified that she had endorsed her entire equalization payment to her
lawyer, to whom she still owes more than $20,000, plus a further $6,000 to an
evaluator.  In order to pay the equalization and his legal expenses, the
husband had to liquidate all of his investments and savings.

[
6
]

The wife has been a full-time homemaker and
mother since the children’s birth.  During the marriage she was totally
dependent on the husband for her support, and since the separation, child and
spousal support have been her only meaningful sources of income.  Apart from
significant capital gains on investments that he liquidated to meet his
obligation to equalize and to pay his legal expenses, the husband’s sole source
of income has been his law practice.  He presented evidence that his practice
had gone into steep decline beginning in 2009 as part of the global recession
and related downturn of the local auto-manufacturing economy.  This evidence
suggested that he has made little or no income during the past several years.

[
7
]

It was against this tragic background that the
parties appeared before me in Oshawa, each self-represented, in a trial that took 24 days over a period
of about six weeks.  The court heard 22 witnesses, and received hundreds of
pages of documentary exhibits in addition to photographic evidence and tape
recordings.

[
8
]

Justice Czutrin’s February 2, 2007, interim Order
had also directed that a custody/access assessment be conducted under
s. 30
of
the
Children’s Law Reform Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. C-12, by Dr Ted Horowitz,
who had been jointly recommended by counsel.  The resulting 149 page custody/access
assessment report (with a further 130 page Appendix) was delivered on July 8,
2008.  Dr Horowitz strongly recommended that the husband have sole custody of
the children.  In response, the wife retained her own expert (Dr Betty
Kershner) to conduct in-depth psychological testing on her and to present a
critique of Dr Horowitz’s report.  Both reports were filed as exhibits at trial.

[
9
]

When all the reports were in, the parties concluded
a settlement by the husband’s January 22, 2009, acceptance of the wife’s formal
Offer to Settle, dated January 20, 2009.  On consent, the terms of the accepted
offer were embodied in the April 16, 2009, Divorce Order.  The issuance of the
final Order was delayed because the court had lost some of the necessary
documentation related to the divorce itself.  In spite of the delay, the
parties conducted themselves on the basis of their settlement.  The matter was
therefore effectively resolved on January 22, 2009.

C.  The Terms of the Original Divorce Order

[
10
]

The Divorce Order granted the parties joint
custody of the children, who were to reside with each parent on a rotating, week-about
basis.  Detailed access provisions divided holidays and special occasions
equally, including three consecutive weeks with each parent in the summer.  During
the time that the children were residing with a parent, that parent was to
provide primary care in all respects.  If the residential parent could not care
for the children for 24 hours or more, that parent was to offer the other the
opportunity of care before arranging it to be done by someone else.  The only
exception was when the children visited with extended family of either party.

[
11
]

The Divorce Order also provided that the parties
were to share the responsibility of making decisions affecting the children,
and were to consult with each other.  The children were to continue their
Jewish faith, and the parties were each permitted to select two
extra-curricular activities for each child.  Where the parties could not agree,
there was to be mediation.  In the event of medical or other emergencies, the
parent with care at the time was to inform the other parent promptly.  Each
parent was to provide the other with up-to-date contact information, and the
parents’ involvement in school and other activities was spelled out in some
detail.  They were each to maintain principle residences within a defined area
of the Durham Region and they were not to remove the children from the Province of Ontario except on consent or by
court order.

[
12
]

Neither party was to denigrate the other or
members of their respective extended families in any communication with the
children or in their presence.  Nor were they to make disparaging or critical
remarks of the other to or in front of the children.  If they had disagreements
about anything touching upon the marriage breakdown, or the terms of
resolution, they were not to communicate it to the children.

[
13
]

On the financial side, the husband was required
to pay the wife $4,198.00 per month for the support of the two children in
compliance with the
Federal Child Support Guidelines
, S.O.R./97-175, based
on an estimated annual income at the time of $340,159.00.  Because settlement had
been reached in January 2008, and income tax returns for that year were not due
until the end of April 2009, the husband’s income from his practice was not
finalized or available.  By June 1, 2009, the husband was to disclose his
actual annual income for 2008 as developed by a named accountant, and he was to
commence payment of
Guidelines
child support based on that amount
commencing July 1, 2009, with adjustment for over or under-payment, and with arbitration
where the parties could not agree on his annual income.  The husband was also
to pay 80% of the children’s extraordinary expenses, and the wife was to pay
20%, subject to appropriate adjustments commencing July 1, 2009, based upon the
husband’s actual annual income for that year, which was to have been disclosed
by June 1, 2009.  The agreement specified that “extraordinary expenses” were:
the children’s private school tuition and related expenses; their music
lessons; their karate lessons and any successor activity; dentistry or
orthodontic treatment; prescription medicines; and, such other expenses as the
parties agreed, or that a court or arbitrator determined.

[
14
]

Commencing on June 1, 2010, and on June 1 of
each succeeding year, each party was to disclose his or her income through the
production of all the information required by the
Federal Child Support
Guidelines
, and the amount of child support would then be adjusted and paid
accordingly, commencing on the next following July 1, with provision for over or
under-payment also to be adjusted, and arbitration where there was disagreement
as to annual income.

[
15
]

The husband was required to pay spousal support of
$7,250 per month, commencing February 1, 2009, and ending on March 31, 2015;
that is, the spousal support would be paid for a term of six years, and then it
would end.  The husband was to maintain specified insurance policies on his
life and obtain new insurance that was specified as security for his support
obligations.

[
16
]

It was provided that $172,911.03 was owing to
the wife in equalization of family property, and that sum was debited and
credited according to advances that had been previously ordered or made,
adjustments for costs in the litigation and pre-judgment interest.  The
matrimonial home was to be listed and sold, with the proceeds divided equally
after adjustments, and accounting for expenses that were set out in some
detail.  On or before March 8, 2009, the husband was to pay the wife $265,000 in
full satisfaction of all claims raised in the litigation, “including, but not
limited to, the balance of the equalization payment owed as described in para.
43 [i.e. the $172,911.03 after applying the specified debits and credits], the
costs ordered by Justice Czutrin, pre-judgment interest, any claim for support
arrears and costs”.  In addition, the husband was to pay the entire cost of Dr
Horowitz’s assessment.

[
17
]

With respect to household contents, para. 50 of
the Order provided:

The parties shall equally divide their
household contents, with the exception of chattels that each of them brought
into the marriage.  The parties shall retain the chattels that they brought
into the marriage.  If the parties cannot agree on a division, they shall have
Mr. Stephen Grant, or another jointly appointed arbitrator, decide the issue by
way of a summary secondary family arbitration.

D.  Specific Changes Sought By Each Party

[
18
]

The parties each presented a written memorandum
setting out of the relief sought at trial.  The husband asked (in Exhibit 2): that
he be granted sole custody of the children; that the wife have access on
alternate weekends “as agreed between the parties” including an equal sharing
of time in the summer; that the wife be prohibited from consuming alcohol while
the children were in her care or smoking while they were in her presence; that
his obligation to pay spousal support be terminated; that all arrears of child
and spousal support be rescinded; that the wife pay monthly child support of
$375 retroactive to April 1, 2009; that he be entitled to 50% of the contents
of the matrimonial home as well as the furniture he brought into the marriage;
that he be permitted to move with the children to the Greater Toronto Area; and
that paras. 3 through 12, paras. 18 and 19, and paras. 31 through 42 of the
Divorce Order of April 6, 2009, be rescinded.

[
19
]

The wife did not specifically request sole
custody of the children.  Rather, she asked that their primary residence be
with her (see Exhibit 65).  She proposed that the husband’s access be on
weekends commencing after school on Friday until the following Sunday at 6:00
p.m., or as otherwise agreed.  The children’s school materials were to be
returned to her with the children after each weekend’s access.  The wife did
not specify that the access be on alternate weekends, so I presume that she was
proposing it take place every weekend.  In addition, the husband would have the
children one overnight at mid-week.  The wife also proposed that each parent
have the children for one month during the summer, with the parent of care
deciding what activities the children would participate in during his or her
month.  She proposed that the husband consult with her before enrolling the
children in extra-curricular activities, but she was content that he had the
final say in the event of disagreement.  He was also to take the children to
all extracurricular activities, except when he was unable to do so, and then he
would ask her before making any other arrangement.  The wife requested that the
children’s residence not be moved from the Durham Region.  Also, they were not
to be moved from their current school, except if Jacob required a specialized
school because of his developmental disability.  In that case, they would have
to agree on the location.  The wife also asked that all arrears of child and
spousal support made under the existing Order be confirmed without change.  She
did not address whether the amounts should change in the future, but the
absence of such comment leads me to presume that she was opposed to any
change.  The husband was to provide her with his Income Tax Notice of
Assessment by May 1 of each year, commencing on May 1, 2012.  He was also to
purchase a “proper bed” for Levi.  In all other respects, the Divorce Judgment
of April 16, 2009, was to remain unchanged and in place, except that the husband
would have the final right to make decisions in respect of the children’s
education and health care.  Finally, the wife asked for costs.

[
20
]

In oral submissions at the end of the trial, the
wife proposed without qualification that the husband make all decisions
regarding the children’s health care, education and recreation.  In summary, it
appears that she was content to have joint custody continue, although the
children’s primary residence would be with her.  The shared custody arrangement
would not continue and instead there would be a form of parallel parenting.

II.

The Questions of Custody and Access

A.   Preliminary Comments About the
Trial Process

[
21
]

The fact that these parties were both
self-represented undoubtedly complicated the trial and made it longer.  The
trial would have been complicated enough, even with experienced counsel
representing the parties, given the history of the dispute and the nature of
the evidence it evoked.  These parties faced the daunting task of presenting
the case in a coherent manner according to accepted laws of evidence and trial
procedure.  Because of its complexity and the fact of self-representation, a
judge very experienced in family law matters was assigned to manage the case
from Toronto.  He guided the parties through the stages of preparing for trial,
including the preparation of trial records, motions and sworn financial
statements.  He also gave some guidance on witnesses that the trial court might
wish to hear (e.g. teachers, physicians, other professional care givers and
Children’s Aid Society workers).  As the case management judge observed in his
December 13, 2010, endorsement (Exhibit 37, Tab1):  “The file is in disarray
and the intensity of the litigation has not subsided since the April 16, 2009
(sic Order).”  He also assisted with the transfer of the file back to the
Durham region where the parties and children lived, and where most of the
potential witnesses were situated.  The case management judge facilitated the
setting of the soonest possible trial date before a judge from out of the
Region because of concerns that will soon be referenced.

[
22
]

The husband is a senior member of the Durham
Region family law bar.  The case management judge observed in his December 10,
2010, endorsement that “The Respondent is not on an equal playing field with
the Applicant.”  She had been denied legal aid.  Her financial situation was
desperate (as will become evident), and she is probably in danger of losing her
only significant asset - her home.  She had no option but to represent herself
as best she could if she wanted to participate.

[
23
]

From the wife’s perspective, the “uneven playing
field” was not just because she lacked legal training, but also because she had
a fundamental lack of confidence in the judicial system given the husband’s
professional status, which she also perceived was a significant threat to her
in the trial process.  She feared that the husband could influence or
manipulate the system against her to his personal advantage.  She had basis for
her concerns.  In a written “Proposal” (Exhibit 39) made shortly after the
separation, the husband had written: “As an aside, you’ll need a lawyer
eventually.  I suspect that any lawyer that takes your case will not be highly
respected by both the judicial community and other lawyers.”  Before the
husband moved out of the matrimonial home, the wife also found a memo that he
had prepared for himself, and left on the desk in his home office.

[
24
]

The husband acknowledged the document in
cross-examination.  In it he had noted talking to a local judge of this court about
moving the case to Cobourg.  The memo continued that the judge was going to
confirm for him what judge was sitting in Cobourg.  The memorandum also
instructed the husband’s assistant not to tell his lawyer about it.  This was
an obvious on-going concern to the wife throughout the trial and she expressed
it a number of times in a number of ways.  I could do nothing more than
acknowledge her concern and that there was a basis for it.  At the same time,
however, I must observe that there was no evidence of interference of any
kind.  The case had been conducted largely in Toronto and the application for change had been managed in Toronto.  I tried to assure the wife that I
had no connection with the judges in Oshawa.  I have also attempted to be sensitive and sympathetic to the
wife’s concerns in this area, including during the trial, in reviewing the
evidence and drafting these Reasons.  During the trial I attempted to be
patient and to give the wife every leeway and allowance so that she could be
assured that I heard and understood her perspective and the evidence she
considered most important.

[
25
]

The wife’s concern about the forum also came out
in the context of her major complaints that the husband was extremely
controlling, both before the separation and since, attacking her verbally and
emotionally at every opportunity, so that she felt that she was always on the
defensive.  She was convinced that as part of his strategy to control, he was
keeping her under surveillance and manipulating people against her.  While the
wife was at times awkward in the presentation of her case, she learned quickly
and was generally very focused and direct in her presentation.  She knew what
evidence she wanted to lead and for what purpose.  She was equally focused in
cross-examination.  I do not think that legal matters were entirely foreign to
the wife because she had completed formal training as a legal assistant,
although I acknowledge that she did not have the skills of a lawyer by any
means.

[
26
]

By contrast, the husband had difficulty prioritizing
his evidence and distinguishing what was important from what was not.  As a
result, his testimony was a long and rambling event.  Also, while the husband
was obviously aware of the law as it applied to family matters, he had almost
no trial experience, admitting that he had attempted to avoid going to court if
at all possible in his practice.  Therefore, I did not find him much more skilled
than the wife in the trial process and presentation of evidence.  In looking
back, I conclude that the “playing field” alluded to by Justice Czutrin turned
out not to be as uneven as he had foreseen.  Because both parties lacked
experience in the trial process, the court had to keep a careful watch throughout
the trial, irrespective of which party was involved in the presentation of
evidence.

[
27
]

Before the commencement of the trial, the
husband and wife were given a ten page memorandum (Exhibit 1) designed to
assist self-represented parties with the trial process.  The memorandum covered
a range of subject matter including the role of the judge in assisting parties
with the process while remaining impartial and even-handed.  It also provided a
procedural overview of the conduct of a trial, including the exclusion of
witnesses, opening statements, procedure for introducing evidence, reply evidence
and closing submissions.  It then dealt with how to present evidence at a trial,
including questioning witnesses, cross-examination, dealing with prior
statements, summoning witnesses, documents as evidence, reading opposing
party’s answers into evidence, making objections, hearsay, and expert
witnesses.  The memorandum concluded with how a party should conduct
herself/himself in the court room, hours of sitting, taking notes, difficulties
in hearing a witness and seeking clarification or further assistance.  As the
trial commenced, the parties acknowledged that they had read the memorandum and
understood it.  I entertained the parties’ questions about it in open court.
The wife was also advised of the availability of legal aid duty counsel in the
court house, and she availed herself of the service on several occasions.  I
also had the impression that both parties had lawyers in the background giving
them advice from time to time but not appearing on the record.

B.  Preliminary Comments About
Evidentiary Issues

[
28
]

The trial was full of evidentiary and procedural
complexities that were difficult both for the court and the parties.  The
husband brought a motion for contempt based on allegations that the wife had
failed or refused to give him certain household contents that he had identified
and claimed had been agreed to.  I was concerned that the wife did not
understand the potential seriousness of such a motion, how to respond and the
process for hearing it.  In the end, it was agreed that the motion would be
dealt with as part of the trial, with the trial evidence applying as the
evidence on the motion.

[
29
]

The wife had surreptitiously taped a number of
conversations between her and the husband, mostly during the period from
October 16, 2006, to February 2, 2007, when they were separated but living
together in the matrimonial home.  The wife wanted to introduce the tapes into
evidence, together with transcripts she had prepared.  At the beginning of the
trial, the husband moved for the exclusion of the tapes and transcripts.  The
wife had also recorded several conversations after the husband moved out, but
she did not propose to rely on them.  Nor did she plan to present tapes made
surreptitiously of Jacob just prior to his being examined for autism by a
paediatrician, and of a meeting with Dr Horowitz after he had disclosed his
conclusions.

[
30
]

The husband made submissions and presented
considerable case law. He was concerned about the fairness and reliability of
the tapes, given that they were obtained without his knowledge or consent.  He
referred to cases where courts had refused to admit such recordings as a matter
of policy in family law disputes.  He was also concerned about the quality and
completeness of the recordings, as well as the accuracy of the resulting
transcripts.  The wife was disadvantaged in her ability to present legal
argument in response, but she clearly articulated what the tapes contained,
their evidentiary relevance and value, and their importance to her case.  It
was her position that they demonstrated the husband’s controlling, hostile and
verbally abusive nature toward her, including in front of the children.  She
wanted to demonstrate these qualities in him as a reflection on his judgment
and ability as a parent.  She submitted that such behaviour (which she
described as the norm) and attacks on her in the presence of the children was
harmful to them.  She also argued that the husband was more interested in “winning”
than in nurturing the children.  The recordings were an important part of the
wife’s case, and on that ground alone (given her concerns about the trial
process and court itself) merited patient consideration.

[
31
]

I concluded that it would be necessary to embark
on a
voir dire
in order to resolve the question fairly.  This of course
required explaining the
voir dire
process to the parties and helping
them prepare for it.  In doing so, it became apparent that the husband had not
heard the tapes and it was not clear that he had even received all of the transcripts.
Indeed, the wife proposed to adduce a selection of transcripts that she had
assembled into a package and not all of the tapes themselves because some were
still in her counsel’s possession.  The husband believed that his former
counsel had listened to some tapes, but he did not know if he had heard all of
them or which ones.  The husband took the position that copies of the tapes had
not been provided to him.  The wife could not say how the lawyers had dealt
with the tapes, although she presented a Consent Order dated June 26, 2007 (but
not entered until August 13, 2007), requiring their production and an
opportunity to listen to all tapes that were in her possession, power and
control.  Curiously, there was no endorsement, consent or entered order to be
found in the court file, and the husband did not have a copy either.  It was
news to him.

[
32
]

I concluded that while production of the tapes
may have been achieved in a technical sense, it had not been done effectively.
I was also concerned that the parties’ ultimate settlement had eclipsed any
legal issues about the tapes that a trial court might have otherwise had to
consider.  It was also not fair to the husband to require him to proceed on the

voir dire
without having had the opportunity to hear the tapes and to compare
them with the transcripts.  Nor would it have been fair to the wife to simply
deny admissibility because of non-production, or for some other reason.  It was
unclear what had actually happened between the lawyers with respect to the
tapes.  The wife was therefore directed to produce all the tapes and
transcripts to the husband, which required her to retrieve some of them from
her former counsel.  The parties were eventually set up in the court room to
review the transcripts and tapes together under supervision of the registrar.
This process took several days, but ultimately the parties were able to agree on
what tapes and transcripts would be entered into evidence.  After hearing them,
the husband also wanted to enter some of the recordings into evidence, even
though the wife could not produce all of the tapes and some tapes had not been
transcribed.

[
33
]

The admissibility of Dr Horowitz’s court-ordered
Custody and Access Report was also a contentious issue.  The wife opposed its
admission because she regarded it as inaccurate, unbalanced, biased and unfair.
The report had recommended sole custody be awarded to the husband.  At the
trial
management conference
, the presiding judge (Mesbur J.) persuaded the
husband not to call Dr Horowitz as a witness, apparently because his work and
report predated the current application for change and should therefore not be
part of the body of facts upon which a determination of change of circumstances
might be made, or be of relevance to circumstances from which a new order might
flow.  However, the
case managemen
t judge directed and supervised the
preparation of trial records.  The husband’s trial record contained Dr
Horowitz’s lengthy report, which I had read along with the rest of the trial
record in preparing for trial.  The wife was thus surprised to find the report
before the court and likely to become part of the evidence, and she quite
properly objected.

[
34
]

I decided that the report was admissible.  It
had been court-ordered.  The assessor had been selected by agreement of very
experienced counsel.  Also, how could a court determine whether there had been
a substantial change in circumstances unless the circumstances predating the Order
could also be reviewed?  Whether there had been a “change” was unfathomable
without the pre-existing situation being known and understood.  Besides, both
parties also intended to call witnesses and submit documentary evidence bearing
on events predating the present application, for example observations of
counsellors, conclusions of physicians, observations of the local Children’s
Aid Society and the tape recordings.  Why would these evidentiary sources be
available if Dr Horowitz’s report was not?  An assessment of the situation at
the time the application for change was brought and only covering the interval from
then to the time of the hearing would be impossible and artificial without the
context of what had come before.  An assessment and determination of the best
interests of the children could not be considered in a vacuum.  Their current
circumstances could not be assessed without full consideration of all the
circumstances that reflected the history of their needs, the progression of
those needs, and the historical abilities and roles of the parents in meeting
them.   I was also aware that the final Divorce Order was based on an offer
that had been made by the wife and accepted by the husband.  There had been no
judicial finding of facts or circumstances upon which the shared custody
arrangement had been based or justified as being in the best interests of the
children.  Also, given the pre-resolution history of extreme conflict, and the highly
litigated nature of the case, I was concerned that the interests of the parents
may have been a major motivating factor.  The primary purpose of the current
process was to determine and meet the best interests of the children.

[
35
]

If Dr Horowitz’s report was admitted into
evidence, the wife wanted the opportunity to submit her critiquing report
(prepared by Dr Kershner), which I agreed was a fair demand that would also
advance the enquiry into the children’s best interests.  However, if the
reports were tendered in evidence, I was concerned that the authors be available
to testify in order to adopt them, explain any portions the presenting party
might think necessary, but more importantly, to be available for
cross-examination by the opposing side.

[
36
]

In this regard, and more generally, I was also
concerned about compliance with the “Rule in
Browne v. Dunn
” ((1893),
1893 CanLII 65 (FOREP)
, 6
R. 67, at p. 70-71 (H.L.)): see  John Sopinka, Sidney N. Lederman & Alan W.
Bryant,
The Law of Evidence in Canada
, 2d ed. (Toronto: Butterworths,
1999), at paras. 16.146-16.148.  A review of the trial record made it clear
that each party was making allegations against the other that would likely involve
questions of credibility, and that each party would be trying to impeach the
credibility of the other.  The Rule in
Browne v. Dunn
states that a
cross-examiner that intends to impeach the credibility of a witness by means of
extrinsic evidence must give that witness notice of his intention by
confronting the witness with the evidence during cross-examination.

[
37
]

Numerous other evidentiary and procedural issues
arose throughout the course of the trial, including these self-represented parties’
constant difficulty with the hearsay evidence rule.   I have outlined some of
the more troublesome questions about the trial process in order to give some
insight into my attempts to deal fairly with the parties given that they were
self-represented, and to give them every opportunity to present their positions
and concerns fully.  In the end, I took a generous and patient view of the
admissibility of evidence, while remaining cognizant during the trial and in
the preparation of these Reasons of the necessity to make findings based on
evidence that is relevant, reliable and admissible in law.

[
38

With respect to the Rule in
Browne v. Dunn
,
the husband might well attempt to impeach the wife’s credibility on the basis
of things she supposedly told Dr Horowitz or that came from his

the basis of the observations or conclusions of Dr Kershner.  There were also
many other reports and records that could be used to the same end.  I explained
the Rule and its underlying concern about fairness, and I urged the parties to
put facts or circumstances to a witness in cross-examination so that the
witness could respond rather than be faced with evidence later that he or she
could not then answer or explain.

[
39
]

The court heard a huge amount of testimony and
received hundreds of pages of documentary evidence.  It is impossible and

and documentary evidence I thought most important, and with what is necessary
to give transparency to my reasoning.

C.  The Law in an Application to Vary Custody and Access

[
40
]

Section 17(5)
of the
Divorce Act
, R.S.C.
1985 (2nd Supp.), c. 3, as amended, gives the court authority to vary custody
or access in an existing divorce orders only if there has been “a change in the
condition, means, needs or other circumstances of the child of the marriage
occurring since the making of the custody order”, and in doing so “the court
shall take into consideration only the best interests of the child as
determined by reference to that change.”   This court must therefore base a decision
to vary on the best interests of the child (
s. 17(5)
), and in doing so, it must
not take into consideration the past conduct of a person unless that conduct was
relevant to the ability of that person to act as a parent of a child (s. 17(6)).
Also, as in making an original order for custody or access, a varying order
must “give effect to the principle that a child of the marriage should have as
much contact with each spouse as is consistent with the best interests of the child
and ... shall take into consideration the willingness of the person for whom
custody is sought to facilitate such contact” (s. 17(9)).

[
41
]

Although it does not apply to custody and access
under the
Divorce Act
, I find it helpful to consider the factors listed
in
s. 24(2)
of the
Children’s Law Reform Act
as a guide to determining
the best interests of a child.  These factors include the following:

•

the love, affection and
emotional ties between the child and each person seeking custody or access to
the child, other persons who reside with the child, and persons involved in the
child’s care and upbringing;

•

the child’s views and
preferences, if they can reasonably be ascertained;

•

the length of time the
child has lived in a stable home environment;

•

the ability and
willingness of each person seeking custody of the child to provide the child
with guidance and education, the necessaries of life and any special needs of
the child;

•

any plans proposed for
the child’s care and upbringing;

•

the permanence and
stability of the family unit with which it is proposed that the child will
live;

•

the ability of each
person applying for custody or access to act as a parent;

•

and, in assessing a
person’s ability to act as a parent, whether the person has at any time
committed violence or abuse against the other spouse or the child (provided not
done in self defence), keeping in mind that this is the only time that past
conduct shall be a consideration in determining a child’s best interests.

[
42
]

Courts have long held that there must be a
“material change” in circumstances before a variation can be granted.  A
“material change” means a change, such that, if the matter which is relied on
as constituting the change had been known at the time, it would likely have
resulted in different terms in the Order.  If the matter relied on was known at
the relevant time, it cannot be the basis for variation: see
Willick v.
Willick
,
1994 CanLII 28 (SCC)
, [1994] 3 S.C.R. 670.  The change must also be more than momentary,
and it must have altered the child’s needs or the ability of the parents to
meet those needs in a fundamental way.  It must impact the child’s best
interests: see
Gordon v. Goertz
,
1996 CanLII 191 (SCC)
, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 27, at paras.
17-18
;
see also
M (B.P.) v M. (B.L.D.E.)
,
1992 CanLII 8642 (ON CA)
, [1992] O.J. No. 2299 (C.A.).  The
test is the same whether the change sought is in respect of custody and access,
or support.  The onus of proof lies on the applicant on a balance of
probabilities, so that if a material change in circumstances cannot be
established, the enquiry ends.

[
43
]

In an application to vary a final order, the
court must assume that the original order was correct and was in the best
interests of the child when it was made: see
Gordon v. Goertz
, at para.

11
;
Crawford v. Dixon
,
2001 CanLII 28121 (ON SC)
, [2001] O.J. No. 466, at para.
10
(S.C.).  This is
so whether the final order was based on a court’s findings after trial or when
the parties’ agreement was incorporated by consent into a final order: see
Miglin
v. Miglin
,
2003 SCC 24 (CanLII)
, [2003] 1 S.C.R. 303; see also David M. Steinberg et al.,
Ontario

Family Law Practice

2011
(Markham: LexisNexis Canada Inc., 2011), at p.
133.

[
44
]

If the threshold condition of a material change
is satisfied, the court will proceed to make a fresh enquiry into the best
interests of the child: see
Young v. Young
(2003),
2003 CanLII 3320 (ON CA)
, 63 O.R. (3d) 112
(C.A.).  In undertaking this fresh enquiry, both parents bear the evidentiary
burden of demonstrating where the best interests of the child lie.  There is no
presumption in favour of a custodial parent: see
Gordon v. Goertz
, at
para.
47
.

[
45
]

In the present case, the husband’s principal ground
for variation of custody was Jacob’s diagnosis of autism or Asperger’s Syndrome
after the offer to settle was accepted and ultimately embodied in the final Divorce
Order.  Although the husband was aware of behavioural problems and that Jacob
was “different”, he had been assured that there were no serious developmental
issues.  In his custody and access report to the parties and the court, Dr
Horowitz had expressed a strong concern that some form of autism was involved
and he urged that appropriate testing be done.  But as will be discussed, this
was ruled out by a paediatrician who examined the child as a direct result of Dr
Horowitz’s concerns.  The paediatrician’s opinion completely undermined the
assessor’s report.  It was only after the Divorce Order was made that autism
was positively identified.  A host of care issues and parenting needs also flowed
from this subsequent diagnosis.  The British Columbia Court of Appeal has held
that the identification of children’s special needs was good reason for a fresh
enquiry into custody: see
Rail v. Rail
,
1999 BCCA 587
, at para.
20
.  I
have attempted to keep all these principles in mind and to apply them in
concluding that there has been a material change in circumstances, and then in
conducting a fresh enquiry into these children’s best interests.

D. Joint Custody

and the Law

[
46
]

Joint custody has become an increasingly popular
parenting model for separated spouses.  Theoretically, it keeps both parents
directly involved in their children’s lives and better fulfils the mandate for
maximization of contact between parent and child.  It is also a very practical
support to working single parents.  In joint custody arrangements, both parents
maintain the full decision making powers they enjoyed during marriage or
cohabitation, and they make decisions together in respect of the children.  Parties
may also share their children’s time and care with a week-about residential arrangement
in what is generally known as “shared custody”. These parties resolved their dispute
with a joint custody arrangement whereby care of the children was also shared
on a week-about basis.

[
47
]

In Canadian law, there is no default position in
favour of joint custody, as each case is fact-based and discretion-driven: see
Growen
v. MacKenzie
,
2008 ONCJ 170
.  Whether it is sole or joint custody, the child’s
best interests remains the primary consideration.  Joint custody is appropriate
where the parents agree to it, although such agreement is not a prerequisite to
ordering joint custody: see
Patterson v. Patterson
,
2006 CanLII 53701 (ON SC)
, [2006] O.J. No. 5454
(S.C.)

[
48
]

However, the courts have consistently held that
there must be a high level of co-operation and communication between the
parents if joint custody is to be a viable option consistent with the best
interests of the children.
Rivard v Rivard
,
2010 ONSC 2711
;
Lawson
v. Lawson
(2006), 81 O.R. (3d) (C.A.);
Roy v. Roy
,
2006 CanLII 15619 (ON CA)
, [2006] O.J. No.
1872 (C.A.);
Kaplanis v. Kaplanis
,
2005 CanLII 1625 (ON CA)
, [2005] O.J. No. 275 (C.A.).  In
Kaplanis
,
the court observed that hoping communication would improve post-litigation or
as the result of a joint custody order does not provide a sufficient basis for
the making of such an order.  There must be some evidence before the court
that, despite their differences, the parents are able to communicate effectively
with one another.  This was re-affirmed in
Giri v. Wentges
,
2009 ONCA
606
, at para.
10
, where the court held:

...as this court has repeatedly held, joint
custody requires a mutual commitment between parents to co-operate on matters
pertaining to the raising of the child, and an ability for the parents to put
their own interests behind those of the child.

[
49
]

A parallel parenting arrangement within the
joint custody model may be an appropriate resolution in situations where the
parties cannot co-operate.  In a parallel parenting situation, the parties may
be solely responsible for decision making in certain aspects of the child’s
life.  For example, the father may be responsible for decisions with regard to
the child’s recreation, and the mother may be responsible for education.  The
areas of decision making are divided up according to what the court thinks is
in the children’s best interests.  Still, the over-riding consideration is the
best interests of the children.
Ursic v. Ursic
(2006),
2006 CanLII 18349 (ON CA)
, 32 R.F.L. (6th)
23 (Ont. C.A.);
Hildinger v. Carroll
(2004),
2004 CanLII 13456 (ON CA)
, 2 R.F.L. (6th) 331 (Ont. C.A.);
Andrade v. Kennelly
(2006),

2006 CanLII 20845 (ON SC)
, 33 R.F.L. (6th) 125 (Ont. S.C.), aff’d (2007),
2007 ONCA 898 (CanLII)
, 46 R.F.L. (6th) 235 (Ont. C.A.);
Cox v. Down
(2002),
2002 CanLII 78080 (ON SC)
, 30 R.F.L.
(5th) 54 (Ont. S.C.), aff’d
Cox v. Stephen
(2003),
2003 CanLII 18571 (ON CA)
, 47 R.F.L. (5th) 1
(Ont. C.A.).
