errands.  Before leaving, he asked her what the children had had to eat so far,
and she replied that they had eaten some cereal and milk.  He said he asked her
quite “gingerly” to cook something for them then took them out with him to pick
up some groceries and a prescription for the wife.  On returning home, he said
he found the wife in tears complaining about how he had talked to her and
declaring that she was leaving.

H.  Questions and Complaints Bearing Upon Custody

[
77
]

At this point I propose to discuss the
complaints and positions of each of the parties in support of their positions
on custody.  I propose to start with the husband’s evidence because he launched
the claim.  The wife’s testimony was both a response to the husband and
statement of her own position in support of the children’s primary residence
being with her.

1.

Health and Development

(a)  Jacob’s Situation

(i)

General Overview

[
78
]

The question that triggered the present litigation,
and that is probably the most important of the many concerns raised, pertains
to Jacob’s emotional and developmental health.  Jacob has always been
“different” in his emotional make-up and the way he relates to people and the
world around him.  It became a focal concern for the husband, especially when
the child eventually expressed suicidal thoughts.  In his custody access
report, Dr Horowitz expressed urgent concern that Jacob was exhibiting signs of
autism or Asperger’s Syndrome that should be explored by an expert.  The wife
took the assessor’s concern to the family doctor, who referred Jacob to local
paediatrician, Dr Christopher Montgomery.  The physician met with the wife and
Jacob, and concluded in a written opinion that the child was not autistic.  On
that basis, the parties settled the case with the joint custody, shared care regime
now in dispute.

[
79
]

However, the husband was not satisfied.  He had
not been included or consulted in the diagnostic process, so he had been unable
to ask questions or know the extent and nature of the assessment done.  On the
verge of trial, it would have been difficult to challenge the unequivocal opinion
of this medical expert.  Yet the husband had questions and wanted to satisfy
himself.  Eventually, he managed to prevail on Dr Montgomery to meet with him,
and once he described the nature of child’s behaviour that caused him concern,
the doctor referred Jacob to Dr Peggy Kirkpatrick, a paediatric specialist in infant
development.  Dr Kirkpatrick diagnosed the child with Asperger’s Syndrome,
which is a form of autism.  This brought a new perspective to Jacob’s behaviour
and the many difficulties he had been experiencing on a number of fronts.  The
husband believed that the wife had deliberately frustrated a valid diagnosis and
this became his principal ground for a change in custody.

[
80
]

The husband testified that Jacob’s behaviour had
been unusual and difficult to manage nearly from the start.  The child had been
non-verbal until the age 2 or 2 ½ years, and then he had been slow to talk.  He
had also lacked eye-contact and exhibited an obsession for wheels on cars or
toys.  When he was shy or nervous, Jacob tended to repeat what was said to him
(“echolalia”), and he was not interested in social interaction with other
children his age.  While the husband acknowledged that he was not an expert,
from his background in psychology and special education he suspected autism
might be involved.  He also had a good friend in British Colombia with two sons
who had been diagnosed as autistic or having Asperger’s Syndrome.  Therefore,
he had some first-hand familiarity with the behaviour of autistic children.  He
said he had discussed his concerns with the wife, and Jacob’s behaviour had
been one of the reasons they had enrolled him in the Montessori program.
Jacob’s first teacher had also apparently been concerned that he might be
autistic.  She had shared her concerns with the parents and recommended an assessment.

[
81
]

Arrangements were therefore made for Jacob to be
assessed at the Grandview Children’s Centre.  The Centre’s report indicated
that the husband had been the source of referral, because he had set up the
intake appointment, albeit at the suggestion of the teacher. At the time of the
assessment, Jacob was 3 years and 4 months old.  The report did not identify
any particular problem, except perhaps some speech delay.  There was no mention
of autism, which the husband concluded had been investigated but was not
indicated or of concern.  He would learn much later that Jacob had not been
tested for autism.  In any event, Jacob was recommended to a speech program and
that was the end of it for the time being.

[
82
]

The husband testified that he accepted the
report with relief, and put his concerns about autism out of his mind.  He indicated
that he was also lulled and encouraged by the child’s improved reading ability
and his growing interest in social contact with peers.  The concern about
autism did not recur until Dr Horowitz expressed his concern in the July 30,
2008, custody/access report to the court and the parties.  In the meantime,
Jacob had many health problems that occupied the husband’s attention and that
probably distracted both parents to some extent from signs of autism. These
other health issues also became an increasingly divisive part of the battle
between the parties.  The wife regarded it as another front upon which her
parenting ability was being attacked, and she was convinced that the husband
was also using it to assert control over the lives of her and the children.
The husband viewed it as another example of the wife’s insensitivity to the
children’s needs, and her refusal or inability to take responsibility.  He saw
the wife’s resistance as a disregard for the children’s health needs
(particularly Jacob’s), and as a result they were being placed in potential
harm; so he pressed all the harder.

(ii)  Early
Post-Separation Situation

[
83
]

After the wife was awarded interim exclusive
possession of the home and interim custody of the children, she took over the
children’s health care and the husband was pointedly excluded.  This in itself
was a great source of frustration and ill will on both sides.  The husband did
not have the children’s health cards when he exercised access and he was not
provided with copies, even though he requested it often and it was a repeated
topic in court affidavits and correspondence.  It was also a practical difficulty
when a child fell ill or suffered minor injury during access, and required
attention at a clinic or hospital emergency department.  The wife never
explained why she did not want him to have their health cards, although I
expect she feared he would use them to take the children to doctors or other
health care givers in the advancement of his complaint to the court that she
was not properly caring for the children.  The husband finally got copies of
the cards when a Dispute Resolution Officer pressed the wife to provide them,
but this was late in the process and not long before the final settlement.

[
84
]

The husband testified that he kept the wife
informed of any health issues that arose while the children were in his care,
be it during the period of his interim access or joint custody.  He documented
it with emails to the wife, for example informing her of trips to walk in
clinics (e.g. when Jacob had a problem with bronchitis), getting prescriptions
for the children, seeking out counselling services for them, and advising of
medical or counselling appointments.  He submitted some of these emails into
evidence at the trial.

[
85
]

On the other hand, the wife did not always keep the
husband informed or involved in her management of their health care.  She did
not include him in appointments with the family doctor, or even inform him of those
appointments or what happened at them.  At times, she was happy to have his
input and support when a problem arose.  At other times she resented it because
she thought he was using the children’s health as a strategic tool to undermine
her in the litigation; and at other times she was concerned that the children
were being exposed to too many health care providers.  The husband admitted
that he had tried to arrange appointments for Jacob to see a psychologist or
psychiatrist without first consulting the wife.  He had done this through a
physician at a local walk-in clinic, and the office of referral had called the
wife for information about Jacob and suggested that he was a “troubled” child
and that he had suffered some trauma.  The wife was either alarmed or offended,
and advised the caller that she would not permit Jacob to attend a scheduled
appointment, so it was cancelled.

(iii)  The
“Pooping” Problem

[
86
]

In April 2007, Jacob started to have what became
referred to as his “pooping problem” – i.e. he would have uncontrolled bowel
movements that could happen at any time or place.  The husband found out how
serious it was when a teacher complained to him.  Jacob had become defiant with
the teacher and was defecating in his pants.  Of course, there would be
objectionable odours that upset the class.  When he was asked about it, Jacob simply
ignored, or even denied that he had soiled himself.  On one occasion he
acknowledged it but said he did not care.  On another occasion, when the
teacher sent him to the washroom to clean up, Jacob spread feces on the
bathroom wall.  He even defecated on a bathroom floor at school.  The husband described
an incident when he was waiting in the school hall one day for Jacob to gather
his things.  He asked a little girl nearby if she was Jacob’s friend, and the
girl replied “no” because Jacob “stinks” and “poos his pants”.  Jacob overheard
the remark but was not the least bit phased, and retorted that he did not do it
all the time.  Jacob did not seem to be bothered by the problem and he did not
have insight into the social ramifications.  The husband picked up on it and
was very concerned.

[
87
]

This problem caused the husband to seek medical
help.  He went to a walk-in clinic, where Dr Lee Sang referred him to Dr Rajah,
a general paediatrician with an interest in infant gastroenterology and
nutrition.  The appointment was for May 7, 2007.  The husband admitted that on
this occasion, he had intended to take the child without notifying or
consulting the wife in advance.  However, she was alerted when Dr Rajah’s
office called her for some information, and as a result she cancelled the
appointment.  It appears that she then spoke with her family physician, Dr
Green, who made an appointment for Dr Rajah to see Jacob on May 22, 2007.  I
note that in his testimony at trial, Dr Green thought Dr Rajah’s involvement
had been in respect of the husband’s concerns that Jacob was failing to
thrive.  He made no mention of constipation being one of the problems, although
he would become aware when he eventually received Dr Rajah’s report following
the May 22, 2007, appointment.  It does not therefore appear that the wife had
raised the issue with Dr Green or had seen it as a problem meriting medical
intervention.  When the husband was not permitted to take Jacob to the
appointments with Dr Rajah, or to be present at them, he met the doctor several
times by himself to express his concerns.

[
88
]

Dr Rajah diagnosed Jacob with “encopresis”,
which is an involuntary fecal soiling secondary to constipation and is not an
uncommon condition in children.  In reviewing the child’s history with the
wife, Dr Rajah was not told that Jacob was acting out at school or having
difficulty with academic performance.  The wife only suggested that Jacob was
demonstrating some oppositional behaviour related to the separation and that
there were no issues at school.  Dr Rajah recommended they give the child a
particular kind of mineral oil.  Eventually the problem was resolved.  However,
it became a part of the battle ground between the parents.  The wife blamed the
soiling problem on anxiety brought about by the husband (she thought it
subsided when the husband was away on vacation).  She also thought that the
husband was over-reacting, and making more out of it than necessary in an
effort to paint her as an unfit mother.  The husband blamed it on anxiety
caused by the wife’s embarking on a relationship with another man who was
spending a great deal of time in the matrimonial home, and who stayed overnight
on occasion.  He noted that the wife had become involved with this man in April
2007, the same time that fecal soiling became a problem.  The wife denied any
impropriety with the boyfriend, who had a daughter the same age as her
children.  She said that the boyfriend came to the house with his daughter in
the context of a children’s play date.  When he stayed overnight, it was in a
room shared with his daughter.

[
89
]

Dr Horowitz also expressed concern that the
soiling was a manifestation of the wife’s new relationship.  Although he
acknowledged that Dr Rajah saw it as a constipation problem, Dr Horowitz thought
it was more related to the wife’s new relationship when also taken in the
context of Jacob’s oppositional behaviour at school.  Dr Horowitz thought there
was an emotional aspect, with the child becoming enraged when another man and
child were brought into the home.  He also thought Jacob was generally angry at
his parents for separating and for the way they were handling it.

(iv)  Failure
to Thrive

[
90
]

From the husband’s perspective, the soiling
problem soon became secondary to the question of whether Jacob was “failing to
thrive”.  Failing to thrive is a potentially serious medical condition where a
child’s growth and weight gain are not progressing as they should.  By early May
2007, Dr Horowitz’ custody and access assessment was well underway.  By then he
had met the parties and the children a number of times.  One of the husband’s
concerns was that the wife had not been feeding the children properly or
adequately.  He was particularly concerned about Jacob, who looked pale, unwell
and had gained very little weight over the previous year (a pound or less over
14 to 16 months).  He expressed his concern to Dr Horowitz, who agreed the
child did not look well.  This became the main focus of Jacob’s medical
relationship with Dr Rajah and one that caused great strife.

[
91
]

Dr Rajah testified that when he first examined
Jacob he was 5 ½ years old and ranked in the 33
rd
and 27
th

percentiles respectively for weight and height.  He had examined the child on
eight occasions between May 22, 2007, and April 13, 2009.  Over the time that
he saw Jacob, the child gained weight and grew sufficiently that he stayed
within those percentile ranges.  As the physician explained to the court, a
child’s weight and height are measured against medically established charts.
Failure to thrive could be a diagnosis if the child deviated from his range on
these charts to a certain degree.  Dr Rajah stated that he was not concerned
about Jacob during the time that he saw him because he maintained his place on
the charts.

[
92
]

However, he also admitted that a parent who
observed little growth or weight gain in their child over a year was properly
concerned and it was worthy of medical investigation.  He agreed that when the
child first came to him he could not accurately assess the problem without the
family doctor’s clinical records where weight and height would be recorded over
prior years.  He had explained this to the husband at their May 25, 2007
meeting and indicated he would ask Dr Green for Jacob’s records.  The husband
followed up with Dr Rajah several times and still no records had been
forthcoming.  Finally, sometime in June 2007, the husband told Dr Rajah that he
intended to make a complaint about Dr Green to the College of Physicians and Surgeons.  However, Dr Rajah persuaded him to
show patience as he made one more request.  The doctor eventually received the
records and it was established that Jacob’s weight and height gains had not
deviated from his place on the chart.  There was no evidence as to when the
records were received.  However, Dr Rajah conceded that it was “some time”, and
it appears they were not received until late spring or early summer 2007.  Dr
Rajah also agreed that Jacob had gained very little weight between 3 ½ and 4 ½
years.

(v)  The
Assessor Gets Into the Fray

[
93
]

All of this precipitated much correspondence
between lawyers and bitter allegations between the parties.  Even Dr Horowitz
got into the battle as he expressed consternation and frustration over the
physicians’ delay in giving a clear answer because of the slow production of records.
Dr Horowitz had personally made numerous attempts to speak with Drs. Rajah and
Green.  As a result, he made unflattering observations suggesting that the
physicians did not want to become involved out of fear of inconvenience or
personal liability.

I am concerned that Dr Rajah, Dr Green and
some of the other key medical players simply do not want to be involved.  They
do not want to sit in a witness chair, give their opinion, and then have a
physician called by ‘the other side’ give a contrary opinion.  Medical
insurance is very expensive.

[
94
]

Dr Horowitz was finally able to speak with Dr
Rajah, although at trial it was clear that the paediatrician had no idea who the
assessor was or what his role was in the situation.  Dr Horowitz reported on how
he had attempted to contact Dr Green, but the doctor failed or refused to
return his calls.  This gave Dr Horowitz the impression that Dr Green had
chosen sides and that his adult patient’s interest in the outcome of the
custody litigation was more important than the best interests and health of the
children.  Dr Green testified that he was unaware of Dr Horowitz’s attempts to
reach him.  He could not understand how he would not have been told about the
assessor’s calls.  However, he admitted that there had been problems in his
front office that had caused him to terminate a manager.  He also admitted that
correspondence or phone calls, other than from patients, were of low priority
and often sat waiting on his desk until he could find time to reply.  Patients’
current needs and record keeping took most of his time.

[
95
]

I accept Dr Horowitz’s testimony on his
difficulties in contacting the physicians.  It was no secret to them that high
conflict litigation was underway.  I am sure they did not want to be involved
as witnesses if it could be avoided.  However, they should not have refused or
delayed to speak with Dr Horowitz.  If there was a question about Dr Horowitz’s
role, they could have sought clarification from their own counsel or by direct
question to whichever one of the parties themselves.  I conclude that Dr Rajah
eventually did communicate with Dr Horowitz but that Dr Green did not.  I doubt
very much that Dr Green would have refused to speak with Dr Horowitz because he
had taken a position in the litigation.  I accept that it was because of staff
problems in his reception area and also that it was a low priority issue to him
because of the demands of seeing patients and keeping their records.  Dr
Horowitz was rightfully frustrated and angry, although I do not think his
comments assisted the situation.  He ought to have been less outspoken and more
neutral.  I wonder why he did not send the physicians a letter, explaining his
role and asking for an opportunity to confer with them directly or by telephone?

(vi)  Asthma
and Allergies

[
96
]

Jacob may also suffer from allergies or asthma.
The husband testified that the child has a chronic cough that they had attributed
to one of these conditions.  Before the separation, a neighbour who held a
senior nursing position had recommended specialists they might want to consult.
However, the separation occurred and there was no follow up.  Sometime later,
the husband took Jacob to a walk-in clinic in connection with a rash, and the
doctor suggested it might be linked to allergies or asthma.  In his report to Dr
Green, Dr Rajah commented on dark circles around Jacob’s eyes that he thought
were likely related to allergies.  There was no evidence that Dr Green had
given it attention by testing, referral, or treatment.  So it is probably still
undiagnosed and untreated, and is therefore a potential fertile battleground
between the parents.  Indeed, it is surprising that one of them had not
followed through on it before trial.

[
97
]

The husband accused the wife of smoking in the
presence of the children, including inside the home, thereby exacerbating
Jacob’s condition.  He characterized this as further proof of the wife’s irresponsibility
and insensitivity to the children’s best interests.  At times the wife admitted
to smoking on a limited basis, while at other times she denied it.  At trial
she acknowledged that she still smoked.  She said that she had done it for a
while in the bathroom.  However, now she does not smoke inside her home at all,
and she never smokes in the presence of the children.  The husband did not believe
her.  The nanny testified that Jacob had reported to her that his mother still
smoked in front of him, but he did not say where it happened.  The wife did not
deny or otherwise respond to this piece of evidence.

(vii)  Behavioural
Problems

[
98
]

In addition to the behavioural problems already
discussed, Jacob presented other troubles.  Although he was eager to make friends
and be part of the group, he lacked the social skills to do so.  He did not
pick up on social cues or understand when he was invading someone’s personal space
or comfort zone.  Because of his desire for acceptance, he was easily led.  Peers
would often take advantage of him, urging him purposely to do and say things
that were inappropriate and that would get him into trouble – for example swearing.
The other children regarded him as being “different” and maintained a
distance.  Jacob’s grade-four teacher, Mr Whillans, testified that at least 90%
of the class had asked him why Jacob was so different.  Because of his
difficulties relating to peers, Jacob tended to play with younger children.

[
99
]

The husband also testified that Jacob often lies.
He would maintain the lie, even though he had been clearly found out or
observed at the time.  He also has an explosive temper that can be triggered by
the smallest thing – for example being told that he cannot play outside until
after supper.  He will rage, say mean or rude things, slam doors or make
threats (e.g. to run away).  The husband described how Jacob likes to negotiate
changes that he wants to rules or directions given; but if one stands ground
with the child, he will often go into one of these tantrums.  According to the
husband, Jacob does this three or four times a week on the average.  He is very
difficult to handle when he erupts, and the husband said the best course is to let
the rage run its course.  Typically, after a half hour or so, Jacob will come back,
acknowledge that he was wrong and apologize.

[
100
]

Dr Horowitz reported on communications with
David Martin, an investment broker living in Kelowna, British Columbia.  Mr
Martin is a long time friend of the husband’s and had helped him earn
considerable money on investments that will be the subject of the support issue
later in these Reasons. Mr Martin described several instances of Jacob’s
prolonged tantrums while they were visiting after the separation.  He reported
that on one occasion, while they were all driving to a ski area, Jacob
threatened to “poop” on his head and to poke him in the eyes.  He observed that
the husband was endlessly patient with the child’s moods and attentive to his
needs.

[
101
]

The husband’s nanny, who he described as a very
quiet and capable individual, is particularly the butt of Jacob’s
explosiveness. Because it is her job to manage the household and help care for
the children, it often falls to her to give direction.  For example, as she
testified, Jacob may explode if she tells him to turn off the television, come
to dinner or do homework when he does not want to.  She stated that she had
been directed to maintain a fairly regimented household routine.  As she put
it, there is a time for homework, a time for meals and a time for play. She
testified that when Jacob explodes at some direction he does not want to follow,
he will tell her she is a very bad nanny and not “Queen of the House”.  He will
threaten to tell his father to fire her, and he will carry through on the
threat, as the husband confirmed.  According to both the husband and the nanny,
she and Jacob have formed a close bond.  Yet when Jacob is unhappy about
something, he can be brutally rude to her, say nasty things, hide or break her
belongings, tell her that he does not have to listen to her, or insist to his
father that she be fired.  The nanny also indicated that the child will usually
cool down after a while, admit that he was wrong and apologize.  Although the
nanny understands Jacob’s situation and special needs, the husband fears that she
can only take so much and may quit.

[
102
]

The husband also described how Jacob could
become fixed on something, or obsessed with an idea or desire to do something.
Again, there is often no reasoning with him when he takes such a notion, and if
pressed, he may explode in anger.  He also has difficulty with spatial concepts
and his eye-hand co-ordination is poor.  There are oddities in the way he speaks,
and he continues to repeat back to people things they have said to him (i.e. echolalia).
Yet he is intelligent and capable of functioning well academically.  These
observations came from the husband, not the wife. The behaviours are also well
documented in records that were entered into evidence and the testimony of
teachers and others who have had dealings with Jacob.  Teachers indicated that
he had to be kept busy and focused on the task at hand, or else he would become
distracted and disruptive.  He requires more attention and supervision than the
average student.

(viii)
Diagnosis of Autism

[
103
]

In preparing his assessment, Dr Horowitz learned
of Jacob’s peculiarities and behaviour from multiple sources. As a result, he
was concerned that Jacob might be developmentally disabled by some form of
autism.  For that reason, he engaged a therapist with experience in dealing
with autistic children to observe Jacob in the classroom.  Although no formal
tests were performed, the therapist suggested that the child may be
experiencing difficulty in processing language and that this explained his behaviour.
She therefore recommended audiology and psycho-educational testing.  She did
not address autism as a possibility.

[
104
]

Still, Dr Horowitz was concerned about autism
and he expressed himself to the parties and their lawyers at a disclosure
meeting, where he also discussed his other conclusions and recommendations.  He
urged the parties to have Jacob tested.  What he did not tell them, and what we
did not learn until trial, was that Dr Horowitz was himself in a parental
relationship with an autistic child nearly the same age as Jacob and
demonstrating many of the same characteristics. Dr Horowitz had taken the
responsibility of dealing with this child’s health care providers and
supervising his education.  He had studied the syndrome and had become very knowledgeable
about it – so much so that had become an advisor and resource to other parents
with autistic children.

[
105
]

The wife thought Jacob’s behaviour was more the
result of speech delay.  She believed he would grow out of it, and that no
special measures were necessary.  Undoubtedly she was hostile to Dr Horowitz because
in his report he had been harsh in his judgment of her, and he had recommended
that the husband have sole custody.  Dr Horowitz’s views at the disclosure
meeting, stated also in his written report of July 30, 2008, revived the
husband’s fears that Jacob might be autistic, and he was anxious to have Jacob
assessed.  I am sure that the wife and her lawyers regarded Dr Horowitz’s
urgings with suspicion.  They accused him of acting outside his area of
expertise and of usurping the role of a physician.  The wife continued to be
convinced that the husband had amplified Jacob’s behavioural issues to the
maximum as part of his strategy of manipulate, attack, control, and marginalize
her.  Still, out of caution, she brought Dr Horowitz’s concerns to the family
doctor (Dr Green), who referred her to a well-respected local paediatrician, Dr
Christopher Montgomery.

[
106
]

Dr Montgomery met with the wife and Jacob on May
7, 14, and June 12, 2008, and he delivered a written report and opinion on
September 16, 2008.  The husband was not invited to meet with Dr Montgomery or
to participate in the diagnostic process.  The physician therefore relied
solely on existing records and information provided by the wife. After noting
that Jacob had been found normal for hearing and speech, he summarized the
wife’s information as follows:

Mom said that he did demonstrate some
echolalia when learning to speak as a younger child but this was not a
persistent concern.  She said he does not exhibit any need for routine or
repetitive behaviours.  She said he was “hyper”.  She also felt he exhibited an
intense interest in cars.  Mom said Jacob could be fidgety and disruptive as
well as hyperactive.  But not loud, impatient or impulsive.  She said he was
easily distracted, absent minded and often failed to complete tasks.  She said
she often has difficulty getting his attention.  Mom had concerns that Jacob
has some unusual habits.  For example she said he will sometimes count cracks
on a sidewalk.  She said he seems to have to repetitively touch objects.  It
was not clear to me by history that this was obsessional behaviour.  Mom said
Jacob is indeed very bright and no one has raised any concerns about his
academic abilities.  There is no concern regarding lying, stealing or
aggression.

[
107
]

After conducting a thorough physical
examination, Dr Montgomery concluded:

In my opinion he does not meet the criteria
for the diagnosis of any specific childhood behavioural disorder including anything
along the autistic spectrum or
[Attention
Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder] (
ADHD).
He shows very strong academic skills.

[
108
]

At trial, Dr Montgomery agreed that his
conclusions were based largely on the history and information provided to him
by the wife, and that he had conducted no tests.  The wife and a teacher had
also filled out questionnaires that Dr Montgomery said supported his conclusion,
although the questionnaires focused more on ADHD behaviours than autism.

[
109
]

Dr Montgomery’s opinion had an understandably undermining
effect on Dr Horowitz’s concerns and his entire report.  The wife retained an experienced
psychologist to do a critique of Dr Horowitz’s assessment report, and to also conduct
extensive psychological testing on her.  In considerable detail, the
psychologist’s report attacked the assessment as unbalanced, biased,
misinformed, and unfair.  The wife’s psychological profile ruled out any mental
illness or personality disorders.  The combination of the critique, the
psychological work-up and the ruling out of autism made the husband reassess his
chances of winning sole custody.  Dr Horowitz’s report seemed totally
discredited and the husband’s concerns about Jacob’s behavioural problems
seemed unfounded.  As a result, he accepted the wife’s proposal for shared
custody and the other terms that were eventually embodied in the final Divorce
Order.  From the wife’s perspective, this was also likely the best she could
hope for without taking a great risk.

[
110
]

In spite of the settlement, the husband was not happy
with Dr Montgomery’s opinion, and particularly with having been excluded from
the diagnostic process.  He did not agree with the information in Dr
Montgomery’s report that credited the wife as the source.  He did not think it
complete or accurate, and it did not square with his many observations and
experiences with Jacob.  He even thought that the wife had purposely lied to
the doctor and that taking Jacob to Dr Montgomery had been a “cynical move”
calculated by the wife and her counsel to overcome the concerns expressed by Dr
Horowitz and thereby undermine his assessment report. Therefore the husband
approached Dr Montgomery to discuss the report, and eventually the physician
agreed to meet with him.  This meeting took place on March 5, 2009.

[
111
]

Dr Montgomery testified that he received further
history and information from the husband that suggested Jacob’s echolalia
persisted and that he was unable to pick up on social cues. Had he received
that information from the wife, the doctor said his conclusion would have been
very different.  As a result, he referred Jacob to Dr Margaret Kirkpatrick, a
local paediatrician specializing in autism and foetal alcohol syndrome.

[
112
]

Dr Montgomery testified that he was aware the
parties were going through a very bitter divorce, although he said he never
felt pressured or manipulated by their lawyers.  He was also aware of Dr
Horowitz and his role as an assessor.  He had the impression that Dr Horowitz
was a social worker and he thought it odd that a social worker would be
qualified to talk about medical issues.

[
113
]

The wife consented to Jacob being assessed by Dr
Kirkpatrick, who saw him on July 17, and 21, 2009.  Dr Kirkpatrick was aware of
all the behaviours discussed above and heard the husband’s concerns too.  She
then assessed Jacob with the “gold standard” test for diagnosing autism (ADOS G
Module 3) and concluded that he was Autistic Spectrum High Functioning.
Although he was technically “high functioning autism” because of certain demonstrated
language problems, the doctor labelled him with Asperger’s Syndrome because it
was a more socially acceptable and understood condition.  Dr Kirpatrick’s
testing confirmed that the boy demonstrated poor eye contact and that he lacked
social skills; he tended to use formal language and was good at carrying on
conversations on topics that interested him, but he was not good at
conversations on topics of interest to other people; while he was creative, he
got stuck on certain topics and had to do things in a certain order.

[
114
]

Dr Kirkpatrick explained that an autistic child
may exhibit behaviours that are not core features of the condition, but are
secondary to it.  Sensory processing disorders were in this category and she
believed that Jacob had issues here in respect of certain foods.  Also,
explosiveness was not a core feature of autism, but autism could be so
stressful to the individual that it caused him to explode in anger and
frustration without remembering what he did.  She observed that when the autistic
individual recovered his equilibrium, he would often remember what he had done
(or do so when told), would accept it and apologize.

[
115
]

The doctor emphasized the importance of
structure, routine, consistency and predictability to autistic children.
Transitions and change are difficult for them because they get fixed on
routines and have difficulty moving on.  The autistic child has to know what to
expect and what is going to happen.  Otherwise he may experience “melt down”
and trauma. While this does not rule out a shared custody arrangement,
structure, routine, consistency and predictability must exist in
each

household for the autistic child to be able to function and thrive.  Dr Kirkpatrick
also thought it was important to inform the autistic child about his condition
as soon as possible and in a positive supportive way so that he could learn how
to advocate for himself and know what works best for him.  Parents of an
autistic child must also be sensitive to the impact of the condition on younger
siblings, who should also be made aware of it; but this disclosure was best
achieved as a family event and in a manner that was positive to and supportive
of both children.

[
116
]

The wife was clearly unhappy with Dr
Kirkpatrick’s diagnosis.  She did not have confidence in it.  At trial she
stated that she would still like a second opinion and assessment.

[
117
]

Since the diagnosis, the husband initiated an
assessment by Lakeridge Community Support Services, an Oshawa agency that works
with children and families in respect of children with developmental problems.
The husband came to them for advice on how to deal with Jacob’s explosiveness
and resistance to direction that he did not like.  As a result, one of the
agency’s consultants conducted a behavioural assessment.  The consultant interviewed
both parents. The wife attended appointments with Jacob only two or three
times.  The husband usually took Jacob, and he met often with the consultant to
express concerns and to seek advice.

[
118
]

The husband detailed the history of Jacob’s
behaviour and diagnosis, as discussed above.  In her interview with the
consultant, however, the wife denied that the behaviours complained of by the
husband and documented elsewhere were occurring when Jacob was with her.  She
said that he would only become angry when he thought he was getting into
trouble for something he did not agree with.  She also claimed that he could be
calmed by reassurance and talking the situation through.  If he became angry,
he would get flushed, purse his lips and become teary-eyed – a very different
picture from that described by the husband.

[
119
]

The consultant visited the wife’s home four
times and the husband’s once (but met with the husband four times at his
office).  She concluded that many of the behaviours were not occurring in either
home at the time, but recommended: that definite rules be established at each
house (not necessarily the same, but defined so that Jacob knew what to
expect); that specific consequences be developed so that he knew what to expect
if he broke a rule; that daily schedules be developed with Jacob each morning
for the day; that a positive reinforcement system be developed in each home so
that Jacob could expect to earn something when he successfully followed the rules
and schedules; that Jacob’s negotiating skills be used by the parents to their
advantage in a manner she then described; and, that the husband refrain from
“giving in” to the child as a way of avoiding conflict, because giving in
reinforced Jacob’s persistence and the likelihood of recurrence of the negative
behaviour. The consultant acknowledged that explosiveness was a common occurrence
in autistic children.

[
120
]

The husband testified that since Jacob’s
diagnosis he has read a considerable amount about autism and Asperger’s
Syndrome.  He has loaned books to Jacob’s teacher and recommended reading to
the wife.  He has also completed a course on Asperger’s Syndrome at Durham
College, which was confirmed by a letter from the College dated January 27,
2010.

(a)

Levi’s Situation

(i)

Question of Incontinence

[
121
]

Levi is generally healthy and suffers from no identified
or chronic mental, emotional or physical condition or disorder, but for one.  At
age six he still “wets” his pants fairly regularly at home, at school and other
places.  The husband testified that Levi knows everyone is concerned about it. He
knows when it happens and is embarrassed.  However, he does not seem to be able
to control it and he has told his father that he cannot sense when it is about
to happen.  The husband thought Levi just seemed to get wrapped up in whatever
he was doing, and did not take the time to use the washroom.  The nanny
testified that she usually has to find out on her own that Levi is wet.  She will
have to check; sometimes she will try to remind him by asking whether he has
taken time to use the washroom, and he will tell her that he is wet.

[
122
]

In typical fashion, the husband took steps to address
the problem by asking the wife to take Levi to the family doctor for
examination, tests and perhaps a referral to an urologist if necessary.  He
asked to be kept informed.  This was documented in an email to the wife dated
April 23, 2010.  The wife made an appointment with Dr Green, who ordered an
ultra-sound.  The test was completed, but the husband was never advised of the
result or of any other tests or steps taken.  He sent the wife follow-up emails
on May 17 and June 14, 2010, and requested a reply, but none came.  The wife
did not deny it or explain why she had not shared the information.  This is but
one of many examples of how the parties could not communicate or co-operate
effectively on a significant child care issue.

[
123
]

The potential seriousness of Levi’s situation
came out in Dr Montgomery’s testimony.  He stated that night time bed-wetting
is not uncommon.  About 15% of children six and seven years old do it.
However, a child of that age who is wetting his pants during the day required
medical attention.  The doctor also commented that an ultrasound was usually of
little assistance.  Dr Green did not address the issue when he testified.

[
124
]

As with almost everything that touched the lives
of the parties or the children during this period, it became a battlefield.
The wife had apparently told Levi’s teacher that Levi only wet his pants the
weeks he was with his father.  The husband found out and complained about it to
the wife in an email sent to her on May 29, 2010.  Again, the wife offered no
explanation or comment about it in her testimony.  Nor did she deny.  In any
event, when the opportunity presented itself the husband retaliated.

[
125
]

Late one Saturday morning or early afternoon in February
2010, the wife took the children skiing.  They skied the entire day and stayed
into the evening while the wife socialized.  The children visited their father
the next day and at some point, the nanny noticed that Levi was wet, so she
asked him to follow her upstairs to clean him up and change him.  As she washed
him with water in the washroom, he cringed and said it hurt.  It was then that
she noticed an angry rash in his pubic area and between his legs.  She called the
husband to observe, and asked him what she should do.  He instructed her to
take photos of it, which she did with a digital camera while the boy laid on
his back exposed in a bedroom.  The husband’s purpose was to preserve the
evidence, which he regarded as another example of the wife’s inattention and
lack of responsibility.  She had failed to take precautions that Levi use the
washroom, had not paid attention and had permitted him to spend a good part of
the day in heavy, urine-soaked clothing, and even into the next day.

[
126
]

Both the husband and nanny testified that the taking
of the photos had not bothered Levi in the least, except that he had worried
about getting his mother in trouble.  The digital camera was left lying
around.  Some days or weeks later, Jacob had a friend over to play.  The boy
found the camera and also discovered the photos.  The boy called Jacob to look,
and together they teased Levi and made fun of him.  Now Levi was embarrassed,
although he said nothing to the nanny or the husband.  The boy told his mother,
and the mother informed the wife.  The wife may have reported it to the
Children’s Aid Society.

[
127
]

The nanny confirmed the sequence of events
described by the husband, and she was quite open about having taken the
pictures and what she had done with them.  She admitted leaving the camera beside
the computer, where Jacob’s playmate found it.  She said she had downloaded the
photos onto the family computer in order to be able to print them.

[
128
]

The wife was outraged that such pictures had
been taken in the first place, and then that they were carelessly left to be
discovered by other children.  She was very upset that they had been downloaded
onto the computer where they could be viewed or even distributed on the
internet.  They were a potential lasting embarrassment for Levi, and a possible
source of mischief.  The husband also admitted that he had given the photos to
the wife’s ex brother in law, in to order to bring up the dates that the photos
were taken.  There was considerable bad blood between the brother in law and
the wife’s family, which was another area of concern.  The wife took the
position that the photos were both inappropriate and immoral, and they might
even be illegal; in her cross-examination of the nanny, the wife suggested that
they were “kiddie-porn”.

[
129
]

The wife did not deny the origins of the rash
alleged by the husband; but she went on the counter-attack, using the photos as
another example of the husband’s poor judgment and determination to win at any
cost.  She regarded it as another instance of the husband’s greater interest in
the contest than the best interests of his children.  When this point of view
was put to him, the husband said he did not think the photos were necessarily a
bad thing, and it had not become an issue until the wife made it one.  He
agreed that he had not informed the wife that he had taken the photos.  He had
obviously taken them with the trial in mind.

[
130
]

The wife did not give evidence about Levi’s incontinence,
except in the context of the photographs.  She did not describe the nature of
the problem when Levi was with her, or explain how she dealt with it, whether
she had sought medical intervention (and the result), or what solutions may
have been suggested or that she proposed to employ.  I am sure that it was as
much a problem when Levi was with his mother as when he was with his father,
and that it had to have been equally challenging.  The wife did not deny that
Levi had skied the day in wet pants and she did not deny that he was wet when
he went to his visit his father the next day.

(b)

Discussion

[
131
]

First of all, it is sad and disturbing that the
health of the children could become a strategic focal point of the battle
between the parents.  The antipathy and mistrust of the parties toward each
other has caused them to be unable to communicate or co-operate effectively on
child health care issues. Although, I accept that the husband could be
controlling, domineering, demeaning and profane (his fighting style, as I will
discuss later), I do not accept that he acted in that manner when dealing with
the children’s health issues.  Probably because the wife feared he would attack
her on this front, she excluded him.  It may have also afforded a degree of
control that affirmed her independence and sense of worth as a parent, as well
as a way of fighting back.  After all, she was the one with considerably less
power in the relationship (e.g. financial resources, education, career status,
age).  She did not consult with him or include him in appointments with doctors
or other health care givers (in particular the family doctor and Dr Montgomery),
who seemed reluctant to meet with him anyway, no doubt in part because they were
aware of the bitter conflict and did not want to become embroiled in it.  I do
not diminish or set aside the wife’s fears about the husband’s attempts to
control, bully and marginalize her in the overall dispute (as I will discuss
later), although I do not think he did it on health care issues or that he used
it as a strategic instrument.

[
132
]

However, I conclude that the wife went too far
and did not act in the childrens’ best interests.  Indeed, it probably hurt
them.  I cannot understand why the husband was not allowed to have health cards
when the children were with him for three out of four weekends every month (plus
additional time on holidays and other times that the wife permitted or
requested).  Although he finally received cards, it was several years after the
separation.  There were times when the children required medical attention
during access.  Although the wife might have been legally within her rights,
her position was neither reasonable nor practical.  There is no evidence that
the husband ever exercised bad judgment in making decisions on health issues,
either in the short or long term.  Indeed, the opposite was generally the case.

[
133
]

The evidence supports that the husband generally
attempted to co-operate with the wife and to help her with child health
concerns.  The husband’s attempts to communicate and consult on these matters were
well documented in the many emails he sent her.  She rarely responded, although
she was technologically capable.  On the other hand, sending those messages
took some effort for the husband because he knows little about the operation of
a computer.  He had to write out or dictate his messages, which were then keyed
and sent by one of his office staff.  There were two occasions when the husband
tried to go behind the wife’s back.  In the one, he attempted to arrange for a
psychologist or psychiatrist to see Jacob and the wife blocked it entirely when
the caregiver’s staff called her for information.  In the other, he arranged
for Jacob to be examined by Dr Rajah, although that was not entirely hidden
because Dr Rajah called Dr Green for copies of the child’s records.  Again, the
wife discovered the appointment in advance and cancelled it.  However, after
consulting with Dr Green, she made a new appointment and carried through.  At
trial, she initially took credit for involving Dr Rajah, although eventually
she acknowledged that the husband took the initial steps.  In both cases, the
husband’s concerns were well-founded and reasonable.  Rather than communicate
with him, however, or try to find out what the concern was, the wife simply
blocked him.  Otherwise, the husband seems to have kept the wife informed of
his concerns.  On health issues involving the children, the husband was also open
to the suggestions and observations of others, be they caregivers, teachers or the
assessor.  The husband was alive to Jacob’s many health issues, including his
“pooping” problem, his behaviour, anger management, weight gain and growth, and
the recurring question of autism.  He took the initiative on most of these
matters, or was prepared to do so.  On the other hand, the wife generally
refused to acknowledge that these matters were significant, or she ignored
them.

[
134
]

The husband was also always concerned about the
effect of the wife’s smoking on Jacob.  She admitted that she smoked, but not
in the presence of the children, although Jacob reported otherwise.  As with
everything else in the dispute, it became part of the war, including the back
and forth allegations by both parties to the Children’s Aid Society.  I
conclude that the wife smoked and that while there was no clear proof that she
did so in the presence of the children, it was probably sufficient to have a
second-hand effect, for example, by tobacco smoke adhering to surfaces in the
bathroom where she admitted to smoking, and on her clothing.  There was also no
evidence that the wife addressed the possibility with the family doctor that
Jacob might have asthma or allergies, even when Dr Rajah alluded to the
possibility.

[
135
]

With respect to the failing to thrive question,
I do not think that the husband was being unreasonable in raising it under the
circumstances, and Dr Rajah agreed it was a fair question for a parent to ask
when a child had only gained a pound or less over a year or more.  Dr Horowitz
was also concerned.  Even Dr Rajah had difficulty obtaining Dr Green’s records
of the child’s past growth patterns for assessment purposes.  Again, it was the
husband who took the initiative to get the child to Dr Rajah, although the wife
participated once it had been arranged.

[
136
]

There is no evidence that the wife raised Levi’s
incontinence with the family doctor until the husband asked her to do so.  Yet
she had to have been aware of it and must have dealt with it often.  Again, the
husband sent her emails suggesting medical investigation and asking to be kept
informed, and as usual the wife gave no acknowledgment or reply.  However, she did
take Levi to Dr Green, who ordered a test that would be of little value.  I
have to wonder how the wife presented the matter to Dr Green because it is
difficult to believe that he would not have picked up on it as the
paediatrician did in court. It is likely that the wife did not distinguish
between daytime and night time incidents.

[
137
]

With regard to the pictures taken of Levi’s
genital area at the husband’s direction, I conclude that it was a carelessly
made decision aimed at advancing the husband’s interests in the litigation.
But for that purpose, I am quite sure there would have been no reason to
photograph Levi, and it would not have occurred.  I am also satisfied, however,
that while deliberate and thoughtless, it was not done to hurt or embarrass the
child in any way.  The wife feared the worst, although I am satisfied that the
photograph has not been distributed.  It is not “kiddie porn” and there was no
pattern of similar failures of judgment by the husband.

[
138
]

The most serious matter was Jacob’s developmental
disability.  Again, the child’s behaviour was well documented.  Yet the wife
did not seem alive to it or able to recognize the signs.  She dismissed it as
something that would clear up in time.  I doubt that Jacob demonstrated the
symptoms any less with his mother than with his father.  Yet those signs did
not register with her as being different or worthy of concern.  As a result,
the information she provided to Dr Montgomery was incomplete.  I do not believe
that that wife does not care or that her concerns once engaged would be any
less than the husband’s.  I do not accept that she purposely tried to frustrate
an accurate diagnosis or to lie for strategic benefit in the litigation.  I
accept that the wife truly loves the children and cares deeply about them.  It is
simply a question of perception and sensitivity.

[
139
]

Dr Montgomery testified that he had relied on the
wife’s information to form his first opinion, and that he would have acted
differently if the husband’s perspective had been communicated to him.  It was
only when the husband managed to see Dr Montgomery (which in itself was
difficult) that the doctor recognized that further specialized investigation
was warranted.  Since the diagnosis, the husband has continued to inform
himself of the condition through reading and course work.  He also tried to
take advantage of other services that became available when a formal diagnosis
had been made (Lakeridge Community Support Services).  I believe that the wife
has also read up on the condition, but not to the same degree because she has
difficulty accepting the diagnosis.

[
140
]

I further conclude that because of his academic
and work background in psychology and infant development, the husband is better
able to understand the nature of autism with its complex core features and
secondary implications.  While his learning in psychology is undoubtedly dated,
he is far ahead of the average person in understanding the discipline and its
terminology.  I am satisfied that the husband will not rest until he has
pursued every possible avenue to better his son’s chances in dealing with the disorder.
The husband is determined and vigilant on this issue.  I am not confident that
the wife sees or understands the problem to nearly the same extent and depth,
or that she has the necessary discipline or strength to deal with it in the
longer term.  As will be discussed in connection with the wife’s psychological
profile, she has a tendency to become distracted or to deny.  In any event, she
has proposed that the husband take charge of the children’s health, which is an
admission and recognition that he is the parent best-suited to deal with it.
She has given this recognition not just with respect to autism, but generally.

[
141
]

Finally, I think that the husband’s knowledge,
experience and stage in life have better equipped him to raise the children in
a setting with the necessary consistency and predictability of routine.  The
husband testified about the regimen that he has established in his home.  He
also has the help of a nanny in maintaining the routine and supervising the
children in it.  While the wife regarded the nanny as an abrogation of the
husband’s parenting role and a renunciation of his interest in parenting, I do
not accept that view.  I am quite satisfied that the husband is consistently
and deeply involved with every aspect of the children’s lives. He sets the
rules and routines, and he maintains close involvement with the children’s
health, education, religious and recreational lives.  He is also well
established in a career.  Although it may have faltered over the last few
years, there is no reason to believe that situation will be permanent.  He has
done reasonably well over his working life and he has the health and stamina to
continue.  On the other hand, the wife must re-establish herself in the work
place.  Whatever the amount, the wife’s spousal support will also come to an
end in the not too distant future, making it even more urgent that she find
gainful employment. While the wife has the benefit of more immediate family
around her than the husband enjoys, the evidence did not suggest or propose
that a family member was prepared to help her care for the children on a daily
basis.  The wife’s family support is more situational and social.

2.

Education Issues

(a)

General

(i)

Jacob

[
142
]

Another of the husband’s big complaints is that
the wife has been generally inattentive to the children’s educational needs and
has fallen seriously short in supporting them.  Jacob started school in
February 2004 at the Blaisdale Montessori School in Ajax, a private school
requiring parents to pay annual tuition fees of about $16,000 per child.  It is
apparently a highly respected school with enriched programs including
recreational.  For the final three years of his time there, Jacob’s teacher was
Gloria Lee Wo. In the fall of 2010 he moved to Winchester Public School in the
neighbourhood where his parents both have homes.  At the time of trial he was
in grade 4.  Levi also started school at Blaisdale, where he finished
kindergarten.  He now also attends the neighbourhood school and at trial was in
grade 1.  Most of the dispute surrounding education related to Jacob because he
has been attending school much longer, and because of his needs arising from
the autism disorder.  However, in the last year or two Levi has also started to
present problems.

(b)

Details

[
143
]

The husband testified at length about the wife’s
short-comings, her lack of involvement, and her ineffectiveness.  By contrast, and
noting the high importance he placed on education, his own academic background
and his teaching experience, he detailed his sensitivity to the children’s
needs, his constant involvement and support of them, and his effectiveness in
achieving positive results.  He testified that he had spent a great deal of
time supervising Jacob and assisting him to learn, and as a result there was demonstrable
qualitative difference between his support and the wife’s.  To prove it, he
presented a table showing Jacob’s results on a weekly spelling and grammar test
over a ten-week period between February 3, and April 7, 2010.  On the weeks that
the child was in his father’s care he scored perfect or near perfect (never
less than 38 out of 40).  Originally the test had been out of 20, but Ms Lee Wo
had “beefed it up” as a challenge to the children.  Not only did they have to
be able to spell the words assigned, but they had to give a definition for each
word and use it correctly in a proper sentence.  On the weeks Jacob was with
his mother, his test scores were a bare pass or failure.  In her testimony, the
teacher confirmed the results.  The wife could not deny them, but she pointed
out that it only covered a ten-week period.

[
144
]

On one occasion, during the same period, Jacob
achieved 36/40 with his mother, but according to the husband that was an
anomaly.  The husband claimed that the child recognized that his grades were
better when he was with his father and he would speak about it.  The husband
claimed that the teacher had also acknowledged it to him, although in her
testimony she was more discreet, acknowledging several times under
cross-examination that the wife had always seemed interested in Jacob’s
schoolwork and open to regular dialogue with her.  Under questioning by the
wife, she agreed the wife had provided Ms Wo with Jewish songs for a holiday
concert, had brought objects from Northern Canada for international day, had loaned
the class a butterfly house and “bugs”, had brought a lizard, then a dog to
school to discuss pets with the class, and had accompanied the class on school
ski outings (as she said the husband had also done).  The wife’s point was to
demonstrate that she had actively participated in special days and learning
activities at the school. Ms Lee Wo also agreed that she never felt the wife
was not supporting Jacob academically, although this general statement was not
explored.  Ms Lee Wo did not speak of the child’s academic performance while
with his mother or the wife’s substantive contributions to his actual academic
progress.

[
145
]

The wife testified that she did work with both
children on their math and reading.  Her style and approach was to
“personalize” it and make it fun.  For example, she said she would cuddle up
with the children at bedtime and read with them.  She also produced a mother’s
day card from Levi in which he said he loved her because she helps him read his
books.  Other than this, the wife’s testimony contained little about the children’s
performance in school or her role in it, and as I have observed throughout this
section, she did not deny most of the husband’s evidence about the degree of his
involvement and leadership in the boys’ educations.

[
146
]

Two of the wife’s sisters testified.  Heather
Orleck said that she had tried to stay neutral in the dispute so that she could
be a go-between for the parties. The husband acknowledged her role and thanked
her for it.  Ms Orleck said that the wife read with the children and did
homework with them, although she did not elaborate on the details or depth of
her awareness.  She observed that the wife enjoyed reading, particularly
history and biographies.  She said that the wife had a large collection of
children’s book at her house – a large enough collection that the family had
stopped giving children’s books as gifts.  The second sister, Michelle Newell, also
testified that the wife read to the children and played games with them.  Again
there were no details, although my impression was that she was talking about
recreational reading.

[
147
]

The husband’s concern was not just the negative
impact of the wife’s academic inattention to Jacob’s school experience, but
also the cost to his self esteem, which the husband thought to be critical in
Jacob’s case because of his disability.  He said that Jacob wanted to excel,
and that he was crushed when he did not do well.  Ms Lee Wo confirmed that
Jacob was highly competitive and very happy when he did well.  She thought he
was capable of being in the top half of the class and achieving grades in the
90% range.  Also, if he was not challenged academically, he became disruptive –
which was a problem that he tended toward in any event.  Ms Lee Wo also
acknowledged that Jacob did not like mathematics at first, but that through the
husband’s work with him at home, the child had improved greatly, enjoyed math
now and did well at it.  The husband testified that he worked regularly with
Jacob to improve his math and that he had obtained supplementary materials to
do so.  In a June 25, 2007, letter to Dr Horowitz, the school observed that the
husband “had always taken a genuine interest in all aspects of Jacob’s
achievements at school” and that he was “a very dedicated and involved
parent”.

[
148
]

The husband also claimed that the wife
continually lost school books and assignments.  He said she would often fail to
send books or assignments to school with the children or to pick them up with
the children from his home when it was her week to care for them.  In
affidavits or other documentation, she made similar accusations of him.
However, in chief he testified that none of these allegations was true, and she
did not disagree when it came her turn to testify.  The husband presented an
email he had written the wife on May 7, 2009, complaining of the on-going
problem and its adverse effect on the Jacob.  The message had been provoked by
the wife’s sending the wrong spelling book with Jacob to his father’s home on a
Friday change day, causing the husband to work with Jacob on words that he had
already done.  As a result, Jacob had scored only 4/20 on the test.  When the
husband went to the school to pick the boy up, the teacher complained about how
Jacob had done and she informed him that Jacob was very upset and afraid that his
father would be angry with him for doing so poorly.  The husband said he had to
spend a great deal of time re-assuring and consoling the boy.  It was a serious
blow to Jacob’s self-esteem.

[
149
]

In the same message, the husband stated that he
had also just discovered that a book report had been assigned three or four

(c)

Discussion

[
176
]

I accept the husband’s evidence that he has
taken the lead in supervising the children’s education and dealing with the
schools.  I also accept that there is a qualitative difference between the
attention and assistance he has given to the children’s educational advancement
in this area and the wife’s.  It is all so well documented that it is difficult
not to accept.  I also accept that because of his own educational background
and the values imparted to him by his family in that regard, he gives education
a high priority.  Because of his area of study and teaching experience, he also
probably has a better grasp than the average person of teaching, special needs
and the education system.  He has been closely involved with the children and
their schools.  He has been constant, consistent and gone to extraordinary
lengths to assure that the boys have the best possible educational experience.
These conclusions should not suggest that the wife has been disinterested or uninvolved.
It is more a matter of quality, constancy, intensity, reliability, and focus.

[
177
]

I am convinced that the wife relegated most of
the responsibility in this area to the husband before the separation, because
the school confirmed in writing that he delivered Jacob to school almost
exclusively and picked him up half the time at the end of the day.  The wife
has also clearly had difficulty getting the children to school on time and most
of their absences have been while they were with her.  She has also had
difficulty in meeting deadlines for assignments and getting forms completed and
in on time.  The husband’s many emails (which she did not deny) have documented
this on-going problem.  The wife seems to forget or become distracted.

[
178
]

She has taken interest in school outings where
she has been a parent supervisor (as the husband has done too), and she has
participated generously and creatively in theme day classes, by loaning or
bringing objects of interest.  However, I do not think that the hard work of
day-to-day homework and study are her areas of strength.  While she may help
the children with it, I do not think that cuddling up in bed with them is the
ideal time or setting. The wife did not give any indication that she maintained
a regular study homework routine that was of high priority. A homework and
study regimen is maintained in the husband’s home, and it is enforced as a high
priority.  While the children (as all children their ages will) would rather
play, watch television, etc., they are directed to school responsibilities
first, and they seem to have benefited greatly from it.

[
179
]

The husband has taken leadership in the
children’s education, and he has demonstrated the same determination he did in
the boys’ health issues.  He is not easily distracted or deterred.  I also
conclude that he has generally been quite perceptive and sensitive to the boys’
problems, particularly Jacob’s as a result of the autism disorder.  When Jacob
expressed suicidal thoughts, he found counselling assistance.  When Jacob was
diagnosed with autism, he took advantage of counselling resources available
within the community and he continues to do so.  I give credit to the wife in
respect of enrolling the boys in the Rainbow Program, although she did not
advise the husband or consult with him as he tried to do with her.

[
180
]

The husband gave Jacob more attention than Levi
during Levi’s early infant years.  However, when it was brought to his
attention he consciously balanced his time and attention.  I am satisfied that
the husband was initially distracted by his efforts to understand and
ameliorate Jacob’s difficulties, which were eventually diagnosed.  Since
becoming aware, I accept that he has given equal attention to Levi’s needs and
as a result, Levi’s progress, with reading in particular, has been very
positive.

[
181
]

Jacob will always present special challenges
because of his disability.  He will demand much attention, time and patience.
I am satisfied that the husband is better able to meet these challenges and
needs in a constant, disciplined way.  Fortunately, and in spite of his
disability, Jacob seems blessed with intelligence.  This intelligence will be
his greatest resource and strength in achieving security, recognition, and
satisfaction as an adult.  His intelligence must be nurtured, encouraged, and
applied with great care and attention if he is to have a chance to succeed in
life.  I conclude that his father’s supervision and direct participation will
be important in this regard.

[
182
]

More recently, Levi has also presented problems
at school.  I fear that he may also be facing the challenge of a learning
disability, although it is still too early to know.  Still, I conclude that he
needs a strong hand and routine in order to progress.  The husband seems to
have been able to address Levi’s educational needs with positive results,
particularly in reading.  Levi has the ability and intelligence to succeed.  He
needs firm support and routine that I conclude the husband has demonstrated he
is best able to provide.

[
183
]

As these boys get older and enter their teens,
they will become more challenging.  That will be especially true of Jacob, as Dr
Kirkpatrick and Mr Whillans indicated with concern.  I am satisfied that the
husband has the strength, insight and discipline to deal with it.  I am not so
confident of the wife’s abilities.

[
184

I also see the brotherly relationship as an
important part of the boys’ lives.  They seem to enjoy a normal sibling
relationship now.  From all accounts, while they have the usual sibling
rivalries, they are close.  This will be especially important to Jacob.  Levi
may be Jacob’s closest and only real friend in life.  It is important that Levi
understand his brother’s disorder and how to deal with it.  Living together in
a home with predictable routines will nurture the bond and understanding
between them.  If it turns out that Levi also has a disability (e.g. ADHD), he
will benefit from the same firm, predictable routine.  He will also understand
that such a disability in school is not necessarily a disability in life.  The
boys will be a support for each other.  I conclude that Jacob and Levi’s best
chance at success in school is with their father.
