(c)

Discussion

[
219
]

I have no difficulty concluding that the husband
took primary responsibility for the children’s recreational lives.  For the
most part, he was the initiator and chief organizer.  The wife allowed him to
take the lead.  Although she took some initiatives, it was exceptional.  She
seemed happy to let him do it.  As usual, the husband’s role was
well-documented.  I accept that he promoted the boys’ recreational activities
with the same constancy that he did their school lives.  I also accept that he
attended most of their activities, even when it was not his week.  He has also
tried to find recreational activities that he can share with them, whether
baseball, running, or skiing.  He has been less successful in that regard with
respect to Levi than Jacob, although I think that is in part because Levi is so
young, and his aptitudes are still forming.  However, the husband seems to
understand Levi’s strengths by comparison to Jacob’s and he realizes and
accepts that there will be differences.

[
220
]

I do not agree that the wife was disinterested
in the boys’ recreational lives.  However, it was not as important to her as it
was to the husband.  She accepts that it is good for the children to have
activities, but she is less committed to them.  If some other opportunity arises,
she may opt to let other scheduled activities go by the side.  It may be that
she prefers spontaneity to routine, or that it does not bother her to break
routine as much as it does the husband.  Whatever the explanation, she is not
as constant or as reliable in getting the children to their activities as the
husband is.  Nor does she feel the same degree of responsibility to carry her
weight in these activities, or to keep in touch with coaches and instructors.
I recognize that she had financial difficulties when the husband reduced the
amount of support he was paying. This was a very real stressor and limitation.
However, I am not sure that this was a real reason for her not getting the
children to activities.  The husband was required to pay for 90% of the
activities and it appears that he paid for all of them (or very nearly all).
Also, the wife could have asked him for assistance when she had conflicts and
he would likely have responded positively.  The evidence suggested that he was
willing to take one or both children when requested.  It would also have been
interesting to see how he would have responded to the wife’s request for a tank
of gas.  Distance and fuel costs did not prevent her from taking the children
to her friend’s cottage or other activities that she placed importance on (e.g.
family gatherings, going out with friends).  She often had other priorities
that she thought took precedence to the children’s scheduled recreational
activities.

[
221
]

The events of May 5 to 8, 2011, demonstrate the continuing
unhealthy dynamics of this couple’s relationship in communicating and
co-operating on the children’s recreational activities.  It is clear that they
cannot communicate or co-operate, even after agreeing to the joint and shared
custody arrangement.  When something goes wrong, they assume the worst about
each other and cannot trust that the other parent has the best interests of the
children at heart.  Rather than communicate, they may rely on what the children
tell them, rather than discuss it with the other parent.  This is dangerous
because the children know how each parent feels about the other and will tell
each parent what the child thinks he or she wants to know.  It is particularly
risky to rely on Jacob for accurate information because he has a tendency not
to tell the truth when it is not to his liking at the moment.  The parties’
relationship is now on such a foundation of distrust and anger that those
feelings take over when there is the slightest problem.

[
222
]

The husband is certainly not perfect.  The
wife’s criticism of him over leaving Tiffany in charge was justified.  Urgent
circumstances may arise from time to time that may cause a parent to scramble
for assistance on short notice.  That was likely the case when the husband’s
mother fell ill and he had to be in Toronto with her.  However, to leave Tiffany in charge a second time was
poor judgment.  At least the husband acknowledged his mistake and indicated it
would not happen again, and it has not.  I am prepared to take it as an
isolated lapse in judgment.  He is also open to strong criticism for not asking
the wife to step in when he needed help.  In fact, when he went on a trip he
was supposed to give the wife the option to take care of the children.  He did
not do so, probably because he did not like her or trust her, or he thought
that it would somehow give her an edge in the litigation.  I saw no evidence,
however, that the wife ever asked for the care of the children while the husband
was away.  The failure of communication and co-operation is a two-way street in
this case.  The anger and mistrust are mutual.

[
223
]

I do agree with the husband’s view of the
importance of recreational activities to the children’s lives in the
circumstances of this case.  Besides keeping the boys busy and giving them the
opportunity to improve themselves physically or in some art or skill, such
activities are important opportunities for social interaction.  This may be
especially important for Jacob who has difficulty meeting people.  Recreational
activities will give him the opportunity for social interaction in a safe
setting.  Recreational activities are also a way in which parents can interact
with their children, share interests, and be a family.  I find the husband’s
priorities in this area of the children’s lives appropriate and in their best
interests.  Because of Jacob’s disorder, routine, consistency, and
predictability are very important.  I believe that the husband is more
committed and more likely to support routine in this area of the children’s’
lives than the wife.  At least, that is what the evidence would suggest.  I am
also satisfied that if called upon by the wife for help, he is more likely to
respond positively than the wife.  There was no evidence that he had ever
denied the wife’s request for assistance in this regard.

4.

Miscellaneous Issues and Complaints

(a)

General Overview

[
224
]

Each party presented a great deal of evidence
that was intended to reflect negatively on the other, either as a person or
parent.  This evidence was scattered throughout the trial and while it provided
context, it was not always very helpful, and it was not at the core of
reasoning for my ultimate disposition.  In a trial with experienced counsel,
much of this evidence might not have been led, if only in the interests of time.
However, I acknowledge that these self-represented parties having lived through
their painful situation, had difficulty prioritizing what was important from
what was not as important.  I will deal with it (although not as
comprehensively as they did) so that they may rest assured that I understood
their testimony in these areas, and the points they wished to make by it.  This
evidence most often confirmed the acrimony between the parties and their inability
to communicate and co-operate.

[
225
]

From the start, the husband complained about the
wife’s abuse of alcohol, her partying, her carrying on with other men, all at
the expense of caring for the children.  It was in this context that he
complained that she did not get up in the morning, did not feed the children
properly or sufficiently, and that she was unreliable, uncooperative and
incompetent in dealing with the children’s health, education and recreational
issues.  He also suggested that she had mental health problems.  For her part,
the wife complained that the husband was more interested in winning the case,
and demeaning and controlling her than in caring for the children.  She
presented him as an emotionally abusive bully whose goal was to belittle her in
front of the children, control her, and marginalize her emotionally, financially
and as a parent. She thought that his care of the children was sub-standard,
and indeed that he did not know how to care for them at all.  In fact, he
really did not care for them himself, but relied on baby-sitters and a nanny.
The wife also depicted him as generally lacking good judgment for the
children’s well-being.

[
226
]

The events and circumstances underlying these
complaints demonstrated on the one hand how parents need each other’s help and
co-operation from time to time; and unfortunately, on the other hand, how these
particular parents simply could not communicate or co-operate. They judged each
other with partial or inaccurate information, and they failed to communicate or
consult directly in order to become informed.  They relied on their young
children for information, which is not acceptable, especially when there is so
much discord, although I recognize that turning to the children would be almost
irresistible when one cannot communicate reliably with the only other direct
source of information.  As I have already observed though, when faced with an
angry or anxious parent, a child is more likely to tell that parent what he or
she wants to hear, or the child may fear getting a parent into trouble by
saying something.  There was considerable evidence that each of these phenomena
was at work here.

[
227
]

There were many instances where the husband and
wife testified about being told something by the children that confirmed a
worst conclusion about the other party, but which may not have been accurate.  One
example was the event just discussed, where the wife believed that the husband
had unilaterally used one of her neighbours as a baby sitter, “pawning” them
off on the neighbour to play, and resulting in their being sent to her residence
when she was neither there nor aware of the arrangement.  She testified that
her belief came from what Jacob had told her.  In fact, it appears that the
children had asked to play with these particular neighbour children.  As a
result, the husband called to clear the play arrangement, speaking with the man
of the house and asking him to call when the children were done. However, it
appeared that neighbour’s wife acted without being aware of the arrangement
agreed to by her husband. Relying on Jacob for information, even if he had it,
was dangerous because he sometimes had trouble telling the truth, especially
when he did not get his way about something – for example not being able to continue
playing.  He would also have been questioned by an irate mother who assumed the
worst.  For Jacob, the path of least resistance could well have been to support
his mother’s perspective.  Had the couple communicated, it is unlikely that the
children would have been sent to their mother’s locked, empty home.  This void
of communication and co-operation created a potentially dangerous gap in the care
of the children and reinforced the parents’ already poisoned views of each
other.

[
228
]

The husband testified about a number of things
he had learned from the children and that had coloured his view of the wife.  He
also described how they became reluctant in some instances to speak because
they feared they might get their mother into trouble.  He also complained that
they regularly blamed him for making their mother poor and denying her money
that they thought he had.  From the testimony on both sides, it was clear that
the children had become sensitized to the litigation and dispute.  It was clear
too from the notes and observations of counsellors.  The children knew far too
much about their parents’ differences, had seen and heard too much, and had
been used and involved by both sides.

[
229
]

In the “Recent Example” just discussed, the wife
believed that the husband was trying to get her into trouble in the eyes of the
court and was “setting her up”, not only in the particular example but
generally.  She had not told the husband that she would not be home because she
was going to a family funeral.  Her reluctance to share information about her
schedule was based in part on her distrust of the husband and her fear of how
he might try to use or manipulate the information against her.  She also wanted
a degree of privacy - a corner of her life that she did not have to explain to
or share with the husband.  Even at trial, the wife took extreme exception to
disclosing or discussing any details about the funeral; and the husband pressed
for it in cross-examination because he did not believe her – or he saw the
stress it caused her as an opportunity.  Sometimes privacy takes second place
in a parenting context.  While sensitivity to reasonable privacy concerns
should be a common courtesy, still when it comes to the care of children in
circumstances such as these, it is prudent to let each other know generally
whether one will be around or not.

[
230
]

I accept that the husband did not intend the
children to be sent to their mother’s house at the end of the play session.
However, had he known in advance that the wife would not be home, he would
likely have told both the neighbour and the children, so that they would not
have gone to their mother’s home.  I am certain that the neighbour lady sent
the children there because it was right next door (or across the street, as the
case may be), and she assumed the wife would be home – as the children probably
did too.  By the same token, I also accept that the husband was always watching
what the wife was doing – ready to pounce on any opportunity he could use to
promote the negative view he had of her.  Similarly, assuming the worst of him,
she could not resist the opportunity it presented in the litigation.

[
231
]

For his part, the husband’s questioning of the
parents of the child that the wife had picked up from ballet class during
Levi’s school performance was unwarranted, and running the wife down with them
was clear mischief, designed to attack her reputation.  It was meddlesome and
malicious, and had no purpose in advancing the best interests of the children.
Again, the obvious conclusion (by understatement) is that this couple simply cannot
and do not trust each other.  They dislike and distrust so profoundly that they
cannot reliably communicate or co-operate.  I believe that both parties looked
for opportunities to get each other into trouble and to make the other parent look
bad in order to advance their complaints about each other.  Unfortunately, the
children have ultimately paid the price emotionally and sometimes in terms of quality
of care.  I cannot say that one parent was better or worse than the other in
this regard.  I take an equally dim view of both.

(b)

Involvement of Children’s Aid Society

[
232
]

The parties’ respective themes of complaint
emerged early in the separation through the involvement of the local Children’s
Aid Society.  CAS records indicated that the husband called the Society in
September 2007 to disclose his concerns about the wife’s consumption of alcohol
and suspected poor mental health.  The couple had seen a counsellor (Mr Danes) through
a Law Society of Upper Canada benefits program.  When the wife did not appear
for a scheduled joint session, the husband kept the appointment himself and told
the counsellor that the wife drank so much that she could not get up in the
mornings.  He also told him that the wife was on medication for depression, and
he was concerned she was bi-polar and possibly schizophrenic.  The counsellor
was alarmed by this disclosure and insisted that the CAS be informed.  If the
husband did not do it, then counsellor said he would have to do it himself.
The husband testified that the counsellor made the call to the CAS and that he
(i.e. the husband) spoke to the CAS in the presence of the counsellor.  The
Society’s records confirmed the nature of the call and that it had been made in
the context of a counselling session. The Society investigated and concluded
that the couple was having marital problems and that the children “were in the
middle of the battle”.  CAS records also noted that Jacob had verified that his
parents “were constantly yelling and screaming at each other”.

[
233
]

In the course of the same investigation, the
wife reported that the husband was feeding Levi four to five bottles of
homogenized milk during the night, and as a result the child would not eat
properly during the day.  The husband admitted giving Levi a bottle just before
bed, and again during the night, but he said it was because the wife was not
feeding the child properly throughout the day, so Levi was hungry and cried for
food in the night.  The wife’s inattention to the children’s proper nutrition had
been one of the issues that had triggered the separation. The CAS cautioned “the
family” that bottle feeding during the night was not good for the child’s
nutrition or teeth.

[
234
]

As for drinking and partying, the Society’s records
indicated that the wife admitted to drinking daily but never to excess in front
of the children or while caring for them.  She told the Society that she
consumed one or two glasses of wine or beer a day.  If she drank to excess, she
said she did it outside the home and would spend the night with a friend.  In
other words, she admitted to going out to drink and to staying out all night.  By
way of justification, however, she complained she had been emotionally abused by
the husband, and as a result felt overwhelmed and unstable due to stress.  She
said that she went out to get away from the husband’s abusive treatment.  She also
indicated that
both
parties were under treatment for depression, and
that
both
were on anti-depressants, which was true.

[
235
]

The CAS concluded that both parties were under
extreme stress, and that they were creating a very unhealthy environment for
their children.  The Society observed that neither party was prepared to move
out of the house; they were in a stand-off.  It proposed that they enter into a
voluntary service contract, but the wife refused.  At trial she suggested that
the husband had persuaded her not to agree because he was not going to agree
either, so she refused the agreement.  She said that the husband had “set her
up” so that she would look bad, but of course the husband denied it.

[
236
]

In early January 2007, the wife told the Society
that the husband continued to abuse her emotionally in front of the children,
and that he was stalking her (although they continued to live in the same
house).  She disclosed that she was taping conversations that she had had with
the husband, in order to substantiate his abusive nature - and she provided
transcripts of the recordings to the worker.  She also complained that the
husband continued to feed Levi bottles of milk in the night, in spite of having
been warned not to. She further complained that he slept regularly with 5 year
old Jacob, although he had been cautioned not to by the previous worker.  The
Society’s report made no reference to a previous complaint that the husband was
sleeping with Jacob or that the husband had been cautioned in that regard.  In
making this complaint, the wife did not directly raise a direct allegation of
sexual impropriety, although there was innuendo. The worker reported signs of
“bottle rot” in Levi’s teeth.

[
237
]

Jacob was also interviewed and at first he said
that his parents yelled at each other every day and night, and that the husband
would say things to the wife that were not nice.  Then he said that the wife
did not yell at the husband.  The child also confirmed that he slept with his
father at night because he (Jacob) wanted to.  He said his dad would read to
him nightly in his own bed and fall asleep reading.

[
238
]

The Society then met with the husband on January
12, 2007, in the presence of his lawyer to explore the complaints.  The husband
again admitted that he gave Levi a bottle before bed and in the night, but he
did it because the child would wake up hungry.  The husband again accused the
wife of not feeding the children properly during the day.  With respect to the
allegation that he was sleeping with Jacob, he explained that he would fall
asleep reading to the child in his (the child’s) bed.  He would eventually wake
up and move to his own bed, but Jacob would follow him after he was asleep
again and in the morning the husband would find Jacob in bed with him.  Jacob also
eventually confirmed to another care giver that this was what happened.

[
239
]

A worker cautioned the husband that he might be creating
an unhealthy dependency in Jacob by allowing him to sleep with him and
suggested that a doctor be consulted, which the husband agreed to.  However, there
was no evidence that the husband or the wife raised the night bottles or
sleeping routines with a physician.  The husband was required to move out of
the home in early February 2007, and the wife was granted interim custody.  The
husband was then unable to take the children to their doctor and the wife did
not include him in their health appointments or permit him to set up his own.
There was no evidence that the night feeding continued to be a problem after
the husband moved out of the matrimonial home, although Jacob’s sleeping
routine continued to be an area of dispute.

[
240
]

During the January 12, 2007, meeting with the
Society, the husband repeated his complaints that the wife did not care
properly for the children because she drank to excess and went out often at
night, including overnight, so that she could not get up in the morning.  He
also repeated his concern that the wife suffered from serious mental illness,
including depression and possible bipolarity and schizophrenia.  He told the
worker that the wife had attempted to hurt herself by slashing her wrists not
long before the separation.  The worker advised the husband that he could not
leave the home while the wife was still sleeping and either child was awake and
otherwise unsupervised by an adult.

[
241
]

As a result of the husband’s allegations, the
worker returned to investigate the wife’s situation.  Again she admitted to
drinking, but only socially and never while she was caring for the children.
She said that her family doctor had been administering random urine screenings
for alcohol consumption.  She admitted again that she went out in the evenings
and sometimes stayed out all night.  However, it was to escape the husband’s
abuse.  She also admitted she had slashed her wrists, which she agreed had been
a stupid way to try to get the husband’s attention and caring.  She also admitted
to suffering from depression, but she gave assurance that she was being treated
and that the condition was under control.  The wife said that her physician
could confirm she was not abusing alcohol, that he had no concern about her
mental health and that she was a good parent.  Dr Green wrote a letter
confirming his positive opinion on these points.

[
242
]

In April 2007, the Society received a “tip” from
a third party alleging that the wife had been seen intoxicated while having a
party at her home, that men frequented her home and that she smoked excessively
around the children.  The Society investigated but the complaint could not be substantiated.
The wife’s lawyer wrote the Society pointing out that on the weekend in
question the children had been with the husband for access, so how she spent
her private time was of no consequence to the children.

[
243
]

The Society concluded that both parents enjoyed
a positive relationship with the children, and that the children would be safe
with either parent.  However, it also concluded that the parties were
demonstrating a high degree of conflict and strife in the children’s presence,
including inappropriate language and conversations.  The overall conclusion was
that if the parties continued to live together there would be a child
protection concern.  When the husband moved out of the home shortly after, the
CAS decided that concern no longer existed, and it closed its file.

[
244
]

That did not end CAS involvement, however.  In
August 2009, the husband took both boys to Levi’s soccer game at the wife’s
request.  The nanny went with him.  When the evening was over, they returned
the children to their mother’s home and watched them enter the house.  As they
pulled away though, the nanny noticed Levi heading across a field by himself at
the rear of the house.  They assumed he was going to a friend’s house.  Levi
was only 5 and it was nearly dark outside. Accordingly, they caught Levi and
made him go inside. One morning a month or so before, the husband indicated that
he had been trying to reach the wife about picking the children up.  When she
did not answer the phone, he and the nanny drove to the wife’s house and found
Levi wandering around alone outside in the front yard.  When they asked him what
he was doing, he said Jacob had locked him out.  The husband and nanny both
testified that they waited with Levi and talked to him for 10 to 15 minutes.
Then they knocked on the door and Jacob answered, confirming he had locked his
brother out in fun.  The wife then appeared and said she had been in the
shower.  Around the same time, Levi had resisted the nanny’s direction to get
out of the bath. She had allowed him to play in the bath for 5 or 10 minutes,
but Levi insisted that his mother let him play alone in the bath for extended
periods of time.  The husband reported the three incidents to the CAS with the
complaint that the wife was not supervising the children adequately.

[
245
]

He repeated his complaint that the wife was still
drinking to excess on a daily basis.  He reported that he had shown up
unannounced at the wife’s home one evening when he had been unable to reach her
on the phone.  She answered the door.  Although she was not intoxicated, he
could smell alcohol on her breath.  He also complained that he thought Dr Green’s
screening tests were ineffective.  The wife’s boyfriend was also in the home,
but the husband did not know if he had been drinking too.  The husband also thought
the wife was taking drugs (cocaine), on the basis of a report from someone who claimed
the wife and her boyfriend had gone looking for it at a specific bar.  He
reported that a family friend had seen the wife doing “sniffing” actions.  He
insisted that the CAS advised him they had warned the wife as a result,
although this did not appear in the Society’s records that were with the worker
at trial.

[
246
]

The Society investigated and the wife denied
failing to supervise the children properly.  She agreed she had been in the
shower and that Jacob had locked Levi out of the house while they were
playing.  However, it was only for a couple of minutes and it was an isolated
incident.  The wife denied drinking to the point of intoxication in front of
the children and said she consumed about four drinks per week at most.  While
she might have been sniffing a lot, it was because of allergies and she denied
that either she or her boyfriend consumed drugs.  The wife also indicated that
she felt that she was being stalked - the husband’s complaints to the Society
being evidence of it.

[
247
]

Both children were interviewed.  Levi acknowledged
that he had been locked out, but he said it was only for a minute or two and it
had never happened before.  Jacob could not recall the incident.  Jacob told
the worker that his mother hardly ever drank in spite of his dad’s frequent
allegations that she did, and that she supervised them continually and would
not let them leave the yard alone.  He complained that his father was “mean”, yelled
at him, and often broke promises.

[
248
]

A worker testified at trial that the Society ultimately
concluded the complaints on both sides could not be verified; that the “locking
out” incident was an isolated momentary lapse; and, that the children were safe
with each parent; that each parent was capable; and, that the children loved
both parents.

[
249
]

The husband was not satisfied with the Society’s
response to his complaints or how it had investigated them.  The CAS worker who
testified at the trial stated that the Society had received seven complaints or
“referrals” in all, of which four had been from the husband.  However, it
turned out that there were also two complaints from the broader community that
had not been included in these seven.  The worker also confirmed that neighbours
or others who purported to know the parties had complained of men going in and
out of the home at night during the wife’s exclusive possession.  These third-party
complainants, some of whom remained anonymous, also told of loud parties and
drinking in the home.  However, the worker said that the Society could not substantiate
the complaints.

[
250
]

The husband testified that when the Society
investigated one his complaints it did not interview him as part of the
investigative process.  In fact, he thought it had confused his complaint with
one from a neighbour.  Also, in respect of the locking-out incident, he
observed that the Society had ignored the nanny’s unequivocal statement in an
interview that they had waited outside for at least 10 minutes with Levi and
not just a couple of minutes as the Society concluded.

[
251
]

The husband also thought the CAS had been
unbalanced in its approach.  The worker admitted to visiting the wife at her
home six times, but had only met once with the husband.  The wife had deposed
that the husband failed to co-operate with the Society by never being home for
an appointment or returning calls to the worker.  However, the worker agreed
under cross-examination that she had never tried to schedule an appointment with
the husband, but had only dropped by his home unannounced, only to find he was
not there.  The worker agreed that the husband had never failed to return a
telephone message, although she could not say whether he had been called.  In
fact, the husband produced a copy of a letter he had sent to the Society,
asking that it contact him if it wanted to meet with him.  The worker had not
seen the letter, and a copy was not in her file.  She thought it might have
gone to the legal department.  She was aware that the husband had been unhappy
with the Society’s handling of the situation, but she was unaware of
correspondence between the husband and the Society in that regard or of
meetings with the husband to resolve his concerns.  Again none of this was in
her file.

[
252
]

Finally, the husband complained that the wife’s
lawyer had obtained disclosure of the CAS file without his consent or his
receiving a copy.  The husband suggested that one of the wife’s lawyers had
been a former CAS employee and that his wife was still an employee at the
time.  The husband suggested that the wife had obtained disclosure through her
lawyer’s connections.  Again, the husband had complained to the Society and he
produced correspondence confirming his complaint, which the worker testified she
did not have in her file and was unaware of.  Although the worker who testified
at trial was the Society’s representative in relation to matters involving
these parties, she did not have the complete file, and she did not even know that
her file was incomplete before the husband demonstrated it.  It was clear that
she was not fully informed.

(c)

Further Complaints About Nourishment and Sleeping with a Child

[
253
]

The husband continued to complain that the wife
did not feed the children properly.  He made the allegation when he took Jacob
for counselling at Family Services Durham in the spring and summer of 2009.  At
trial, he said that the children had often told him that they had to make their
own breakfasts when they were with the wife, because she would sleep in the
mornings.  He also testified that when the children came to him they were often
hungry because meals had not been regular. The nanny also testified that when
the children came to the house after a week with their mother they would
immediately ask for food, and then more food.  However, she said that they were
very guarded and defensive if asked specific questions about meals at their
mother’s home.  On the other hand, Dr Green testified that he had never had a
concern that either child showed signs of failing to thrive.  Both were
consistently within their appropriate weight ranges.

[
254
]

The wife’s complaint that the husband was
sleeping with Jacob blew up when the wife observed Levi playing with his penis
on October 23, 2007.  She testified that when she told him he should not do it,
Levi replied that his dad did so both in bed and when walking around.  She testified
that Jacob advised her that his father slept naked with them in bed.  Dr
Horowitz took the allegation to have a sexual context from a letter from the
wife’s lawyer complaining about it, but he noted that the lawyer had not asked
him to contact the CAS.  The husband testified that in spite of the wife’s
complaint with its sexual innuendo, she still permitted him to have the
children over the following weekend and regularly thereafter.  Dr Horowitz was
also aware that access was continuing without interruption in spite of the
allegation.  He agreed with the wife that it would not be appropriate for the
husband to sleep naked with a child sharing the same bed.  The husband did not
deny that he did not wear clothing in bed or indicate whether the children
joined him while he was unclothed.

[
255
]

Apparently the children continue to sleep
occasionally with the husband.  The nanny confirmed that Jacob still crawls
into the husband’s bed now and then, and very occasionally Levi will join him
too.  She testified that Levi sometimes crawls into her bed, but Jacob never
does.  None of the medical experts who testified were asked whether permitting
Jacob or Levi to sleep in a parent’s bed would be harmful, and if so, why.

(d)

The Nanny

[
256
]

The husband believed that the wife had reported
the pictures taken by the nanny of Levi’s rash (and genitals) to the Children’s
Aid Society, although the worker who appeared at trial said nothing about it
and there was no documentation to indicate it had been reported.

[
257
]

While the trial was on-going, the Society had
been called by the school when Jacob alleged at a Rainbow Program meeting that

[
258
]

The husband also testified that Jacob had often accused
the nanny of hitting or kicking him.  This happened when the child became angry
about not getting his own way and went into one of his tantrums.  The husband
was certain that the nanny had never assaulted either child, and he said that

witness that there had been no assault.  Again, when the child had an

apologize.

[
259
]

The nanny testified that she had not been
interviewed by the Society, although she was aware of the allegation.  She said
that she had never kicked either child or physically disciplined them, although
Jacob had kicked and hit her in his rages when she had directed to do something
routine that he did not want to do at the time.  When discipline was necessary,

reported at school and to the Society, she said the husband had instructed her
not to discipline the children at all

and she was following that direction.
The husband confirmed he had directed the nanny not to discipline the children,
but he said he had done it at the request of the Society.  The Society did not

[
260
]

The wife ultimately questioned the quality of
the nanny’s care of the children and also the husband’s judgment and degree of direct
involvement in their day to day lives.  Under cross-examination, the nanny
admitted she had opened a Facebook account in Jacob’s name and that to do so
she had had to lie about his age.  One was supposed to be at least 18 years of
age to have a Facebook account.  Opening an account for Jacob and lying about

explained that she had eventually opened an account for Jacob because of his
interest in a game called “Farmville” that she played on the site and that

The nanny was aware that

Dr Horowitz interviewed Peter and Sheri Ferkl,

(f)

Alcohol Screening and Depression

[
273
]

The wife was aware from the start of the
separation that the husband would allege that she abused alcohol, and that she had
mental health issues, all of which adversely affected her fitness as a parent.
She approached Dr Kevin Green, her family physician since June 1997, for his
assistance.  He was aware of the marriage breakdown, the resulting high
conflict and the husband’s allegations.  He counselled the wife on eight
occasions between November 21, 2006, and October 5, 2007, in relation to the
separation.  He also arranged for her to receive therapy from a psychologist in
his office during the same time period.  The therapy with the psychologist
eventually ended because the wife could no longer afford his services.

[
274
]

Dr Green also undertook a course of “random”
alcohol and drug screening.  This involved taking urine samples which were then
sent for analysis.  Ten screenings had been done, all of which proved
negative.  Dr Green presented copies of the reports of analysis at trial.

[
275
]

By letter dated December 10, 2006, Dr Green
reported that he was aware of the marriage breakdown and the husband’s
allegations that the wife was mentally ill and abusing alcohol or drugs, all of
which it would be argued undermined her parenting abilities.  He also reported
that she had been attending his clinic on a regular basis for therapy with a
psychologist and “regular random urine drug and alcohol screens”.  He then
expressed the opinion that there had been no evidence to suggest a drug or
alcohol problem, and that she was an excellent mother who was fit and able to
care for her children.  At trial he expressed the same opinion and stated that
based on his years of treating the wife, there was no evidence of mental health
problems.  He confirmed that she had been taking the antidepressant medication,
Prozac, under his care since October 2001 to control chronic depression, which
it did successfully.  He testified that his opinion about her parenting
abilities was based on his observation of her with her children when they came in
to see him.  Dr Green’s letter had been provided to the CAS and he had spoken
with the Society too.

[
276
]

Under cross-examination, the doctor agreed that
“random screening” meant he would take a sample from the wife without
forewarning her when she came to his office to see him or the counsellor.  He
agreed that all of these dates had been on a Tuesday or Wednesday.  Therefore
the wife would know that if a sample was going to be requested, it would be on
a date scheduled in advance.  Dr Green admitted that he had never tested her on
a weekend or on a Monday morning.  He testified that alcohol could be detected
for about 24 hours after ingestion, but not longer.  Therefore, the wife would
be able to consume alcohol and let it clear her system in time for a medical appointment
that she knew was coming.

[
277
]

As it turned out, the husband had also been
taking a mild antidepressant for many years.  He testified that he probably did
not need it any longer, but he had not talked to his doctor about it.  The wife
produced a prescription bottle for bromazapam, which the husband admitted had
been prescribed to him.  Dr Green described bromazapam as a mood-altering
drug.  The husband said it was a sedative prescribed one time only to help him
with anxiety.  The husband criticized the wife for making it sound as though he
was permanently on the prescription.  The wife responded that she had not
suggested he was on it constantly (although she had not said he was on it for a
short time either).

Allegation of the Cause of Levi’s Aggressiveness

]

The wife testified that Levi’s aggressiveness in
grabbing the privates of other children or pulling down pants at school was as

Complaints Going to Reliability, Responsibility, and Character

The parties both had a litany of matters that

The husband also complained that she had “stuck”

(i)

Surveillance and Harassment

[

]

From shortly after the separation, the wife was

]

some point she considered it a serious potentially long-term relationship.  Adrian
had his own home in Scarborough,
which he kept.  It does not appear that he and his daughter ever took up
full-time residence at the matrimonial home although they spent a lot of time
there, including overnights – enough time, according to the husband, that Jacob
referred to the little girl as his sister.  The wife testified that when the
husband found out about Adrian,
he raged in the usual way and made harassing calls to the man.

[
303
]

The husband testified that moving a new man into
the house particularly upset Jacob.  He said that Jacob told him that his
mother and Adrian were sleeping in the same bed.  Jacob also felt that Adrian’s daughter was getting more
attention than him, resulting in jealousy, resentment and a feeling of having
been displaced.  The husband was sure this was a major reason for the boys’
acting out.  Sometime in the spring or summer of 2007, the husband telephoned
Adrian, left a message and Adrian called back.  The husband said he complained to
Adrian about being in the home
and sleeping with the wife so soon after the separation and while the children
were under the same roof.  He told him that the children had reported that the
couple shared the same bed.  He also suggested to Adrian that he was only one of a number of men that had been in the home.
The conversation was taped and introduced into evidence at the trial.

[
304
]

Ultimately the relationship between Adrian and
the wife soured and ended.  Adrian charged her with breaking into his home and stealing something.  Criminal
charges were laid, although the details did not come out at trial.  It appears
that some charge was withdrawn and an absolute discharge was granted in respect
of another.

[
305
]

The relationship with Adrian was on-going while the assessor was doing his investigation.  Dr
Horowitz visited the wife’s home while Adrian, his daughter and the boys were all
present.  He reported that the boys seemed comfortable with the arrangement.
They were well behaved and quiet.  However, he observed that they were much
more animated and verbal by comparison when he visited them with their father
at the paternal grandmother’s home.  Both boys were also comfortable in that
setting and were very active in seeking their father’s attention.

[
306
]

In the end, Dr Horowitz could not form a solid
opinion as to how the boys felt about Adrian’s presence in their lives, or how Adrian truly felt about them.  Collateral
sources had reported jealousy and resentment on Jacob’s part towards Adrian’s daughter, although Dr Horowitz
indicated that he had not observed it himself.  He did conclude though that the
wife’s new relationship was one of a number of destabilizing factors in this
high conflict marriage breakdown.  He stated: “I would suggest that whatever
ability Jacob and Levi’s young minds have had in terms of forming expectations
for the immediate future were compromised by the conflictual and changing
environment of the Rapoport household.”

[
307
]

Under cross-examination by the husband, the wife’s
psychological expert, Dr Kershner, agreed that having Adrian and his daughter
stay overnight at the house within a few months of the husband’s moving out was
not good judgment on the wife’s part or in the children’s best interests.  She
regarded it as an example of the wife’s tendency to reach conclusions too
quickly based upon her own view of what was socially acceptable.

[
308
]

After Adrian, the wife met and then commenced
cohabitation at her home with “Glen”.  The wife indicated that their
cohabitation had been motivated in large part by Glen’s ability to contribute
financially to the household (because the husband was not paying the amount
ordered because he claimed that his income had declined substantially).  The
wife testified that they broke the relationship off and Glen moved out just before
the trial although they might get back together.  The husband was aware of the
relationship but did not say much about it.  His criticism had been directed at
the wife’s taking the children to Glen’s cottage rather than following through
with previously agreed, prepaid summer activities.

(j)

Discussion

[
309
]

The evidence about CAS involvement is of limited
value.  Although I conclude that the husband did not initially intend to
involve the Society, it is clear that once the Society had become involved,
both parties used it as a weapon.  If the Society with its investigative
resources could not verify the various allegations at the time, this court
certainly cannot do so.  However, I agree with the Society’s ultimate
conclusion that the children enjoyed close relationships with both parents and
that they would be safe with either parent.  The balance of the evidence that
this court heard at trial supports that conclusion even now.  I also agree with
the Society’s other conclusion, namely that the children were caught in a
bitter dispute that threatened their well-being if the parties continued to
live together in the same home.  The situation was alleviated when the husband
moved out of the home in February 2007.  However, the bitterness of the parties
toward each other and their extreme distrust and dislike of each other has not
abated.  The continuing conflict cannot be in the children’s best interests and
it is not difficult to conclude that it has probably caused them significant
emotional harm.

[
310
]

As I have already observed, I cannot resolve the
truth of the various complaints.  However, I accept that there was probably
some basis to them.  There is no doubt that the husband fed Levi at night and
that he slept with Jacob (or that Jacob slept with him).  I also accept that
the husband had some basis for concern over the children’s nourishment.  Jacob
gained very little weight over the time in question, and as Dr Rajah
acknowledged, the father’s concern was reasonable.  It was not suggested that
the husband was waking the child to feed him.  It was his testimony that he
responded to the child’s crying for food before bed or in the night.  Yet, this
does not mean that the wife was not feeding the children properly, although as
the psychological evidence would disclose, she might become distracted and not
be tied to a particular feeding routine.  If Levi was truly hungry, what parent
would not respond?  On the other hand, he might have wanted food when he did
not need it.  I cannot resolve these questions beyond accepting that they
existed at the time and they were worthy of exploration, including beyond the
question of the effect on the child’s teeth.  Already the parties’ relationship
had become so conflicted that they were more inclined to blame each other and
escalate their battle than to co-operate and communicate in getting to the
bottom of it.  There was no evidence that the problem continued after the
husband moved out of the home.

[
311
]

I do accept that the husband cannot cook and
that he is generally unable to operate common household appliances.  He does
not prepare meals beyond toast and cereal in the morning and probably heating a
can of soup or making a sandwich for lunch.  I am sure that this was another
reason that he hired a nanny, i.e. to support him in caring for the children –
not to replace him.  Otherwise, he would have had to learn to cook, use a
dishwasher, washer and dryer.  However, I am sure that these would not be
overly difficult skills for a man with a PhD and law degree.  I also accept
that the wife is probably a good cook, although I am not persuaded it is her
passion.  I do not regard the issue of who can cook what or how well as a
significant factor here.

[
312
]

With regard to Jacob’s sleeping with his father,
I accept that the Society gave good advice that the child should be discouraged
from sleeping in his father’s bed.  I am satisfied that there was no abuse of
any kind or other impropriety, although that was the innuendo – again useful
mainly for stepping up the battle.  I accept that the husband read to Jacob in
the child’s bed.  The wife also admitted that she would snuggle up with the
children and read to them in their beds.  The difference is that the husband
fell asleep and the wife did not.  However, I accept that it was an involuntary
response on the husband’s part.  Should he have stopped reading to his son(s)
at bed time out of fear that he might fall asleep?  I’m not sure, but it might
be an extreme solution.  In any event, the real difficulty was that Jacob
wanted to be with his father during the night.  The child crept into his
father’s bed when the father was asleep.  He is not easily dissuaded when sets
his mind upon something.  The husband can hardly be blamed.

[
313
]

The other aspect of this issue is that although
the fact it happened was thoroughly explored at trial, why it happened was
not.  It was clear and substantiated that Jacob wanted to be in his father’s
bed at night, but no one seems to have explored why he wanted to be there – at
least there was no evidence of it.  It did not seem to catch the concern of the
counsellors.  Counsellor Fledderus was aware of it.  There was no evidence that
either the husband or wife were sufficiently concerned about it at the time to
take it up with the child’s doctor or the various paediatricians who were
eventually involved.  In any case, as both the husband and Dr Horowitz
observed, the wife continued to permit the husband to exercise access
throughout the period.  Also, Jacob’s disability and his associated tendency to
fixate on an idea and become stubborn about it is an added dynamic.  Had I been
a parent to Jacob, I might well have considered this a small problem in the
larger constellation of difficulties with him and the surrounding conflict.  The
issue raises many questions that I cannot resolve.

[
314
]

With respect to the nanny, I am satisfied that
she is experienced and capable.  I do not believe that she has kicked or
otherwise inappropriately disciplined either child.  I expect that the CAS
reached the same conclusion.  Otherwise it would have taken action, which it
did not.  Given Jacob’s autism and accompanying disposition, it is more probable
that the nanny has been a victim of Jacob’s physical outbursts and temper.  I
accept the husband’s testimony in this regard because it is consistent with
Jacob’s behaviour in other settings.  He will lash out verbally and physically
if he is required to do something he does not want to do at the time.  He is
likely to say or allege whatever comes into his mind if he thinks it will
advance his own will.  The nanny’s job is to run the husband’s household and to
be sure that the children follow the routines he has established.  The nanny is
not only a caregiver, but she is also an enforcer to some extent.  From the
evidence I heard, she is very experienced and capable.  The husband and
children are fortunate to have her, although I do not know how the husband can
afford her.  I suspect he has received financial assistance from his mother or
sister.  In any event, I conclude that she is a positive force and asset for
the husband and children.

[
315
]

I do not agree that the nanny’s presence is
evidence that the husband is disinterested in parenting the children or is
removed from that role.  The evidence of his consistent and active involvement
in their education, health and recreation underlined that he was very involved
in the day to day lives of the children.  I accept that he cannot look after
the children every minute of the day.  He must earn a living to support himself
and meet his considerable financial obligations arising from this case.  The
wife will face the same challenge.  Still, he has adjusted and limited his work-day
in order to be an active parent.  Sometimes he has had to have the children
taken to his office, but his staff had assisted him and the children seem to
have enjoyed their time there, which was occasional.  I am satisfied that the
husband is also home now and then for lunch with the children if one or both
are likely to be there.  He also has supper at home in the evenings and is
there to assist the boys with homework and participate in putting them to bed.
When they have activities, he takes them and is there.  He is also often
present even when they are with their mother, especially when it involves
sporting events.  I agree with the wife that on the two occasions that he
allowed a friend’s daughter to take them to swimming and she failed to stay or
return on time was an unacceptable lapse.  However, it was not intentional on
the husband’s part.  He ought not to have allowed the woman a second chance and
he did not allow her a third.  I am satisfied that this was an isolated
incident and that he has taken great care since.

[
316
]

Sometimes emergency situations arise.  On the
one occasion he had to care for his elderly ailing mother.  The second
instance, however, gives me more concern – not only because of the sitter’s
lapse, but the fact that there was a sitter in the circumstances.  The final Order
provided that the other parent have care of the children if the one they would
normally be with could not care for them for 24 hours or more.  The husband was
holidaying the second time the sitter failed to meet the children on time at
the pool, and he had apparently gone away on other occasions during one of his
weeks and left the children with the nanny.  He ought to have asked the wife to
care for them while he was away.  In my view, this was a serious breach.
Unfortunately, the full details and surrounding circumstances were not explored
or revealed in the trial.  It appears that the wife may have put the situation
to the nanny after the husband was away and the nanny advised the wife that she
could not let the children go without the husband’s approval and direction.
This was an appropriate response on the nanny’s part and buttresses my impression
of her strength and reliability.  However, the wife did not indicate that she
ever communicated the issue to the husband.  I cannot safely reach a
conclusion, other than to warn the parties that it is a sensible provision that
I intend to maintain.  They should be careful to respect it.

[
317
]

I accept that the husband and nanny did see Levi
sneaking across the field behind his mother’s home in August 2009, probably in
an attempt to see a friend.  He saw an opportunity and on the spur of the
moment he took it.  He could as easily have attempted to escape his father’s
attention as his mother’s.  One could also criticize the husband for not seeing
the child into his mother’s presence, rather than just dropping him at the
door.  But of course the parties had as little face-to-face communication as
possible, and it was a mutual predicament.  I also accept that they found Levi
locked out of the home and wandering around in the front yard on another
occasion.  Jacob locked his brother out as a prank while his mother was in the
shower.  I am certain that the wife would have discovered what had happened in
short order and responded appropriately.  I am sure that she dealt with Jacob
appropriately and effectively once she found out, because it never happened
again.  The CAS investigated and found nothing improper, concluding that it was
an unusual, momentary lapse.  I do not accept that the wife is inattentive to
the children’s safety or that she does not generally supervise them closely and
appropriately when they are with her.  In my view the husband is equally
attentive to the children’s safety and that he supervises them appropriately
too.

[
318
]

As for the husband’s differences with the
Society, there is little I can say about it.  He chose to expand his war for
reasons that seemed important to him at the time.  On the basis of the evidence
I heard, it may well be that like many large organizations, this Society’s
right hand may not at times know what its left hand is doing.  It may be the result
of the apparent separation of the legal from the social work parts of the
file.  However, the husband was represented when he confronted the Society (one
or more meetings occurred in the presence of his counsel).  I also wonder
whether he might have been a bit paranoid about it all.  The fact that the
Society met more often with the wife than with him might indicate where the
Society’s concerns lay at the time rather than being a question of giving equal
attention.  While the wife may have alleged that the husband was not co-operating
with the Society that was her personal allegation.  There was no evidence that
the Society ever thought the husband was uncooperative.

[
319
]

I do not accept that the husband assaulted Jacob
at the Terry Fox run.  It appears that the police and CAS were involved and did
not take action.  I cannot explain what happened, other than to observe that it
was at the height of the conflict after the husband had moved from the
matrimonial home and the complaint was initiated with the wife.  I am concerned
that it was another instance of using public authorities as instruments of
battle.  It may have also been a manifestation of Jacob’s disability.  I do not
know and I cannot speculate.  The overwhelming balance of independent evidence
supports the husband’s being a kind and gentle parent.  At trial I put the
question of the husband’s profane, aggressive and abusive outbursts with the
wife to Dr Horowitz.  The assessor described the husband as a very direct “in
your face” type of person, but his direct observation and the observations of
collateral sources presented the husband as being very gentle and sensitive
with the children (“sweet” according to Dr Horowitz).

[
320
]

Dealing with these children has been very
difficult because of the surrounding high degree of conflict, Jacob’s condition
and Levi’s youth.  Counsellor Fledderus described the husband as having
“reputational” problems with Jacob, and she tried to coach him on how to
improve his reputation.  The husband’s direct and forceful personality was
probably reflected in his communication with the children, in particular
Jacob.  However, one must also remember the context of the counsellor’s
observations.  The husband was the parent primarily pressing Jacob and Levi to
complete homework assignments and to generally improve in scholastic areas
where they were having trouble.  He was also trying to establish routines,
including in recreational activities.  If he had not done so, the children
would not have performed nearly as well as they have.  In fact, they have gone a
long way to successfully addressing their most serious academic shortcomings.  I
do not doubt that he often had to deliver unhappy news to the boys about their
performance in school, and to cajole them and even require them to apply
themselves.  The same holds true of household, social and recreational
routines.  Yet he has persisted, sought help, taken advice and achieved
considerable success.  His efforts may have been regarded by Jacob at times as
uncomplimentary and aggressive.  Yet it has worked, and it appears that even
Jacob has acknowledged it.  Except for arguments with the wife in front of
them, there was no credible evidence that the husband has been physically or
otherwise inappropriately aggressive with the children since the separation.
Indeed, the overwhelming balance of the evidence has been to the contrary.  I
accept that the husband may have occasionally slapped the children, especially
prior to the separation.  However, it is unsubstantiated that he has done so
since the marriage breakdown, including spanking a child in front of someone –
especially to the point of black and blue.  I regard that as “whole cloth”.

[
321
]

The nanny’s driving without a license was an
exercise of poor judgment, and I have difficulty believing that she did not understand
that she needed a fully-licensed driver in the car with her.  However, I am
satisfied that it was an isolated incident.  There was no evidence that it was
ever repeated or that she has been charged for a driving infraction.  Nor was
there evidence that she had ever driven with the children without the
supervision of another fully licensed driver.

[
322
]

The wife was not unreasonable in being upset
about the photographs taken of Levi’s genitals.  This was not good judgment on
the part of the husband or the nanny, who was following the husband’s
direction.  The husband and nanny got carried away in their zeal to preserve
the evidence, although in the context of the conflict I can understand the
husband’s concern that the wife not be able to deny the rash’s existence,
although she could still have denied its origin.  The difficulty was compounded
by the nanny’s carelessness in leaving the camera lying around where Jacob or
his friend could find it.  However, I do not think that this photograph will
ruin Levi’s life or do him great harm.  It can be set right by destroying the
photos and I hope that the husband will do so completely.  That way they can
never embarrass Levi and in any event I am sure they will soon be forgotten.

[
323
]

Nor do I agree that the photographs had anything
to do with Levi’s aggressive sexualized behaviour, either at home
(touching/playing with his penis) or grabbing at the private areas of other
children.  With respect to the aggressive behaviour at school, I accept the
husband’s evidence that these incidents predated the discovery of the photos by
Jacob and his friend.  It is therefore difficult to make a causal association.
With respect to the child’s playing with himself at home, I again fail to see
the connection and there was no evidence making that link.  I expect it was a
childhood phase.  The wife does not seem to have sought help or guidance from
any professional.  Rather, she has used it for strategic purposes in this
litigation through innuendo.

[
324
]

It may be that a Facebook account should not
have been created for Jacob.  The nanny takes sole responsibility for doing
it.  While I understand the wife’s concerns about child predators using social
networking systems as a means of reaching innocent children, I do not think
that was a danger here.  The nanny’s reasons for opening the account were
innocent enough and well-intentioned.  She wanted Jacob to be able to play his
own game, rather than simply watch the nanny play it.

[
325
]

I accept that whenever he plays or uses the
internet the nanny is sitting beside him supervising him.  Jacob cannot get
into much trouble as long as he is supervised this closely.  The direct
internet supervision described by the nanny in her testimony is the appropriate
standard of care for a child of Jacob’s age, while still giving the child
computer access which has become an important part of our culture.  It would be
a different story if the nanny had created an account for Jacob then left him
to use it when and as he liked.  Therefore, while the wife’s concerns are
well-placed, I do not see Jacob being in danger where he is supervised while
using the computer.  Also, at some point the wife complained to the husband and
from then on I am satisfied appropriate steps were taken, if only because of
the pending litigation.

[
326
]

By her own admission, alcohol was a daily part
of the wife’s life.  However, I cannot conclude that she had a dependency on
alcohol.  The husband testified that he would detect the smell of alcohol on
her breath in the home, but he never complained that she was intoxicated.  I am
certain that alcohol was probably a feature of her socializing and that she
probably did drink to excess on occasions.  However, there was no evidence that
she drank to excess in the presence of the children or while caring for therm.
Nor was there evidence of use or abuse of non-prescription drugs.  I am
satisfied that this was an allegation the husband was conveniently able to use
against the wife with the Society, although its source was second hand from a
person also at conflict with the wife’s family.

[
327
]

I do accept the husband’s submissions that Dr
Green’s alcohol and drug screening prove little, except that on the day the
samples were taken, and the 24 hours before, the wife did not ingest alcohol or
non-prescription drugs.  The wife knew that samples would be requested at
appointments she had with the doctor or another care giver at his clinic.  She
was aware well in advance of appointments, which were usually 48 hours or more
after the end of the weekend.  The wife could well have planned consumption
around the screenings, although there is no evidence she did so.  My point is
that the screenings were not truly random, so the results are not able to give
much confidence.  Dr Green’s opinion must be weighed in this context, although
I am certain it was very helpful to the wife in dealing with the CAS.  Still,
while the wife certainly consumed alcohol regularly and enjoyed doing so, there
is no hard evidence substantiating that she did so to excess.  One might say
the fact that she had difficulty getting up in the morning supported the view
that she drank to excess.  However, not being able to function in the morning
could equally be a result of her being up late or all night.  The more serious
aspect of the husband’s allegation is the wife’s inability to wake in the
morning, care for the children when they awoke and get them off to school –
which I think has been well established.

[
328
]

With respect to the questions of depression and
mental illness, while both parties are taking medication, I am satisfied that
the conditions they were intended to address are well controlled.  The husband
has been taking a prescribed medication for mild-depression for some time.  The
circumstances underlying that prescription were not clear from the evidence at
trial.  At some point around the time that Jacob was born, he was prescribed a
tranquillizer for anxiety, but it was a one-time prescription.  There was no
allegation that the husband suffered from any mood or mental health disorder.
The wife’s questions about these medications were intended to counter the
husband’s allegations against her and to emphasize that medications for
depression were entirely proper and effective.

[
329
]

The greater issue was the wife’s mental health.
The husband alleged that she was chronically depressed and perhaps bipolar or
even schizophrenic – in other words, that she might suffer from a major mental
illness that was not being treated, that accounted for some of her alleged behaviour
and impacted negatively on her parenting ability.  I can understand how the
concern about possible bipolarity arose.  The wife herself reported that at 17
years of age she had been diagnosed as bipolar by a psychiatrist.  She reported
this to Dr Kershner and probably to others too, including the husband.  It is
commonly known that depression is a fundamental part of bipolar disorder.
However, apart from the wife’s report, there was no real evidence that she had
ever been diagnosed, and Dr Kershner’s extensive psychological testing ruled out
bipolarity or any other major mental illness.  The wife has suffered from
chronic depression since she was a teenager, but it has been successfully
managed with medication.  I am satisfied that the wife’s day-to-day life is not
seriously affected by the condition. There was no evidence that she suffered
from schizophrenia or any other major mental illness.  I am sure that the wife
felt more depressed at times than at others, but who would not be depressed by
the conflict of the situation and by the financial and child care issues at
stake?  I conclude that the wife’s ability to parent is not impaired by reason
of poor mental health.

[
330
]

The husband’s complaints about the wife’s
incurring debt or expenses in his name or promising to pay for things or compensate
him if he paid them are probably true.  I am sure that they angered him greatly
and that the wife may have even taken some satisfaction in taking advantage of
him.  However, I regard these incidents more as a dynamic of the conflict than
character flaws.  There was no evidence that the wife has been financially
irresponsible in general in the community.  I do not think that the husband
paid her any more than he had to and the fact that he was the family’s sole
source of income gave him power that the wife recognized and feared.  Once
settlement was reached, the husband only paid full support for a short period
of time then started to fall into arrears ever more deeply because of the
decline of his law practice.  This put the wife into very difficult financial
straits.  By then she had purchased a home and established a life style based
on the child and spousal support it had been agreed would be paid to her.
However, she was soon living well beyond her means when the husband fell into
arrears.  It became a question of survival for her, and of course the parties
could not co-operate or communicate to find a way to get through or adjust.

[
331
]

I also accept that in the months after he moved
out of the home, the husband may have sent the children home after access with
soiled clothes as the wife complained.  He may also have been inattentive to
the children’s bathroom issues.  However, I conclude it was more a matter of
inexperience and that eventually it was resolved.  This was not a complaint
expressed to the CAS or investigated by them, and again the wife permitted the
access to continue.  I accept that the husband may also have gotten one or more
speeding tickets; that he may have run out of gas with Jacob in the car in
winter; and, that he may have taken Jacob for a ride in his sports car as the
wife alleged.  However, I am satisfied that they were isolated incidents, or in
the case of returning soiled clothing, the situation ameliorated with time.
These have not been issues since 2007 or 2008.  They have little or no bearing
on the present case.

[
332
]

It is difficult to know what to make of the
wife’s concerns about being under surveillance.  It may well be that the
husband had surveillance conducted, although there is no clear evidence of it.
Given the nature of his complaints that she was out drinking, partying and
running around with other men, I am sure he was trying to keep an eye on her
one way or other in order to substantiate his suspicions.  However, I am not
persuaded that his attempts were as sinister as the wife suggested.  There was
no evidence that he “bugged” her car or residence, and indeed the wife’s own
evidence contra-indicated it.  On the evidence, it was at best a fear or
suspicion.  It may be that some of the neighbours reported things they saw or
suspected to the husband, which does not make it reliable either.  This was
another dynamic of the conflict between the parties.  One thing I am sure is
that if the husband had discovered something significant through professional
surveillance, the court would have heard of it.  It did not.

[
333
]

I accept the wife’s testimony that male hair
removal clients and workmen who came to the home may well have terminated their
association with the wife or location.  However, the reasons are less clear.
The wife testified that it was because of harassing calls or other
communications from someone, and of course she suspected the husband.  On the
other hand, the husband also complained that he had received calls complaining
of the wife’s behaviour or suggesting that her involvement with male clients was
more than professional.  I appreciate the implications on each side and how
they might well reflect on the other party.  However, I cannot resolve the
conflicting positions on the evidence presented.

[
334
]

While I appreciate the wife’s concerns and do
not minimize them (especially if there was stalking or threats), it may be more
complicated than she presented.  The neighbours may not have been very happy
about a business being run out of the matrimonial home, and so they may have
been watching and complaining.  The matrimonial home was described as a very
nice one in a new subdivision.  I assume it was a residential area, zoned
accordingly.  Although there was no testimony as to the propriety of a business
being run out of the home or whether the requisite permissions or licences had
been obtained, it may not have been popular with the neighbours.  If there were
loud parties at the home, neighbours may have been similarly upset.  There was
evidence that neighbours or other third parties made complaints against the
wife to the CAS.  I accept that something was going on to provoke the
complaints on both sides.  However, there was insufficient evidence to reach a
reliable conclusion.  The court cannot divine a conclusion.

[
335
]

There is no doubt that the wife formed a new
relationship not long after the husband moved out of the home.  She introduced
Adrian and his daughter to Jacob and Levi, and they spent a great deal of time
at the home, although they did not take up permanent residence.  In the
beginning of this relationship the wife may have introduced Adrian and his daughter to the boys in the
context of a play opportunity, and Adrian and his daughter may have shared a bedroom one or more overnights.
However, I am satisfied that eventually the wife and Adrian were sleeping
together as the husband said Jacob reported to him, and which the wife did not
deny.  Nor did the wife deny that the boys started referring to the little girl
as their sister, or that Jacob may have complained of feeling displaced or losing
his mother’s attention to the little girl.

[
336
]

There is no doubt either that after she broke
off with Adrian, the wife soon
formed a relationship with Glen.  He took up residence in the wife’s home,
motivated in part by the wife’s financial need.  While that relationship had
been discontinued by the time of trial, it was not clear that it was over as
much as on “pause” until the court case was over.

[
337
]

Dr Horowitz thought the relationship with Adrian and introducing him into the home
showed poor judgment and reflected adversely on the wife’s parenting because of
the destabilizing effect it had on an already highly conflicted situation.  He
was concerned with the upsetting effect it must have had on the boys’
expectations about their futures.  Their relationships with the most important
figures in their lives were threatened, uncertain and in disarray; and they
were surrounded by hostility and distrust.  Dr Kershner did not approve either,
although circumstances might have ameliorated it for her.  I agree with Dr
Horowitz.  It was the introduction of another male figure in the household so
soon after the separation and in the context of such conflict that was harmful
to the children, especially Jacob who directly experienced his parents’
hostility to each other and seemed sensitive to the implications of the custody
dispute.  It could not have reassured the children when their mother’s
relationship with Adrian also
ended in conflict.

[
338
]

The wife also admitted that she went out at
night with her girlfriend and perhaps others.  The wife enjoyed and needed
social contact with other adults.  There is nothing wrong with that as long as
it does not interfere with child care responsibilities.  The evidence did not
suggest that she was leaving the children in the care of babysitters or family
on a regular basis, and when she went out in the evening after the separation
she left the children in the husband’s care at home.  I accept the wife’s
testimony that getting out of the home when the husband was there was a way of
escaping or avoiding the high level of conflict between them – although I think
it also coincided with her desire for wider adult social contact.  Again, I
cannot resolve the issue in terms of right and wrong or good and bad.

5.

Taped Conversations

[
339
]

Partly in response to her surveillance concerns,
the wife decided to tape record conversations with the husband.  She testified
that she took advice first from a private investigator on how to do it within
the law.  She hid a small tape recorder in her clothing, under a pillow, in her
purse or wherever, and surreptitiously recorded their conversations.  The
recordings started in October 2006 shortly after the separation and continued
until the first week of February 2007 when the husband moved out.  After he
moved out, she said that she made occasional recordings when he called or came
to the door, but it stopped sometime in the summer of 2007.  She admitted that
she had also taped Jacob in May 2008 just prior to his seeing Dr Montgomery.
She further admitted that she also taped Dr Horowitz at a meeting after he disclosed
his conclusions but before delivering his written report.  The tapes were an
important part of the wife’s case to show how contemptuous, abrupt, insulting,
demeaning and profane the husband had been toward her, including in the
presence of the children.

[
340
]

The husband challenged the admissibility of the
tapes from the start.  Surreptitiously obtained private communications may be a
criminal offence contrary to
s. 184
of the
Criminal Code
, R.S.C. 1985,
c. C-46, absent
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

considerations
(which only arise in acts involving the state).  There are no statutory
provisions governing the admissibility of evidence illegally obtained by private
parties. The common law leans toward inclusivity of evidence if it is relevant
and advances the court’s truth-finding mandate, irrespective of how it was
obtained: see
The Law of Evidence in Canada,
at para. 9.1.

[
341
]

However, in the family law context the
authorities are divided.  In
Reddick v. Reddick
,
[1997] O.J. No. 2497
(Gen. Div.)
, surreptitiously obtained tape recordings were allowed into
evidence.  The court held that if the tapes were reliable, relevant and of
probative value to a determination of what was in the best interests of the
children, they were admissible irrespective of their repugnance to the court as
to the manner in which they were obtained.  See also:
G.B. v. D.B.
,

[1998] O.J. No. 5375 (Gen. Div.)
;
W.L.D. v. R.C.D.
,
1999 SKQB 178
; and
L.C.M.
v. C.A.V.
,
[2000] O.J. No. 2591 (S.C.)
.

[
342
]

On the other hand, in
Hameed v. Hameed
,
2006
ONCJ 274
, the court excluded such evidence in a family law case for policy
reasons.  The court observed that surreptitious recording of telephone
conversations by litigants in family law cases should be strongly discouraged
because it only heightened the usual high degree of conflict that already
existed in such cases and diminished the chances of restoring sufficient trust so
that the parties could co-operate in the care of children.  See also:
S.C.
v. J.C.
,
2009 SKQB 87
;
Norland v. Norland
,
[2006] O.J. No. 5126
(S.C.)
;
Shaw v. Shaw
(2008),
2008 ONCJ 130 (CanLII)
, 62 R.F.L. (6th) 100 (Ont. C.J.);
Luckov
v. Taylor
,
2008 ONCJ 795
.  This line of cases observed that: the admission
of such evidence could prejudice the administration of justice; it tended to be
highly unreliable and susceptible to manipulation; it was generally repugnant
because of its surreptitious and possibly illegal nature; and that it was
divisive in family law cases and should be discouraged as a matter of policy.

[
343
]

Accepting the
Reddick
line of cases as
the applicable law, I concluded that I could not rule on admissibility without
hearing the tapes to assess their reliability, accuracy, the context of their
making and their probative value in terms of the custody issue and what was in
the best interests of the children.  However, by the time it became necessary
to actually conduct a
voir dire
