, the husband had decided that he also
wanted the tapes admitted into evidence. The parties had agreed which tapes
would be admitted, and they had approved the accuracy and admissibility of
transcripts previously prepared by the wife.  The tapes and transcripts were
therefore put into evidence and the parties were allowed to testify about
them.

[
344
]

Many of the recordings were of very poor quality
– so much so that in listening to them with the corresponding agreed
transcripts it was impossible to say that the transcript captured or even
resembled what had actually been said.  I was not prepared to admit purported conversations
that were so bad that it was impossible to compare the recorded voice with the
paper transcript.  It was also impossible to capture tone and context.  It was
better that the parties simply testify about whatever they say may have
happened in a particular situation purportedly recorded but incomprehensible on
the tape.  Therefore, a number of recordings were not admitted into evidence.
In respect of those that were, I maintained and exercised the court’s usual
right to determine what weight should be given to a recording as a piece of
evidence.

[
345
]

In her evidence in chief, the wife played Tape Number
5, which it was agreed recorded a conversation on the morning of December 22,
2006.  Jacob was with the couple in the kitchen, eating breakfast and talking
to his mother about playing.  The husband was upset about the wife having been
out all night, and he accused her of partying with her friend Cheryl, another
woman and three men.  He claimed she had gone out that night and on other
occasions over the previous two weeks when one or both of the children were
sick, and he claimed that Jacob had been congested and fevered that night.

[
346
]

In speaking to the wife, the husband used considerable
profanity, and he addressed her in an insulting and contemptuous manner.  With
repeatedly vulgar language, he accused her of sexual escapades.  It is
unnecessary to quote the language.  The reader must simply imagine the worst
possible; and it was all spoken in front of Jacob, who was chirping throughout about
various things of interest to him.  While Jacob may not have understood all the
language used, he certainly understood some, because at one point he said that
if his grandfather George “...hears daddy talking like that then he’ll drive his
car all the way to this house and spank my dad’s butt.”  The husband also told
the wife to get out a number of times, again in front of Jacob.  His tone was
blunt, mocking, insulting, angry, and full of contempt and disgust.

[
347
]

The wife denied the husband’s justification that
she had selfishly left the children when they were sick, and they argued about
it both in the taped conversation and at trial.  There is no question that the
wife went out, but on the conflicting evidence presented, I cannot determine whether
one or both of the children were sick at the time.  No matter what had
happened, the husband’s recorded language and behaviour in front of Jacob was
unjustifiable for any reason.  While the language was bad enough, it was the
inclusion of the child in the argument and his listening to the angry and
demeaning tone of voice used against his mother that was truly terrible.
Whatever was in the husband’s mind, it was not the welfare of his child.  There
can be no doubt but that the husband engaged in verbal abuse and that the wife
was a victim.

[
348
]

That being said, I note that the wife was trying
to capture the husband’s language and demeanour in order to advance her own
interests and cause.  Also, this was not the entire conversation.  It was
impossible to know what had preceded the moment when the recording started.
Had there been an argument?  Did the wife provoke the husband into saying what
he did?  This is where the mischief of surreptitious taping becomes a concern.
Also, if the husband was in such a foul mood that he was directing verbal poison
at the wife, why would she stay there to take it – other than that she had an
interest in capturing his performance for her own strategic purposes?  Whenever
an outbreak of verbal abuse occurred, she could have largely avoided it by
going to another room or leaving the house, and taking the child with her.
Instead, she argued with the husband and seemed to egg him on.

[
349
]

At one point she said: “Can you hear him?...This
is, ahhh, this is how he talks in front of them.”  She was speaking to the
recording device, highlighting the vulgar drama that was unfolding in front of
her child and that she seemed to want to happen so she could record it.  It was
important to the wife’s position that the husband’s language and behaviour was
taking place in front of the child, and she was intent on letting it go forward
so that she could capture it – to “add value for her”, as the husband put it.  I
agree with the husband’s observation, although it does not excuse him in any
way.  In pursuing her strategy, the wife was also not thinking of Jacob’s
welfare or the potential effect on him.  It also demonstrated the care with
which a court must approach such recordings, and the importance of weighing them
carefully.

[
350
]

This (and other) recordings had a “staged”
feeling to them that require the court to be very careful in drawing
conclusions.  In this case I think I can safely conclude that the husband
engaged in verbal abuse with the wife when they were arguing.  However, I cannot
determine how long it had gone on.  At some point, the wife started recording
the conversations and at that point she was also submitting to some extent, and
likely encouraging it for her own strategic reasons.  By January 2007, the
husband was suspicious that he was being recorded.  From that time forward I
think he was much more careful about how he spoke to the wife, so from then on
he was not likely verbally abusive toward her.  There was also likely no verbal
abuse after the husband moved out of the matrimonial home in early February
2007.  For a period of time after he moved out there was little or no direct
communication between them and access exchanges were supervised.  When this
ended, the husband communicated with the wife mostly in writing by email.

[
351
]

The wife also introduced Tape Number 8 into
evidence (recorded on December 25, 2006).  The wife’s most important point here
was to show that the husband had taken Jacob to the house where, she said, she
and Cheryl had gone with several men after a bar had closed and they wanted to
continue talking.  On the tape, the husband indicated that he had pointed the
house out to Jacob and told him that his mother liked to go there.  The couple
argued about it in the recording and the wife asked Jacob to confirm to her
again what he had seen.  Jacob was able to describe the colour of the house and
its numeric address.   At trial, the wife testified that it was all very
confusing and unsettling for the child, which is understandable.  It was clear
that the husband had been involving Jacob in the details of the dispute and
using it as a way to harass or threaten the wife, and to undermine her in
Jacob’s eyes.  Again, however, the wife allowed the conversation to take place
as it did in order to capture evidence that might favour her, and she thereby took
part (probably unwittingly) in reinforcing Jacob’s sensitization to the
situation and the details.

[
352
]

The husband also referred to the tape
recordings.  He started with Tape Number 1, which he thought had been made just
before the February 2, 2007, interim motion.  It recorded a call from the wife
to his cell phone.  She started in immediately about the way he had been
talking in front of the children, and she asked him not to do it.  He denied
that he had spoken inappropriately in front of the children, but the wife
insisted and repeated the kind of language she said he had used (focusing on
her having sexual relations with “Dan”).  The husband was suspicious that she
was taping the conversation and said so, including that he was not going to let
her set him up again by taping and that she was not going to get anything more
out of him that way.

[
353
]

He stated his suspicions and concerns about
taping at least four times, and at one point the wife admitted it.  The husband
said several times that he did not want to speak with her, and at one point she
told him not to hang up.  Although he was very abrupt, direct and sarcastic, it
was obvious that the wife did not want to let him go, and she kept coming back
to the same subject, and several others that she raised.  She showed no
hesitation, and indeed, in this conversation she was the aggressor.  The
husband used profanity, but so did the wife.  It was clear that she was not
uncomfortable with such language.  She kept pressing the husband and it was my
impression that she wanted an argument – probably to see if she could get him
to say something more compromising.  Eventually, he hung up on her.

[
354
]

Tape Number 10, recorded on January 10, 2007,
was an important piece of evidence for the husband, although it was of poor
quality and would have been very difficult to follow without the aid of the
transcript that both parties agreed was accurate and that I was also able to
understand.  The husband explained the context.  He said that he had been on
his way to work while the wife stayed with the children.  He had left the house
and gone to the next door neighbours (the Ferkls) “to say hello”.  The wife
followed him, leaving the children alone in the house – although it eventually appeared
that Levi followed her over.  The wife was concerned about Sheri Ferkl
preparing an affidavit against her and she confronted Mrs Ferkl about why she
hated the wife.  This sparked a mild exchange between them in which Mr Ferkl
denied hating her, but expressed concern about Jacob’s behaviour and the wife’s
leaving him with the Ferkl’s when he had been ill.  The wife then turned her
attention to the husband, complaining about his involving strangers in their
dispute, including teachers.  The husband was abrupt, unfriendly and sarcastic
as usual, but again he told her he did not want to talk to her and he voiced
suspicion that she was taping him.  He asked her to go home to look after the
children.

[
355
]

He said he then left the Ferkl’s and went to the
car, but the wife followed and blocked his entry into the car; so he went back
to the house, but she followed again.  He said he kept asking why she was
following him, and once inside he again headed for the door to go to work.
However, she blocked him by standing in the door with her arms spread wide, and
she had a smile on her face as she did it.  The husband testified that at this
point he thought she was taunting him and trying to get him to hit or push her,
but he did not do so.  Then he said she whispered: “It’s too bad Hitler didn’t
kill your parents.”  He said he was astounded, speechless and unable to believe
what he had heard.  He said he asked her to repeat herself, and she whispered
it another time.  Again, he thought she was trying to get him to react
physically, but he was speechless and frozen.  This part of their interaction
had not come out on the tape, according to the husband because it had been
whispered, and of course their movements could not be viewed.

[
356
]

With respect to this recording, again it was not
difficult to conclude that the wife was the aggressor.  She followed him to the
Ferkl’s, where she drove the conversation and was argumentative.  She did not
show any fear or hesitation.  At trial, the wife did not deny the husband’s
testimony or interpretation of the tape, except for the alleged whispered
comment against his parents.  She denied that she had said it, and several of
her witnesses testified that she had never exhibited racial, religious or
cultural prejudice.  I am satisfied that the wife is not a bigot and that she
makes a conscious effort to be open to other cultures, religions and races.  I
accept that her conversion to Judaism was sincere, that she is committed to it
and supportive of the children benefiting from their religious cultural
background.  This is admirable and she deserves credit.  As a committed member
of the Jewish faith she would hardly support the Holocaust.

[
357
]

However, I conclude that she probably did make
the comment – not out of bigotry or bias, but rather to hurt the husband.  She
felt threatened and generally vulnerable because of the husband’s career,
income and professional influence.  There were not many ways she could hurt him,
but this was one, and it certainly worked.  I have come to my conclusion in
part because of the husband’s testimony.  At one point, when he was attempting
to explain to the court what had happened, he became so visibly upset and
agitated that he could barely speak, and he had difficulty maintaining his
composure.  Having watched the husband testify and speak over the weeks, I am
satisfied that his reaction was real, involuntary and in no way staged.  I have
come to this conclusion with great awareness of the dangers of demeanour in the
decision making process.  In this case, however, the circumstances, context and
the husband’s reaction make it credible and likely on a balance of
probabilities.

[
358
]

The husband referred to other tapes and
recordings.  However, I do not consider it necessary to summarize or review
them because they were of such poor quality or they did not add to matters
already commented upon.

6.

Involvement of the Children

[
359
]

There was considerable evidence that the
children had been told too much about their parents’ dispute, that they felt
caught in the middle and at times pressured to take sides. Levi’s teacher from
last year testified that she sometimes thought the legal proceedings had hurt him,
although she did not give reasons.  There was also considerable evidence of
child involvement in counsellor Fledderus’ notes.  She observed: that Jacob was
anxious that his mother might lose her home; that he wanted his parents to stop
arguing about money; and, that he wanted his dad to stop “picking on” his
mother.  Another time he expressed fear that his father would lie to the police
about his mother and she would be arrested.  This seemed like a baseless fear,
because there was no evidence that the husband had ever approached the police
and in fact it was the wife who had called them to allege assault by the
husband on Jacob on one occasion.  In the same meeting, Jacob advised the
counsellor that he had been on his father’s side when he was younger, but that
he now encouraged his mother to fight back against his father, so that she
might “win”.  Jacob had expressed a fear that if his father won, his mother
would be “a goner” emotionally.

[
360
]

On another occasion, the husband called the
counsellor because his wife had reported to him that Jacob had told Ms
Fledderus that he “hated” his father as a result of the separation.  The husband
said that Jacob told him exactly the same thing, but only after being coached
by the wife and informing him that she had told him to tell Ms Fledderus.  The
counsellor’s records did not note that Jacob said this to her, but the
husband’s report about it was noted, and she counselled him on how to handle
it.

[
361
]

I conclude that the children felt caught in the
middle and that the highly conflicted marriage breakdown caused them great
anxiety – especially Jacob, who being older understood more, and being autistic
was more prone to harm from uncertainty in his life.  Without doubt, they had
witnessed a great deal of conflict between their parents.  It must have been
very upsetting and worrisome to them.  I agree with Dr Horowitz that this may
have had a significant bearing on their acting out at school.

[
362
]

I am also satisfied that the parents expressed
very negative points of view about each other directly to or in front of the
children.  Raising matters such as a strange house that the wife liked to go to
without the children, and hearing about it in anger and argument must have been
very disturbing.  Whenever he spoke of the wife, the husband’s tone ranged from
anger to contempt.  This could not have escaped the attention of the children
and they must have felt pressure to be negative about her too as a sign of
affection toward their father when they were with him.  I am sure that the
mother complained greatly and often to the children about her financial
problems and that it was the husband’s fault.  They seem to have voiced this
fear often, including to their father.

[
363
]

In spite of this, I am satisfied that the
children enjoy close loving relationships with each parent.  To their credit,
each parent has allowed the children to visit the other when it was not the
other’s week of care, and have even permitted the children to stay overnight if
the children asked or if the party had some specific need.  Levi’s teacher
testified that at times she thought he was closer to his mother than his
father.  This may also be reflected in the fact that when he is living with his
mother for a week and visits his father, he rarely wants to stay overnight with
his dad.  On the other hand, when Jacob visits his father during one of the
wife’s weeks, he often wants to stay overnight, and is usually permitted to do
so.  Jacob also enjoys skiing, running and baseball with his father.  During
the fall of 2007, Jacob had to decide whether to go to a child’s birthday party
with his mother or to a professional baseball game with his father.  It was a
difficult decision for him, but in the end he opted for the baseball game with
his father. Jacob relies on his father to guide his studies and
extra-curricular activities. Levi has been too young for most of the period
since the separation to be engaged in such activities with the father.  He skis
with the father and his father accompanies him regularly in his recreational
pursuits.  I am sure that the husband will find ways to engage Levi to the same
extent as Jacob.  He has acknowledged the need for balanced and equal time with
each boy.

[
364
]

Dr Horowitz could not determine the views and
preferences of either child.  There was no obvious or overt preference on the
part of either child.  I am sure that they did not want the separation.  In
fact, Jacob told counsellor Fledderus that he wanted his parents back
together.  I am satisfied that both parents love their children very much and
enjoy spending time with them.  There is no evidentiary basis upon which a
reliable conclusion can be founded as to the children’s preferences.

7.

Three Unusual Incidents

[
365
]

The husband related three incidents where the
wife exhibited unusual behaviour.  The first occurred on October 5, 2006, when
she took Jacob to a Party Giant Store at a nearby mall in order to return a
Halloween costume she had purchased for him.  The store’s policy required that
the receipt be presented with the merchandise to be returned.  The wife did not
have the receipt so the store refused the return.  The wife became very angry
and went to the back of the store where she started trying to sell the costume
to other customers.  Jacob was with her the entire time and observed everything.
The clerk told her that she could not sell the costume in the store but she
insisted on doing so unless the store gave her a refund.  The clerk then asked
her to leave but she refused.  The clerk called the police who arrived and had
to escort her off the mall property.  The husband testified that she was banned
from the mall.  The wife did not deny that the incident occurred essentially as
the husband had described, but she stated that she had only been banned from
the store rather than from the entire mall.  Dr Horowitz was aware of this
incident and had received communications from the manager and clerk of the store
as part of his investigation.  He thought her behaviour had been “bizarre” and
that it demonstrated “her extraordinarily poor judgment as a parent”.

[
366
]

The second incident occurred in April 2009,
after settlement had been reached.  The wife wanted to speak with the husband
so he agreed to meet her at a Tim Horton’s restaurant.  They met and took a
table.  The husband said he asked her if she was recording their conversation.
The wife reacted to the question angrily by standing up in full view of everyone
in the restaurant, pulling her top up to expose her bra and asking him in a
loud voice if he wanted her to pull her pants down too.  The husband said she
started to scream his name, yelling that he was a lawyer who was not providing
any money for the children so that they did not have food.  The husband
testified that he got up and left the restaurant but she followed, blocked his
entry to his car and spit at him.  The police were called and wanted him to
make a complaint against her for assault, but he refused.  Again the wife did
not deny the incident.

[
367
]

The third incident occurred in the summer of
2010.  The husband testified that he had learned the wife been had picketing
the front door of the Oshawa Court House with a sign stating his name, that he
was a lawyer and that he was not paying support for his children.  When the
police were called she became agitated and had to be placed in their car until
she calmed down.  The wife did not deny this incident either.

[
368
]

At the very least, these incidents reflect on
the wife’s temperament and judgment.

8.

Dr Horowitz’s Access and Custody Report

[
369
]

Dr Horowitz strongly recommended that sole
custody of both children be awarded to the husband, with substantial access to
the wife (which he spelled out in considerable detail).  Dr Horowitz had conducted
16 interviews lasting approximately one hour each with each party.  In
addition, he conducted a joint interview of the parents, and observed the wife
with the children once and with the husband twice.  On two occasions he observed
Jacob at school and he engaged a social skills therapist with extensive
experience in dealing with autistic children to observe Jacob at school also.
He arranged for the husband and wife to be assessed by a psychologist, who
submitted a written report, and he met several times with the psychologist to
discuss and understand his findings.  He also met or spoke with numerous
collateral sources, including family on both sides, neighbours, friends,
members of family, the Children’s Aid Society of Durham, counsellors, teachers
and such caregivers as would respond.

[
370
]

Dr Horowitz’s report was itself 149 pages long
plus another 129 pages of reports, letters, memoranda or other documentation
from collateral sources.  It took him 16 months to conclude the report.  He
testified that he took extra time to review and consider his opinion, which he
knew would be controversial because of its strong language and unequivocal
conclusion – not to mention that he would be under the scrutiny of very skilled
and experienced lawyers.

[
371
]

I will not review the report in detail, but will
attempt to summarize the assessor’s core reasoning.  In doing so, one must
remember that the time frame of his investigation was from the point of
separation in October 2006 (or shortly before) until his disclosure meeting
with the parties on May 23, 2008, and the delivery of the written report on
July 30, 2008.  Events leading up to the resolution in January 2009, and
thereafter, were not on his screen.

[
372
]

Dr Horowitz measured each party’s parenting
abilities on the basis of seven basic parenting components:

(i)

Role Constraints, which
involved the daily demands and significant restrictions placed on a parent
(particularly a single parent), including loss of freedom, autonomy and
privacy.

(ii)

Attachment, which
involved the ability of the parent to see a child for who he was, including
possible behavioural problems and developmental challenges.  This component
also considered the parent’s “craving company” with the child and the extent to
which the parent integrated the child into his/her life and lifestyle.

(iii)

Parenting Skills
Knowledge, which involved testing (through interviews) the parent’s skills in
dealing with both hypothetical situations and situations actually facing the
particular family, including the ability to recognize and address the
children’s emotional or psychological needs.

(iv)

Competence, which
weighed the parent’s confidence in his/her ability to manage and make decisions
regarding the children, including openness to seeking information, opinions and
advice, then making the effort to make decisions and adapt accordingly.

(v)

Support Network, which
considered support networks of family, friends and colleagues who are available
when needed.

(vi)

Former Spouse, which
considered the relationship between the parties with a view towards their
ability to co-parent and co-operate.

(vii)

Other Life Stressors,
such as maintaining or finding a job or career, forming a new relationship, and
handling the effects of the old relationship.

[
373
]

Dr Horowitz found the wife wanting in almost all
areas, and no better than the husband nor worse in some.  He concluded that she
had great difficulty meeting the demands of parenthood, including providing
reliably for the children and making her own freedom, autonomy and privacy
secondary to their needs.  Until the husband moved out of the house, she had
abdicated the children’s morning and after-school routines to him, and she had
let him take the lead in dealing with Jacob’s school.  She had also “given away
a huge chunk” of parent/child time to the husband in allowing him three out of
four weekends for access.  Also, once the husband had moved out of the home,
she had difficulty getting Jacob to school on time, supporting him regularly
and reliably in his studies, and getting both children to their activities.
The psychologist engaged as part of the assessment process had also convinced Dr
Horowitz that the wife’s psychological makeup was such that she could have
difficulty putting the needs of the children before her own.

[
374
]

The assessor concluded that the husband’s
attachment to the children was normal.  In spite of the behavioural and
possible developmental issues, the husband had accepted those challenges as
part of who the children were and had made a great effort to integrate them
into his life.  He “craved” their company.  He participated in activities with
them, followed their daily activities, and made them the centre of his focus.
He had not sought out another relationship; he drew the children into his
world, for example bringing them to the office where they got to know staff and
played; and he closely monitored and directed Jacob’s education and attempted
to do so with child health and emotional issues.  Dr Horowitz did not believe
the same was true of the wife, as just mentioned.

[
375
]

Dr Horowitz also concluded that the husband was
sensitive to the emotional and psychological needs of the children,
particularly Jacob, who was posing the greatest difficulty at the time.  The
husband had recognized the child’s difficulties and taken steps to find help,
which he then acted upon.  The wife’s primary response was denial and
avoidance.  She did not seem able to recognize the problems or appreciate the
threat they posed.  She had revealed this to Dr Horowitz both in her actual
response to the problems and also in her response to hypothetical situations
posed to her in the interview process.

[
376
]

In Dr Horowitz’s opinion, the wife’s
shortcomings negatively affected her competence in parenting.  If one could not
recognize needs, one could not minister to them.  She also seemed to lack the
confidence necessary to deal with the children’s emotional and developmental
growth.  Her relative lack of involvement in important daily aspects of the
children’s lives also spoke to her parenting ability.  On the other hand, the
husband was very confident in dealing with these issues and he had not
hesitated to do so.  He had done research, and then acted upon it to seek
help.  He was able to understand the advice given, act upon it reasonably and
to keep searching for ways to improve the emotional and developmental lives of
his children.

[
377
]

Dr Horowitz recognized that both parents had
access to support networks, although they were very different.  The wife’s
support network consisted mainly of her large family and a few close friends.
Yet he thought that her potentially most reliable support was the husband –
probably because he was so dedicated in dealing with school, recreation, health
and developmental issues.  The husband’s network included a much smaller family
(not all of which was nearby), friends and colleagues.

[
378
]

With respect to the nature of the relationship
of the spouses after their separation, Dr Horowitz recognized that the parties
were mutually hostile, antagonistic, and resentful of each other.  In his
opinion, there was no indication that they would achieve a good level of
co-parenting or co-operation in the near future.  Both spouses also faced
stressors apart from the high conflict divorce they were going through.  The
husband was coping with an elderly parent who was also seriously ill.  The wife
was coping with maintaining a new relationship and also probably having to
think of re-entering the job market.

[
379
]

After a lengthy review of the psychologist’s
test results, Dr Horowitz reached the following conclusions about the wife:

That sketch depicts a woman who lacks
empathy; is grandiose; often fails to accurately recognize her own situation;
is interpersonally exploitive; denies responsibility and blames others; tends
to be disinhibited which includes seductive behaviour, sexual promiscuity and
substance abuse; has been self-mutilating; is self-centred, self-indulgent, and
intensely dependent on others; projects her own unrealistic, fantasized
intentions onto people with whom she is involved; is emotionally shallow to
avoid distress; and has difficulty understanding herself or others (including
her children) in any depth; and whose selection of marital or sexual partners is
often highly inappropriate.

After defining the psychological term “personality disorder”, he
accepted the psychologist’s finding that the wife had a “histrionic personality
disorder (HPD)” characterized by a pattern of excessive emotionality and
attention-seeking, including an excessive need for approval and inappropriate
seductiveness, usually beginning in early adulthood.

[
380
]

This was a very harsh judgment of the wife that
would provoke the strong reaction it did, both by the wife and her very capable
litigation team.

[
381
]

Dr Horowitz recognized the husband as “a neurotic
individual with a sadistic personality style” that affected his interaction
with others, but was not chronic, and did not cross the line into pathological
personality disorder (which would have been potentially serious).  As a result,
the husband liked to be in charge and in control.  He feared psychological
weakness and submission, and he preferred functioning within non-ambiguous
structures and rules.  Thus he tried to keep his interpersonal life in a
simplistic frame unencumbered by complexity.  On this level, there were fewer
grays in the husband’s life.  He also tended to try to dominate interpersonal
relationships and reacted aggressively to challenges to his authority.  He had
little tolerance for uncertainty and ambiguity, thus he sought to define issues
and find ways to address and solve them.  He showed “good reality testing” and
an adaptive capacity to think logically and coherently.  Yet he was also at
risk of thinking and acting impulsively because he tended to have difficulty
coping with internal and external demands placed on him.  This impulsivity was
likely to manifest itself in the form of aggression towards people who
threatened him with loss or defeat.

[
382
]

Dr Horowitz recognized the husband’s aggressive
and controlling behaviour toward the wife, who was at the receiving end of his verbal
abuse and desire to maintain a position of power and control.  He wanted to
“win” because the separation and potential loss of home and family threatened
his internal/external coping mechanisms and offered up uncertainties outside
the simple, defined structures and set of rules he preferred to operate
within.  The husband’s psychological profile made him a very unpleasant
opponent in the divorce proceeding, yet it also made him a source of strength
and support as a parent in the circumstances of these particular children and
the challenges they faced.

[
383
]

Thus Dr Horowitz “strongly” recommended that
sole custody of both children be awarded to the husband.  He then structured an
elaborate access plan whereby the wife would have access on alternate weekends
from Friday after school until Sunday morning at 9:00 a.m., so that the husband
could take the boys to their Jewish school.  She would also have them on the
“off” Thursday from after school and would take them to any scheduled
recreation activities that evening and return them home after.  She would also
be able to have them for dinner after school on Mondays following her weekend
access.  Holidays and special occasions were divided fairly evenly.

9.

Dr Kershner’s Critique of the Horowitz
Report and Psychological Assessment of the Wife

(a)

Dr Kershner’s Opinions and Testimony

[
384
]

Dr Betty Kershner is a highly experienced
psychologist with many years of practice in the Toronto area.  She is a
specialist in conducting psychological assessments and parenting capacity
assessments, and she was qualified as an expert in those areas.  Dr Kershner is
particularly interested and skilled in assessing attachment issues.  She was
retained by the wife’s counsel to do a psychological assessment of the wife and
a critique of Dr Horowitz’s report.  Accordingly, she conducted extensive
testing of the wife (requiring about 14 hours of face to face contact).  She
also did a critique of Dr Horowitz’s methodology in the context of parenting
capacity but she did not comment on the custody and access aspects of his
assessment, although no doubt her criticism of his methodology was intended to
undermine his conclusions.  Dr Kershner has had no experience in doing custody
and access assessments or reports, and she did not purport to do that here.
The basis of her information was documentation and selected affidavits provided
by the wife’s counsel, and Dr Horowitz’s report (together with the documents
included in the appendices of his report).

[
385
]

Dr Kershner found Dr Horowitz’s report wanting
in the way it treated the wife.  She thought he had been biased and unbalanced against
the wife, and that he had not treated her fairly or on the same basis as he had
treated or measured the husband.  She also thought he had failed to consider
important issues, that he had misinterpreted or unfairly interpreted others
against the wife’s interest, and that he had misunderstood, misused or failed to
properly use the psychological assessments that he had obtained.  I will review
and comment on some of Dr Kershner’s principal complaints.

[
386
]

Much of her criticism that Dr Horowitz was
biased, unfair and treated the spouses unequally, was based on the section of
his report entitled “Brief Historical Data” at the beginning of the 149 page
report.  In this section, Dr Horowitz briefly described the personal background
of each of the husband and wife from birth until the separation.  He presented
about three pages of historical information about each party.

[
387
]

Dr Kershner criticized Dr Horowitz generally for
insufficiently addressing each spouse’s relationships with other important
persons in their lives, especially parents and other partners.  Parents are a
model for their children.  How the child relates to the parent may give insight
into the kind of parent he or she will be.  The psychologist identified this as
an important gap in respect of the husband, especially his relationship with
immigrant parents who were survivors of the Holocaust.

[
388
]

She observed that the trauma of Holocaust
experiences often results in the family being dysfunctional.  Also, the
husband’s father had become seriously ill when he was very young, and the
father had died when the husband was a young man.  She wondered how all this had
affected the husband, because such factors often left scars and unresolved
relationship issues in the child so that when he matured it would often have a negative
effect on his own ability and approach to parenting.  Dr Kershner pointed out
that there was a great deal of research about the children of Holocaust
survivors, who it was found often have a deep need to care for their parents in
order to compensate for how the parents had suffered.  Children of Holocaust
survivors may be good achievers and earners because of the need to compensate
for their parents’ hardships.  However, it may also adversely affect their
ability to maintain intimate relationships and healthy parenting
relationships.

[
389
]

Dr Kershner observed that the husband was on his
third marriage, which might have been an effect of his relationship with his
own parents and father.  Dr Horowitz only reported that the first marriage
ended because his wife had been unfaithful to him, and that the second marriage
ended because of unspecified fidelity and trust issues.  But whose fidelity and
trust?  The psychologist thought that much more attention should have been
given to the husband’s relationship with his parents and former spouses,
because these relationships would probably shed light on his general ability to
maintain intimate and parenting relationships.  She thought Dr Horowitz’s
review in this area was superficial and inadequate.  She also criticized him
for presenting the husband’s family’s situation and struggles as heroic.

[
390
]

Dr Kershner was also very critical of what she
thought was the assessor’s unfair and unfounded review of the wife’s
relationship with her parents and other partners. In describing the marriage
breakdown of the wife’s parents, Dr  Horowitz had observed:

Susan states that her father was a
tremendous father, a good man, a philanderer, and “a pig” due to his many
infidelities.  She adds that “he was her hero”.  When she was 3 years of age
her father went on a skiing trip during which time his best friend, George, a
married man, moved to Oshawa with Susan’s mother and all her children.  Susan
believes that her mother went with George out of spite but then fell in love
with him.  George got divorced and the two married.

[
391
]

Dr Horowitz then made the following comment
about the effect of the marriage/family breakdown on the wife:

Everything seemed to have a good and bad
side or, without a value judgment, perhaps a black and white side.  This is
clear, of course, in the dichotomy of her father being her “hero” and a “pig”.
The duality that seems to have dominated her young life was not always quite so
clear, but appears to have still been there nonetheless.  For example, [the
wife] stated that her father began drinking when his wife left him and that he
often made disparaging remarks about her.  As a young woman sensitive enough to
label her father a “pig”, I would think she found it at least unpleasant to
hear her father badmouthing her mother?  And if dad was a “pig,” what thoughts
did she have about her mother leaving dad behind while she moved in with his
best friend?  Or what were her thoughts about dad’s best friend?  If dad was a
philanderer what was George, the man having an affair with a married woman who
happened to be Susan’s mother?  With all that, she still maintained her
paradigm by indicating there was “no downside to her parent’s divorce as she
then had two dads”.  Although she had two dads she only had one mother.  She
indicated that she was primarily raised by her sisters and at times felt
abandoned by her mother.  To their credit, both George and Ruth [the wife’s
mother] left everything to the spouses they abandoned.

[
392
]

Dr Kershner thought this was a very unbalanced
and unfairly critical view of the wife’s mother.  It implied that she was the
unfaithful one who had caused the marriage breakdown, whereas in fact her
action was a response to a husband who was chronically and repeatedly
unfaithful.  Dr Horowitz had glossed over the biological father’s multiple
prior infidelities.

[
393
]

In the same historical passage, Dr Horowitz
reported the wife’s self-admitted lack of motivation to do well in high school
because of her desire to become a gymnast, in which she failed. He then made
the following comment: “With aspirations of becoming a gymnast no longer on the
horizon, [the wife] began working as a welder in Scarborough.  The career
aspirations and choices remain a reminder of the thread of duality that runs
through the fabric of [the wife’s] life.”

[
394
]

Dr Horowitz then described the wife’s first long
dating relationship (five years) with a young stockbroker, their cohabitation
for six months and their separation when the boyfriend began to date another
woman.  He made the following comment:

Although still a young woman, the imprints
of [the wife’s] past are already beginning to invade and color her life.  She
has moved from father to father to father, back and forth unable to remain
“faithful” to either one.  When she settled down with Mike, it was only six
months before she, like her father, was coping with infidelity.  The impression
is that Susan, seeking the stimulation necessary to feel good, kept herself
moving.

[
395
]

Dr Kershner interpreted this comment as reinforcing
negative and unfair blame to the wife’s mother, and implying that the wife was
also unfaithful when there was no evidence that she had ever been unfaithful in
any relationship.  Nor was there evidence that the wife had moved back and
forth between father and partner, one father and the other, or from one man to
another.  As a teenager, the wife had lived for a while with her biological
father, which Dr Kershner observed was not at all unusual in these
circumstances.

[
396
]

Dr Kershner saw no evidence either that the
wife’s relationships were all with older men.  She suggested that Dr Horowitz
had implied that the wife had been unfaithful to the husband too, and that this
had been an important theme or tendency throughout the wife’s life.  Dr
Horowitz had also observed that the
wife
married a man 23 years her
senior.  Dr Kershner saw this phrasing as an example of gender bias.  She asked
why Dr Horowitz had not framed it as the
husband
marrying a woman 23
years younger than him.  In short, the psychologist found Dr Horowitz’s
historical description inaccurate, unbalanced, biased, unfairly negative toward
the wife, and showing gender bias.

[
397
]

Dr Kershner was also critical of Dr Horowitz’s
attitude toward other professionals and suggested that he had expressed
opinions and made suggestions that were not within his area of professional
competence.  Here, she was referring to the assessor’s criticism of several of
the physicians who had failed to respond to his calls, or did not show
appropriate concern.  The following are some of Dr Horowitz’s comments:

(a)

In respect of Jacob’s “pooping problem”:

The medical practitioners, with some
exceptions, have treated this as a constipation issue.  It is obviously far
more than that and volumes have been written about the type of behaviour Jacob
is displaying.  It is far more likely that the pooping is symptomatic of anger
and rage that Jacob cannot express in any other way.

(b)

In respect of Jacob’s lack of weight gain:

Dr. Rajah, a paediatrician, for reasons
which are astounding and defy comprehension, states that he is not concerned.
I do not know if he weighs children at every office visit like every other
paediatrician in North America, but a lack of weight gain is not something one
would ignore.  Jacob is beginning to look like a failure to thrive child
(secondary type) who may have to become dangerously ill before taken seriously.

(c)

In respect of Jacob’s professional caregivers generally:

I am concerned that Dr. Rajah, Dr. Green,
and some of the other key medical players simply do not want to be involved.
They do not want to sit in a witness chair, give their opinion, and then have a
physician called by “the other side” to give a contrary opinion.  Medical
malpractice insurance is very expensive.  Dr. Green, however, may have a
different agenda. [...]  To date Dr. Green has refused to return calls from my
office or from CAS.

[
398
]

Dr Horowitz also expressed strong concern that
Jacob was exhibiting signs of autism or Asperger’s Syndrome, which he strongly
recommended be assessed by an expert.  Dr Kershner opined that Dr Horowitz’s
observations were professionally inappropriate and beyond his expertise.  Dr
Kershner’s opinion had been formed after Dr Montgomery’s examination of Jacob
and his formal written opinion that Jacob was not autistic or suffering from Asperger’s
Syndrome.  So from Dr Kershner’s perspective the “proof was in the pudding”.  She
thought that Dr Horowitz was sounding alarms that he was not qualified to do,
expressing views beyond his professional competence – views that had been
proven wrong by Dr Montgomery’s opinion.

[
399
]

Dr Kershner also accused Dr Horowitz of being
contradictory.  In a letter sent to the lawyers in May 2008, he had expressed
concern that the boys’ current level of care and supervision was sufficiently
deficient that if not improved in the near future could put them at risk of
emotional and physical harm so that he might have to notify the CAS.  Yet he
had taken 16 months to prepare his report.  While he had expressed urgency he
had not acted as though it was urgent.

[
400
]

Finally, Dr Kershner was critical of Dr
Horowitz’s understanding and use of psychological tests completed on the
parties by Dr K. Wiedermann in September 2007.  She noted that Dr Horowitz had commented
that he usually did not call upon psychologists because their role was to
assess mental illness or disturbance rather than parenting capacity.  However,
he thought that certain personality disorders (narcissistic personality
disorder, borderline personality disorder, and histrionic personality disorder)
might severely and negatively impact a person’s ability to parent, and he
suspected the presence of such a disorder in the wife.  Dr Kershner testified
that Dr Horowitz was not correct in his assessment of the value and role of
psychological testing.  In fact, it was an effective tool for objectively
measuring a person’s personality and parenting ability because it “got under
the skin” of the individual.  It was reliable because validity scales were
built into the tests so that the person could not lie or hide.  On the other
hand, in clinical interviews, a person could mislead or hide things, so that
the interviewer might miss something or be fooled.

[
401
]

Having decided to call upon psychology in this
case, Dr Kershner both reported and testified that Dr Horowitz had then misunderstood
and misapplied the test results received from Dr Wiedermann.  She charged Dr
Horowitz with concluding that the wife had narcissistic and/or histrionic
personality disorders, when in fact Dr Wiedermann had only found that she had
“features” of these disorders.  On the other hand, Dr Horowitz clearly pointed
out that Dr Wiedermann concluded that the husband had a sadistic personality
style, and specifically that it was
not
a personality disorder.  In Dr
Kershner’s opinion, this was another example of the assessor’s biased and
unbalanced interpretation.  She testified that her tests of the wife had been
far more extensive and included cognitive testing and attachment analysis,
which Dr Wiedermann’s tests had not done.  Also, she had found scoring
irregularities in her review of Dr Wiedermann’s raw data, although it did not
have a major impact on the results.  Dr Kershner generally agreed with Dr
Wiedermann’s conclusions.

(b)

Discussion

[
402
]

I have thought carefully about Dr Kershner’s
observations since the trial.  Dr Kershner was an impressive witness who spoke
confidently and with authority.  She had obviously taken considerable time in
analyzing the assessor’s report.  She is an expert in her field whose testimony
and opinions merit respect.  From her perspective and with the information she
had at hand, her criticisms made sense.  She did her job well.  However, when
she did her assessment, Dr Montgomery’s opinion that Jacob was not
developmentally disabled had been delivered.  To Dr Kershner it was proven that
Jacob was not autistic, and Dr Horowitz’s concern seemed misplaced,
disrespectful of other professionals and even audacious.  He had been proven
wrong!  The medical finding and Dr Kershner’s report had a powerful effect on
the husband’s view of the custody and access assessment report, and therefore
also on Dr Horowitz’s recommendation on sole custody.  The husband testified
that it caused him to re-assess his position and his confidence in a favourable
outcome.  There was no reason to disbelieve the husband.  The combined effect
of Dr Kershner’s and Dr Montgomery’s reports undoubtedly brought about the
settlement that was embodied in the divorce judgment.

[
403
]

But of course, events have developed and there
have been further twists and turns.  Jacob was eventually diagnosed as autistic.
Dr Horowitz was right to be concerned.  When I stand back and consider Dr
Kershner’s criticisms against all of the evidence that has been received at
this trial, I conclude that while she did an excellent job with the information
she had, it was ultimately based on incomplete and inaccurate information –
particularly the diagnosis of autism and the events since her report.  When one
considers her criticisms in the light of the events that followed, I do not
think they are correct or ultimately bear much weight.  In reaching this
conclusion, I am not including her psychological report of the wife.  That is
another matter that will be addressed shortly.

[
404
]

Many of Dr Kershner’s complaints about the
custody and access report related to Dr Horowitz’s observations made in a very
brief historical outline of the parties’ early years.  This historical outline
was an introductory portion to the larger report.  While I accept that how one
frames a problem reflects upon and affects its subsequent analysis, I think Dr
Kershner may herself have misinterpreted or read too much into it.  This
particular introductory section of the assessment report was intended to provide
a brief historical overview, without detail and supplying a very general
context to each spouse’s formative years.  It was done with a “broad brush,”
light on details and very general in nature.  I expect these outlines reflected
what each spouse had told Dr Horowitz about those years, and their particular
recollections and concerns.  I am also sure it was discussed in much greater
detail at the time, and that the wife presented herself as she wished and as
she saw her own formative history.  There is no evidence and I do not believe
that Dr Horowitz made any of it up.  Each background was of approximately the
same length (just under three pages each).

[
405
]

I have read the passages referred to in
paragraphs 390, 391 and 394 above a number of times.  I do not see them as
saying anything bad about the wife’s mother or blaming the breakup on her.  Dr
Horowitz stated several times that the biological father was a “philander”, and
I am certain that the wife’s reference to him as a “pig” was a derogatory
reference to this fact.  Dr Horowitz did not “gloss” over it.  All he was
trying to say (as I read it) was that the family break-up and reconstitution
was a confusing, troubling experience for the wife.  It was full of
contradictions – or “dichotomy” and “duality” as Dr Horowitz termed it.  On the
one hand, her father had been an unfaithful “pig” (and with many women if he
was a “philanderer”).  Yet the wife loved him and in many ways he was a “hero”
to her.  Dr Horowitz acknowledged the wife’s mother’s observation that the
biological father was a good husband in every other way.  He was also an otherwise
good father, and the wife remained close to him throughout her childhood and
until today.

[
406
]

Against this background of a “philandering”
husband, the wife’s mother struck up a relationship outside the marriage that
ultimately led to her leaving the marriage for her husband’s best friend, and
their relationship bloomed while they were still married to others.  The wife’s
mother was not a philanderer, and most people would probably have great
sympathy for her.  Yet it is a fact that she struck up a relationship outside
her marriage, which she left.  She was part of this complicated and confusing
situation.  The wife was also very close to her mother and to her stepfather George,
who has been a very good father.  All of the wife’s parental figures were
unfaithful to their original spouses.  It must have been very confusing for the
wife and she must have felt conflicted as to how to regard family institutions
and her models in life.  How did she reconcile all of this and digest it?  She
was faced with a conundrum that she probably did not understand but that caused
her much confusion and thought, which was what she was reported to have told Dr
Horowitz.

[
407
]

In Dr Horowitz’s view, these family circumstances
posed two sides – good and bad, black and white - which he saw the wife viewing
without many greys.  That is how I read his comments.  I do not see it
reflecting badly on the wife’s mother or the wife.  Indeed I do not see any
value judgment being made of the wife’s mother.  Dr Kershner testified that the
wife had also expressed strong feelings to her about not having been taken care
of properly or her needs met when she was a child.  While the wife was and
still is very close to her mother, her mother had to work full time during the
wife’s childhood years.  So she was not home a lot to look after the wife.  The
wife was lonely at times.  This was just another unfortunate fact of her early
life, and she acknowledged it.

[
408
]

Dr Horowitz thought he saw this “dichotomy” or
“duality” appearing in other parts of the wife’s life.  Her dreams and goals
were one thing, but how things turned out was another – for example the dream
to become a gymnast, which did not pan out, leaving the wife to graduate from high
school without great marks and finding herself welding in Scarborough.  The
dream was ambitions and romantic, while the ultimate reality was much less so –
i.e. a stark contrast.  As I read Dr Horowitz’s remarks in this passage, they
reflect a certain sadness about the wife’s progress through this stage of her
life.   Nor do I see the reference to the wife moving “from father to father to
father, back and forth unable to remain ‘faithful’ to either one” as referring
to the
wife
being unfaithful in a sexual context.  He was attempting to
highlight the wife’s confusion about her family situation and how the pattern
or “duality” followed her into later years, and how it complicated her
relationships and the quality of commitment she seemed to receive.

[
409
]

I would fault Dr Horowitz for his style, which
he attempted to give a literary flavour, perhaps to make it more readable or
engaging.  However, he may have gotten carried away with his metaphors.  This
dramatic style removed some of the
gravitas
of the situation, giving it
a feeling of being unreal.  I can see the wife, who bore the brunt of the
assessor’s criticism, thinking that he might even be mocking her.  Also, I
found the focus on the theme of “duality” and “dichotomy” as having a
“psycho-babble” flavour, and I wondered how Dr Horowitz was qualified to
theorize in this manner.  His questions were good, but the way he articulated them
may have detracted from the message he was attempting to formulate.  Although
it might not have been as interesting for the reader, Dr Horowitz would have
done better to express his views in a more neutral and conventional manner.  It
would also have been better not to have embarked on metaphorical theorizing to
explain personal history because it was difficult to separate one from other,
and it opened him to the criticism that he did not understand or get the facts
right.

[
410
]

The dramatic passage in question was fairly enigmatic.
I agree that it is difficult to know with certainty what Dr Horowitz was trying
to say.  The reader should not have to parse metaphors.  However, after reading
it many times, it is my interpretation of the passage that from the wife’s
perspective her close relationships with men were with father figures, whether
her biological father, her step-father or her partner.  To her they were all
father figures, who for one reason or another were both attractive and imperfect.
She could not give her natural father up, but neither could she stay with him.
Because of her attachment to her biological father, she was not always close to
her step-father.  There were issues of conflicting loyalty, even though both
men were good parents; and when she lived with the young stockbroker, he was an
authority figure (a father figure) who let her down by becoming involved with
another woman.  I thought Dr Horowitz was attempting to identify a common
thread in the wife’s life with respect to her close relationships with men.  I did
not regard it as a suggestion that the wife was sexually promiscuous or
unfaithful.  By the way, in Dr Kershner’s report she also observed: “[The wife]
sees a mate as a father-figure.”

[
411
]

I do not think the wife’s sexual fidelity was an
issue between the spouses before the marriage breakdown.  At least there was no
evidence to support that it was and I do not think Dr Horowitz suggested
otherwise.  After, however, it was a frequent allegation by the husband –
usually in the heat of argument.  Dr Horowitz was aware that the wife had
formed a relationship with Adrian, and had introduced him (and his infant daughter) to the boys.
While Adrian and his child did not live at the matrimonial home, they were
frequent guests, including overnight.  This greatly upset the husband, and Dr
Horowitz was critical of it.  Even Dr Kershner expressed concern about the
potential negative effect on the boys by introducing them to a relationship so
soon after the separation and bringing another man into the home.

[
412
]

As for the criticisms of Dr Horowitz exceeding
his professional expertise by commenting on physicians, health care issues and
complicated psychological questions, events have proven him right.  There is no
question that he was frustrated by the response or non-response of physicians
either to him or to the husband. I do not doubt that Dr Green failed to take
his calls or respond.  Why would Dr Horowitz make that up?  From his testimony,
Dr Green was clear that his time was at a premium.  He took care of patients
with appointments first – and that took the most of his time.  Paper work and
reports sat on his desk until he could get around to them.  He also testified
that he had experienced problems around the same time with an office manager.
Although he did not have recollection of receiving calls from Dr Horowitz, I do
not doubt that he did.  Also, Dr Green was pretty squarely in the wife’s
corner.  That was not a bad thing.  A physician should advocate for his patient
and be sympathetic to her.  However, he should have responded to the court
ordered assessor whose mandate was to determine the best interests of the
children.  I note that Dr Green had responded to the Children’s Aid Society.

[
413
]

Dr Rajah responded to the husband’s concerns
about Jacob’s weight loss and “pooping” problem, but I had the impression that
he was not very communicative with Dr Horowitz.  Again, I understand that
physicians are very busy and that reports are standardly slow and usually
written.  The assessor’s criticism that Dr Rajah did not weigh Jacob was not
fair.  I am sure that he did, and when he had done it a number of times over a
number of months he had a basis for his opinion.  However, I wondered how he
could tell whether or not the child was failing to thrive in the early months of
his examinations of Jacob without first reviewing Dr Green’s records of weight
and height.  Both Dr Green and Dr Rajah explained how the condition is measured
by relating growth to a plotted curve for children of the same age, weight and
height.  The husband knew that Jacob had put on little weight or height over
the preceding year and even to Dr Horowitz the child did not look nourished or
well.  In testimony, Dr Rajah agreed that a parent was properly worried if his
child had only gained a pound in a year.  I conclude that the husband’s concern
was well-placed and that Dr Horowitz’s concern and support on that issue was
equally well-founded.  Although the assessor may be criticized for being outspoken,
his concern was proper.

[
414
]

I conclude that Dr Horowitz’s concern about the
possibility of developmental disability was equally well based.  What the
physicians did not know was that Dr Horowitz had first-hand experience with an
autistic child and had become a resource on the condition within his own
community.  This came out in testimony.  Also, Dr Horowitz had worked for a
number of years as a psychotherapist.  So while his background was more on the
social work side, he was not without knowledge and experience in mental health
issues.  When one thinks of it, social workers must often work closely with
mental health care givers in dealing with mutual patients.  Dr Kershner made
assumptions about Dr Horowitz without having all the information and on the
basis of professional stereotypical assumptions.  When one reads Dr Horowitz’s
report closely, he was strongly advocating that the question be explored.  He
was not giving a diagnosis although I am sure he thought there was a strong
likelihood.  His expressions of concern were very direct and urgent.  Surely there
was nothing wrong with that.  Had he not been so strong and direct, the husband
might not have persevered and Jacob might not have been diagnosed.  Dr
Kershner’s criticisms were not justified in this area.

[
415
]

After hearing Dr Kirkpatrick’s (the paediatric
specialist who diagnosed Jacob with Asperger’s Syndrome) testimony and reading
her report, it was clear that Dr Horowitz understood the signs and
characteristics of autism and Asperger’s Syndrome.  It is also clear that he picked
up on many of those signs and characteristics in Jacob, and that they were also
confirmed by collateral sources who had had close contact with the child.  The
husband had seen the same signs some years earlier but had accepted the
assurance of a professional who tested a much younger Jacob that there was no
difficulty.  As a result, the husband took comfort and turned his attention
away from autism, although the problems did not abate.  When Dr Horowitz
identified his concerns, the husband saw dots connected and renewed his concern.
Had he not been as determined, the diagnosis would not have been undertaken and
confirmed.

[
416
]

This pointed up a strong difference between the
husband and the wife.  The wife was either in denial or simply did not see the
signs and symptoms of the condition. She did not or could not relate them to Dr
Montgomery and because of control issues or mistrust, she could not let the
husband (who did recognize the danger signs) participate in the medical
investigative process.  As a result, Dr Montgomery was not given sufficient
information to warrant closer investigation.  This reflects on qualities and
weaknesses that the assessor identified in the wife in reaching his conclusion
that sole custody to the husband would be in the children’s best interests.  I
conclude that Dr Horowitz was correct in these observations.

[
417
]

I agree with Dr Kershner’s criticism that the
report took too long.  It was indeed inconsistent and contradictory to express such
urgency (with the threat of reporting to the CAS) when the report itself had
taken over a year to that point.  On the other hand, this was such a conflicted
proceeding and the parties’ positions were so far apart that thorough
investigation was justified.  I had the impression from Dr Horowitz’s testimony
that he felt considerable pressure both from the changing dynamics of the
conflict and the strength of the lawyers.  He testified that he took extra time
to be sure that his conclusion was supported by his findings because he
realized that his report and recommendations would be controversial and that
they would make the wife very unhappy.  I also had the impression from Dr
Horowitz’s testimony that he did not often reach such strong conclusions, so he
took additional time to contemplate and feel assured of his views.   Still, it
took far too long to complete the assessment, although that did not take away
from the quality of the result.

[
418
]

I do not want to get into a discussion of the
relative merits of one discipline over another.  Dr Horowitz is not a
psychologist, so while I would not expect him to minimize or belittle that
science, neither would I expect him to use it regularly as a tool in his own
arsenal.  I do not think Dr Horowitz was casting aspersions on the strengths or
applications of psychology within his own discipline, but rather he was identifying
it as an extraordinary measure that he had called upon in this highly
conflicted case.  I accept Dr Kershner’s observations on the value of
psychology as a means of “getting under the skin” of a subject and its strengths
in objective analysis because of proven validity scales.  It may be that Dr
Horowitz did not appreciate these advantages.  However, that does not detract
from his own discipline and approach.  His experience and qualifications are
equally as impressive and extensive as Dr Kershner’s, but in the area of
custody and access investigations.  He was selected by the parties’ counsel who
are themselves highly experienced and leading practitioner’s of family law in Ontario.

[
419
]

It may be that Dr Wiedermann’s reports were
superficial, although Dr Kershner agreed generally with their results.  I have
carefully reviewed Dr Horowitz’s reading and use of those reports.  It is true
that he expressed concern about certain personality disorders, for example:

There are, however, certain personality
disorders which in my opinion severely impact on the ability to parent.  As I suspected
the presence of such in [the wife], the referral for testing was necessary ....

The personality disorders which, when
present concern me, are narcissistic personality disorder, borderline
personality disorder, and histrionic personality disorder.  Dr. Wiedermann
diagnosed [the wife] as having
features
of two of the three disorders
identified as problematic.  [The husband] was found to have none. (emphasis
added).

[
420
]

In fact, Dr Horowitz did not suggest that the
wife had been diagnosed with narcissistic or histrionic personality disorders
but rather that she exhibited features of those disorders.  In fact, Dr
Wiedermann diagnosed the wife with a “mild to moderate obsessive-compulsive
personality disorder with narcissistic and histrionic features”.  He did therefore
diagnose a personality disorder, which Dr Horowitz correctly referred to in
another part of his report:

Dr. Wiedermann diagnosed [the wife] with
obsessive compulsive personality disorder with histrionic and narcissistic
features.  While her obsessive thoughts and compulsive actions are the
underpinning of her personality, it is the histrionic and narcissistic features
that present the greatest concern in terms of parenting ability and parenting
conflicts.

[
421
]

It does not appear that Dr Horowitz was as
concerned with the obsessive compulsive personality disorder as he was with the
related features.  How these features played out in the wife’s parenting style
was the concern, and he looked for actual behaviour and actions that might show
the presence and strength of those features.  Having listed important
characteristics of histrionic and narcissistic features, he concluded:

A review of the events and incidents
detailed in this assessment report that reflect [the wife’s] thought patterns,
use of logic and reason, and her behaviour in various circumstances will result
in providing at least one example of every item listed above in the classification
of both histrionic and narcissistic features.  This list is an impressively
accurate psychological character sketch of [the wife].

[
422
]

To be sure that he understood the implications
of Dr Wiedermann’s reports, Dr Horowitz indicated that he interviewed Dr
Wiedermann twice and that he also had several other brief telephone conferences
with him.  In the course of and as a result of these meetings, he was advised
that on the basis of the psychological profiles that emerged from the testing,
the husband had the ability and desire to put the children’s needs before his
own.  On the other hand, the wife might not.  Dr Horowitz then stated:

I asked Dr. Wiedermann to repeat this to me
on two separate occasions to absolutely confirm what he was saying.  My own findings
are in complete agreement with this conclusion and examples of this can be
found throughout the entire report.

[
423
]

It could not be clearer that Dr Horowitz was
very careful to understand the implications of Dr Wiedermann’s reports and he
did it directly by questioning the psychologist not once, but twice.  Also, the
opinion was Dr Wiedermann’s not the assessor’s.  Furthermore, Dr Horowitz
observed that Dr Wiedermann’s observations agreed with his.  In other words, Dr
Horowitz had come to the same conclusion through his own discipline and
investigation.  Dr Wiedermann’s test results confirmed what Dr Horowitz had
otherwise observed and concluded.  I am satisfied that Dr Horowitz would have
reached the same conclusions without Dr Wiedermann’s testing and that he did
reach those conclusions independently, but that the testing confirmed them.

[
424
]

Regrettably Dr Kershner was unable to test the
husband or the boys.  I accept that her battery of tests and results were much
more thorough and complete than Dr Wiedermann’s and I accept her opinions over Dr
Wiedermann’s.  I will deal with her findings shortly.  It would have been
worthwhile having her analysis of the entire family had it been possible.
Unfortunately she was able to give only a partial picture.  The collaboration
of experts such as Dr Kershner and Dr Horowitz would have been a powerful combination
for a case such as this.

10.

Psychological Reports

(a)

General

[
425
]

While I do not think it was necessary to have
psychological testing in order to come to sound conclusions in this case,
nevertheless they have provided information that gives insight into how these
parties operate and react, including in their dispute.  These psychological
profiles also help explain why the dispute has been so toxic and why the
parties have had such difficulty communicating and co-operating given their
views of each other.  I will briefly summarize the results, relying on Dr
Wiedermann for the husband (as he was the only source) and on Dr Kershner for
the wife (who was much more thorough).

(b)

Dr Wiedermann’s Results

[
426
]

Dr Wiedermann reported that the husband
functioned in the neurotic spectrum, i.e. he showed no personality disorders or
other serious psychological pathology.  His most notable feature was a sadistic
personality style.  As a result, he tended to fear psychological weakness or
submission, so that he tried to look confident and in charge when tested or
challenged.  He might therefore also deny weakness in himself and try to shift
blame to others when he encountered a problem.  Dr Wiedermann opined that such
individuals try to dominate interpersonal relationships and react aggressively
when their authority is challenged.  They feel insecure unless they are in a
position of power.

[
427
]

This personality style also tends to avoid
introspection, processing feelings, and emotional stimulation.  The quest for
power and domination of threatening situations is also a defence against
feelings of depression and self-criticism.  Underneath it all, the psychologist
thought that the husband likely had a poor self-regard and feared that he had
weaknesses.  This might make him vulnerable to episodes of depression, which he
would generally deny to himself (in keeping with suppressing his feelings), but
which were not likely of serious proportions in any event.  This type of
personality also often attempted to avoid emotional stimulation and maintain a
narrow simplistic interpersonal life.  Dr Wiedermann thought that the husband
did not tolerate ambiguity and uncertainty well; and he might have a simplistic
way of looking at the world.  He might also often have difficulty establishing
close and rewarding intimate relationships.

[
428
]

The psychologist did not do cognitive testing,
so there was no measure of the husband’s intelligence.  However, given his
academic and professional accomplishments, there is no doubt that he is of
superior intelligence.  That was Dr Horowitz’s assessment and from observing
the husband during this long trial, I agree.

[
429
]

Dr Wiedermann’s tests suggested that the husband
had a firm grip on reality, although his preference for simplification of the
world around him gave him a tendency to favour simple solutions to complex
problems.  He also demonstrated a coping deficit, although not serious.
Together with his other personality characteristics, this might be an “Achilles
heel”.  In situations of emotional overload or affect, he was at risk of
thinking and acting impulsively – and probably in an aggressive manner.

[
430
]

This profile explains the husband’s aggressive
and dominating behaviour from the start to the present.  He takes control and
is threatened when he does not have it.  Defiance, aggressiveness and resistance from the wife caused him “to raise
it a notch” in an attempt to control the situation and to dominate.  His
reaction was to put the blame on her, rather than to appreciate that her needs
were not being met.  Rather than trying to charm her out of her desire to
separate, his reaction went the other way – toward domination, control, and
winning submission.  His answers to the problem focused on simple, clear
causes:  alcohol abuse, smoking, sleeping in, failing to get up in the
mornings, etc.  However, his preference to avoid self-introspection probably
also focused his attention not only on blaming the wife for her shortcomings and
behaviour, but also on his children’s troubles and needs.  When he identifies
an external problem, he looks for answers (preferably clear and simple ones).
He problem-solves with equal aggressiveness and determination, and when he
meets resistance, he seeks to overcome and control.  I hesitate to go too far
with these types of comments.  However, I am sure the reader can make his or
her own connections.

(c)

Dr Kershner’s Results

[
431
]

Dr Kershner administered cognitive tests that
placed the wife in the normal average range.  Her strength was in verbal
reasoning and expression.  She demonstrated weakness in non-verbal areas,
including hands-on manipulation, visual-spatial and perceptual skills.  Her
judgment and recognition of social norms were good, although personality
characteristics could distract her from exercising good judgment or social
skills.  She also demonstrated poor memory.  This had a negative effect on
verbal and non-verbal performance and might have been due in part to emotional
distraction.  Although some of the documentation and history provided to Dr
Kershner suggested that the wife may have suffered manic episodes, the
psychologist could not detect signs of mania.  The wife was of average
intelligence.  Dr Kershner also thought that the wife was a highly motivated
individual because of her great desire to care for people.  This could be a
parenting asset.

[
432
]

In terms of personality, Dr Kershner believed
that the wife had some problems and limitations, but not to the extent of being
personality disorders.  She testified that the wife was extremely anxious –
high anxiety being a function of her dependency need.  The anxiety was further
amplified by the high conflict marriage breakdown.  Dependency needs were a
major factor in the wife’s psychological profile.  This meant that she had a
great requirement to feel safe and taken care of by someone who was
trustworthy.  Her dependency needs took priority in a relationship and caused
her significant anxiety.  She needed constant reassurance.  As a result, her expectations
of relationships could be inappropriate, unrealistic and make her vulnerable.
She would allow others to treat her inappropriately because she hoped they
needed her and would take care of her.  She might also have serious difficulty
understanding social boundaries, for example recognizing when she did or did not
have the right to impose herself on others.

[
433
]

Dr Kershner explained that the way the wife dealt
with her dependency needs was through distancing, denial and idealization.  She
tended to have a narrow frame of reference to things in order to become deeply
involved in them and she tended to remain emotionally detached from
situations.  She also preferred to rationalize and rely on thoughts rather than
feelings to come to conclusions, which made her seem unmotivated, undemanding
and bland.  She might also act quickly to meet her needs, so that they did not
remain unsatisfied.  Self-gratifying behaviour could also lead her into
problems.

[
434
]

The tendency to frame things in an overly narrow
fashion could cause the wife to overlook important details in social or
interpersonal interactions so that she might misread situations.  In an effort
to avoid unpleasantness, she could ignore important information or fail to
recognize behaviours that were expected or required in certain situations.  Dr
Kershner gave an example of this tendency.  At the time of their first meeting,
the wife and Adrian had made three phone calls to the office about parking and the
meeting place.  When Dr Kershner finally met the face-to-face, she commented on
the numerous calls.  However, the wife insisted there had only been one.  When
the psychologist listed them with detail, the wife finally agreed.

[
435
]

Dr Kershner thought that the wife had been so
focused on the final call that she forgot or overlooked the others.  Her
anxiety and need to look good in the eyes of others had lead her to misspeak.
Her poor memory and tendency to focus narrowly on what was on her mind at the
moment augmented this tendency.  Dr Kershner had the impression that the wife
acted this way all the time.  It had become a habit and was probably the reason
that Dr Horowitz thought she was lying to him, when in fact she was not.  In Dr
Kershner’s opinion it would be “slightly off” to label the phenomenon as
lying.  This is an interesting analysis and justification, but from the point
of view of individuals at the receiving end and who did not have the benefit of
sophisticated psychological information, it was surely a distinction without a
difference – and one that has probably brought the wife much criticism and has
negatively complicated her interaction with others.

[
436
]

The wife idealizes things and relationships.
She wants them to be perfect and supportive.  She wants to believe that
