everything is really good.  She wants everyone, including herself and her
children, to be happy.  As a result, mundane necessities and tasks of everyday
life may not take high priority.  As an example, Dr Kershner observed that the
spiritual fulfillment of the children and making sure they were happy would be
very important to her but she could be sloppy on the details of dinner or other
such mundane parts of household life.  Dinners might be late, and other such
tasks might lag.  This tendency to idealize so as to see the good and not the
bad also caused distancing and denial of reality, and as a result made her
vulnerable to victimization – especially as her personality’s urge was to
please others rather than herself.

[
437
]

She was also prone to focus on the needs of others
(in order to please them in the hope of being loved and cared for herself),
leaving herself open to exploitation and being slow to recognize it.  She
worried about how other people viewed her, and she sensed that she sometimes did
something wrong to upset other people, or that she did not clearly hear the
message others were giving her and that she would then do the wrong thing.  She
was unsure of her own capabilities and feared failure.  While she liked to
think of herself as confident and secure, really she was not.  She also tended
to take a “black or white” view of things with the result that she could come
to decisions or conclusions too quickly.  She tended to see what she wanted
rather than what was there.  Dr Kershner reported as follows:

[The wife] presents an unusual combination
of seeing and not seeing what is in front of her and moving without notice from
one point of view to the other.  She picks up on a small detail but then may
decide to ignore it due to an arbitrary definition of her own, of how things
should be.  In other words, she may think that something should not be there,
so even though she sees it, she ignores it.  She does not forget about it but
she may deny its existence at one moment and then accept it the next, when for
some reason the equation in her mind changes and it does fit in.

[
438
]

Dr Kershner thought that the wife was a
perfectionist and that her expectations of herself were extremely high.  She liked
to look at and think about things from different angles.  She valued non-conformity
and thought of herself as living creatively within her own set of rules,
picking and choosing how she would fit into the larger society.  This was
another aspect of her tendency to idealize.

[
439
]

She also had grandiose tendencies that were “fragile
and easily lost.”  Dr Kershner did not disagree with Dr Horowitz about this
characteristic; but she thought that the example that the assessor had given of
the wife’s grandiose tendency was over-stated and incorrect.  Dr Horowitz had
reported:

At the age of 23, [the wife] met a woman
from Ottawa and decided to move there as well, an experience she likened to
going to University.  After living there for about a year, she then moved to a
“controlled community” in the eastern Arctic.  [The wife] worked in a hotel
there and then a gift shop.  She reported that she encouraged her fellow
employees to have a different and better outlook on service and in so doing
“raised the bar”.  Her recounting of this adventure in her life is filled with
grandiosity.  After fourteen months she decided that it was enough and returned
to the GTA in 1996.

[
440
]

Again, I conclude that this is a matter of
interpretation.  I read the reference to “grandiosity” in this passage as
relating to “this adventure in her life”, which was the larger move to Ottawa,
then to the Arctic and all that happened over that period.  I think that Dr
Kershner may have read it too narrowly.  In any case, grandiosity involves the
manner and tone of the telling.  One probably had to be there to hear it.  In
her own report, in describing her first meeting with the wife, Dr Kershner
stated that: the wife “had a dramatized, histrionic quality”; her impulse
control appeared limited; there was a childish quality to her presentation;
and, “she pontificated about what she thought was the right answer.”  I do not
think there was a great difference between her judgment and Dr Horowitz’s on
the point.  I conclude that these professionals were capable of identifying the
characteristics they reported, which was part of their training and expertise.
The point still remains that the wife tends toward “grandiosity”, which may
make sense if she is idealizing her view of the world, seeing herself as
“special”, trying to present herself in the most favourable light, and wanting
to please others so that she in turn will be loved and cared for.

[
441
]

Dr Kershner also reported that the wife “views
men as protectors who can compete with, and challenge each other, over women,
set off by silly things”.  The wife also regarded mates as father-figures.  In
the interview portion of her report, Dr Kershner observed:

[The wife’s] description of [the husband’s]
appeal is similar to her description of her decision to live with her
biological father when she was 16: she thought that he needed her.

[
442
]

Although some of the reports supplied to Dr
Kershner suggested that the wife might be manic, and the wife reported to her
that she had once been diagnosed as bipolar, Dr Kershner did not think it was
so.  While the wife spoke very quickly and at times had a manic affect, she did
not write with speed or hypertensity (as would have been expected with a
bipolar individual).  Also, while she had suffered chronically from depression
since her teens, her medication had successfully regulated the condition over
the years. Dr Kershner did not believe that the wife’s condition negatively affected
her ability to function in daily life or to assume the role of a parent.  She
did observe, however, that the wife had stopped taking her medication for about
three months, including when she had been tested by Dr Wiedermann.
Accordingly, depression may have been a greater factor in Dr Wiedermann’s
report than it was in fact when the wife was taking her medication.  The
interruption had been a short one in this instance because of financial issues
relating to the dispute with the husband.

[
443
]

Dr Kershner’s overall opinion of the wife was
that while she was not a perfect parent, she was good enough.  I do not disagree
with that.  During the trial I found the wife to be refreshingly direct,
generally well-prepared, and appropriately vigilant of her interests and
rights.  I had no question about her intelligence or ability to understand what
was happening in the court.  While she demonstrated a high level of anxiety
much of the time, it was not inappropriate under the circumstances.  She was also
polite but firm when she thought she should assert her rights.

[
444
]

However, it is clear that the wife is a very
complicated personality.  From Dr Kershner’s testimony and report, one can see
why the wife may have acted or reacted as she did over the period of the
dispute.  It may explain her inattention to the details of the children’s
schooling, homework, recreation, and health issues.  Her idealization of the
world around and tendency not to see or to deny what is not in that idealized
picture, may explain why she did not see the signs of Jacob’s autistic
behaviour in order to report it accurately to Dr Montgomery.  The need to
please and be seen in the right light by others may explain why she left in the
middle of Levi’s concert to pick up a friend’s child.  There are many other
examples that could be given.  I am not a psychologist and do not want to engage
psychological analysis, other than to observe that there is a clear connection
between the wife’s complicated psychological make-up and her behaviour during
this highly conflicted dispute.  I also conclude that the husband’s psychological
make-up aggravated the wife’s anxiety and dependency characteristics to the
extreme.

11.

Conclusion on Custody and Access Issues

[
445
]

I am satisfied that there has been a material
change of circumstances sufficient to warrant a fresh inquiry into the custody
and access of the children, and I have undertaken that fresh inquiry in the
observations and discussion that precede.  The matter was settled and the final
Order made on the basis that Jacob was not developmentally disabled.  I
conclude that the husband’s agreement to the joint and shared custody
arrangement in the final Order was predicated on his belief that Jacob was not
autistic.  I think that was a key component on both sides.  However, everyone
accepted the false negative diagnosis and the wife used it to great effect to
undermine Dr Horowitz’s report and recommendations.  The fact that Jacob is
autistic significantly changes the care and attention he must be given.  It
also affects Levi and the necessity to give him special consideration because
of his brother’s condition, although it does not appear consideration was given
to separating the boys.  Jacob will require consistency and routine, so that he
may know as much as possible what to expect at every level of his life.  He may
be more difficult to handle as he grows older, and this will have an impact on
everyone in the family.  An assessment of both children’s best interests is
very different with autism as a significant consideration than not.

[
446
]

I also conclude that there is a second basis for
finding a material change in circumstances insofar as custody and access are
concerned. The husband’s acceptance of the wife’s offer and the final Order
that embodied it were intended to bring peace and establish a situation where
the children could thrive in the care of both parents, and the entire family
could normalize life.  From my earlier review of the law, I also conclude that
joint and shared custody assumes that the parents can communicate and
co-operate to a reasonable degree in the day-to-day care of their children.
That does not mean that there will not be differences and disagreements, or
that the parents will like each other.  However, overall there must be
fundamental trust and respect of each other’s ability to care for the children,
and the parents must be able to communicate and cooperate in that regard.  Unfortunately
that has not been the case here.  The strife has continued at the same high
levels of conflict and mistrust as before.  It is a situation that cannot
continue and it is not in the best interests of the children.

[
447
]

I am satisfied that the love, affection, and
emotional ties between each child and both parents is normal and strong.  Both
parents obviously love the children and want the best for them.  If love,
affection, and emotional ties were the measure of who should have custody, both
parents would measure up equally.

[
448
]

It has been impossible to determine the
preferences of either child for a parent.  Dr Horowitz could not offer help on
this factor because of the children’s ages and the way in which they were
caught in the middle of the conflict.  One of the teacher witnesses thought that
at times Levi was closer to his mother, although she did not elaborate.
Another teacher witness noted Jacob’s common interests with his father and
there was uncontradicted evidence that Jacob preferred his father’s support in
academics.  However, these were vague indications and probably based more on
situation.  I conclude that the children love each parent equally and that they
require the company and affection of each equally.

[
449
]

I have considered whether these boys should be
separated so that one lives with each parent.  However, it was not difficult to
decide that this would not be in their long term interests.  These brothers do
not have much other family of their age.  While they have a number of cousins
on their mother’s side of the family, those children are all much older than
Jacob and Levi, and for the most part are of university age.  These boys are
good friends now and they will need each other as they mature and become
adults.  Jacob does not have many friends because of his disorder.  Levi may be
his best friend in life and the one who understands him best.  The relationship
should be encouraged and nurtured.  Separating the boys would only cause
further and greater fracture of the family than has already occurred and might
have a long-term negative effect on them as adults, particularly on Jacob.

[
450
]

Unfortunately I cannot say that either child has
lived in a stable home environment.  The on-going conflict, hostility, and
distrust between the parties have undermined the children’s environment both
before and after the underlying order.  The week-about care situation has not
brought peace and I am concerned that the routines and standards in each home
are so different that the nurturing of the children has been threatened.  This
is especially so with regard to Jacob.

[
451
]

While I am satisfied that both parents could
care for the children and therefore each could manage custody, I am persuaded that
the husband is better equipped and that the children will do significantly
better in his full-time care.  I conclude that he is best able to manage the
children’s academic, recreational, and health situations.  He has demonstrated
his abilities in these areas.  He has consistently taken the lead in dealing
with schools and supervising the children’s daily education programmes.  He has
been consistently involved and deserves much credit in improving both boys’ academic
performance and interest in learning.  Jacob seems to be an intelligent child.
His teachers have said that he is capable of doing well.  His ability to
achieve academically may be his best chance of compensating for his disorder.  This
may be critical to his leading a productive adult life and achieving financial
independence.  The husband understands the academic programme, stays on top of
it and persists both with the children and the schools.  His effectiveness and
consistency have been well demonstrated.  I am also satisfied that he has the
strength to keep the boys on track, if anyone can.  It will be an increasingly
difficult task, but one that I believe the husband is the best equipped of two
to achieve.  While Jacob’s disorder has been identified, Levi may also pose a
problem.  His inability to focus and stay on task has raised concerns that he
may suffer from ADHD.  One of his teachers suspects that is so, although Levi is
still too young to assess.  Whether or not the diagnosis ensues, Levi will
require a strong hand and close supervision.

[
452
]

I do not think the wife has been as involved or
committed to the children’s education programmes or to nearly the same degree as
the husband.  She has not participated in core subjects to the same extent and
I am not convinced that she is as committed to supervision and performance as
the husband is.  She is interested and has done what she can, but there have
been many gaps as discussed.  In my view, the husband has significantly greater
depth and understanding.  He is more consistent and reliable.  There was also
credible evidence that the children did not perform as well when they were in
their mother’s care as when they were with their father.  The wife has conceded
that the husband should direct education issues.  The husband values education
greatly and he has achieved a very sophisticated level of education himself.
The wife’s educational experiences have not been as deep or rich.

[
453
]

The husband was most sensitive to Jacob’s
unusual symptoms that were ultimately identified as autism or Asperger’s
Syndrome.  Without his persistence, the disorder would not have been
identified.  Indeed, the wife was unable to describe the child’s unusual
symptoms to Dr Montgomery with the result that he concluded that Jacob did not
have a disorder.  I do not believe that this was purposeful on the wife’s
part.  It was more a matter of sensitivity and/or avoidance.  I am certain that
the wife did not want her child to have a disability.  What parent would?  So
she failed or refused to recognize the characteristics that must have been
present when the child was with her and which must have been equally
problematic for her as for the husband or anyone else who had dealings with the
child.  Even though it has been many years since the husband obtained his PhD,
he has the educational background to understand the issue and deal with it.
His personality style is to focus on something until he finds the best solution
and to persist. He is prepared to seek out and accept advice.  The wife has not
shown that flexibility or openness.  It is in the children’s best interests to
have a parent with the husband’s insight, persistence and flexibility in
dealing with both major and minor challenges.

[
454
]

The husband has also directed the children’s
recreational activities.  He recognizes the importance of balancing their lives
with activities outside of school, where they might achieve physical fitness,
expand their horizons, learn the discipline of team or individual sports and
competition, and have opportunities for social interaction in a structured
setting.  This is particularly important for Jacob because his disorder also
limits his social skills and opportunities.  Again, the wife has conceded this
area to the husband.

[
455
]

While the wife is committed to Judaism and took
the initiative to enrol the boys in a Jewish school, the husband has the richer
religious and cultural background.  He has been more involved in taking the
boys to religious school, until recently when the decision was made to enrol
them in a school in their own community.

[
456
]

Dr Kirkpatrick testified that children with
Jacob’s disorder require consistency, routine, and structures that allow them
to know what to expect in their day-to-day lives.  I am satisfied that the
husband has best provided the necessary discipline of household and routine,
and that he has consistently followed it with the boys and required their compliance.
I conclude that structure and routine are more a part of his personality style
than is the case with the wife.  Having a nanny has helped him establish clear,
consistent routines and expectations in his home.  The husband has demonstrated
an ability to provide a constant plan of supervision and care when he cannot be
at home during the day due to work.  He has also shown a willingness to make
his work fit his home schedule, for example by restructuring his work day so
that he could pick the children up or take them to activities or appointments.
While he must obviously work in order to support himself and meet his financial
commitments, he has consistently maintained a strong involvement and presence
in his children’s lives.

[
457
]

The wife also faces the prospect of re-entering
the work force, which will introduce considerable uncertainty and stress to her
life.  Until now, she has chosen not to work, but her personal support is
scheduled to terminate in a few years because of the relative shortness of the
marriage.  Given her age and experience, I am sure she would eventually want to
find employment in any event.  I am also concerned that the wife is easily
distracted, that she may not see situations developing, or that she may fall
into denial or avoidance when there is a situation or problem that she does not
like.  The evidence demonstrated examples of this while the children were in
her care (both during interim custody and the final joint/shared custody
arrangement).  The psychological evidence suggested that this was her
personality style.  On occasion, she is also prone to bad judgment, and she may
not be realistic in her assessment of social situations and how to respond
appropriately to them.  A number of examples were discussed in the review of
the evidence.

[
458
]

I have put my mind to whether the husband’s conduct
should reflect negatively on his parenting ability.  I found that he was
verbally abusive to the wife early in the separation.  His behaviour was
completely unjustifiable, especially because it occurred on occasion in front
of one or both children.  Such behaviour was evidenced directly in a tape
recording.  If I thought this was behaviour that would be repeated with the
children I would not grant him custody.

[
459
]

I am convinced that the behaviour was probably situational
and limited to the period between the marriage breakdown in the fall of 2006
and his moving out of the matrimonial home in early February 2007.  He treated
the wife in this unacceptable way in the context of the extreme stress and
hostility between them.  Once he was aware that the wife was recording their
conversations the behaviour probably ceased.  There were still arguments.  The
wife did not shrink from argument and in fact she was probably the aggressor on
occasion, including with the use of profanity.  Once the husband moved out of
the matrimonial home, the behaviour stopped entirely.  From then on, most
communication has been written.

[
460
]

As Dr Horowitz testified, the husband is a very
direct individual who is not afraid to express himself strongly.  However, the
assessor’s investigation revealed that the husband was “very sweet” with the
children, sensitive to their emotional needs and personalities.  There was no
credible evidence that the husband has been abusive of the children in any
way.  Therefore, I do not think conduct is a consideration in this case.

[
461
]

Many other issues were raised and complaints
levelled on both sides.  I have reviewed and discussed them because they seemed
of great importance to these self-represented parties.  I did not want them to
think I had ignored the issues or failed to give them careful consideration.
However, the core of my decision is as I have just stated.  Because of the
ongoing conflict and mistrust between the parties, and also because of the
wife’s concession in the direction of education, recreation and health care
issues, I do not think that parallel parenting is a meaningful consideration or
likely to work either.

[
462
]

Finally, I saw no evidence that the husband
would oppose or interfere with the children having as much contact with their
mother as is reasonably possible.  He recognizes that this contact is necessary
to their healthy development.  Thankfully this is one area where there has been
little conflict.  Both parents recognize the importance of contact with the
other parent and have generally facilitated it.  Neither parent has attempted
to frustrate the children’s contact with the other parent.

[
463
]

For all these reasons I have concluded that it
is in the best interests of the children that they be in the sole custody of
the husband.  However, the wife’s access to the children should be as great as
possible without disrupting their normal weekday routines.  I am also concerned
that they maintain contact with the wife’s immediate family, which according to
the evidence, seemed to get together most often on week-ends and special
occasions.

12.

Order to Be Made in Respect of Custody and Access

[
464
]

Therefore, for all these reasons, paras. 2
through, and including, para. 30 of the Order granted April 16, 2009, shall be

III.

Child
and Spousal Support

1.

General Background

[
465
]

The April 16, 2009, Order required the husband
to pay child support of $4,198 per month based on estimated annual income of
$340,159 in 2008, and spousal support of $7,250, all commencing on February 1,
2009.  Therefore, the husband would be paying total monthly support of $11,448.
Because of the timing of his business tax year end, he was to produce all
information necessary to calculate his actual 2008 annual income under the
Federal
Child Support Guidelines
by June 1, 2009, then start paying the resulting
appropriate monthly amount of
Guideline
child support commencing July 1,
2009.  Any underpayment or overpayment of child support from February 1 to July
1, 2009, would be adjusted accordingly.  The parties were to exchange income
information again on June 1, 2010, and on June 1 of each year following,
presumably so that the child support could be adjusted on July 1 of each year.

[
466
]

In addition to the monthly child support, the
husband was to pay 80% of the children’s special and extraordinary expenses in
2009, with the wife paying the other 20%.  In following years their respective shares
of these expenses was to be adjusted on July 1 of each year based upon their
respective annual incomes as disclosed through the June 1 income disclosure
process.  “Special and extraordinary expenses” were specifically defined to be
the following child expenses: private school tuition, uniforms, books and
related fees; music lessons; karate lessons and any successor activity;
dentistry and orthodontic treatment; prescription medicine; and, such other
expenses as agreed or determined through arbitration or court order.

[
467
]

The husband testified that he produced his 2009
income information (including income tax returns) to the wife’s counsel.
However, it does not appear that there was any adjustment or change as a result.
The wife did not dispute that the information had been produced.  It appears
that around the same time the wife’s relationship with her counsel began to
fail because of non-payment of accounts and by August or September 2009 they
were indicating that they were getting off the record.

[
468
]

The husband testified that his income went into
steep decline in 2009 because of the national economic downturn which had a
great impact on Oshawa’s local manufacturing economy.  He explained that he
practiced family law almost exclusively and that he limited it to consultations
and negotiated settlements.  He tried to avoid court work and had only gone to
trial twice in his career.  Also, he did not work in the area of family law
enforcement or for clients whose views of their obligations were unreasonable.
He relied heavily on telephone yellow page advertising as a source of clients,
spending $4,000 annually for local directory advertising.  When his volume of
work declined in 2009, he said he increased the amount of directory advertising
to $6,000 that year but it did not have an effect.  He advertised that the
first short consultation would be free, and as a result he would see 10 to 12
people a day, many of whom would become clients.  When the economy went bad in
2009 that decreased to 10 or 12 consultations per week in a good week.  The
husband observed that he was also facing competition from younger family
practitioners who were charging hourly rates of about $175 whereas his rate was
$350 per hour.

[
469
]

The husband testified that his practice had not
recovered appreciably by the time of trial. He described many cutbacks that he
had had to make and detailed cash flow difficulties, including substantial
income tax arrears.  In order to meet obligations he had borrowed large amounts
of money from his mother and sister ($50,000 from his sister on March 3, 2010,
and $250,000 and $100,000 on January 5, 2009, and July 14, 2009, from his
mother).  He had cashed all his RRSP’s and investments in order to pay
equalization of about $400,000 to the wife, legal fees and other debts.  By the
time of trial he had few assets of value.

[
470
]

The wife filed a sworn Family Responsibility
Office (“FRO”) Statement of Arrears showing amounts of support paid by the
husband from June 1, 2009, to April 4, 2011.  It appears that the husband paid
the ordered $11,448 in June and July 2009 then started to fall into arrears
which totalled $32,220.39 by January 7, 2010.  From February through July 2010,
he paid $4,000 per month and since then he has paid $2,000 per month.  Sometime
in late summer or early fall 2000, he obtained a refraining order in that
amount from the court.   According to FRO, by April 6, 2011, the husband was in
arrears of $149,752.87 in child and spousal support under the April 16, 2009, Order.

2.

Calculation of Annual Income for Purposes of Child Support

[
471
]

The husband presented Mr Ohran Gobrin, Chartered
Business Evaluator (with the firm of Duff & Phelps, formerly Cole &
Partners), specializing in economic and family law valuations, including the
calculation of annual income for child support
Guideline
purposes.  Mr
Gobrin was qualified as an expert in accounting for purposes of determining the
husband’s income for support purposes.  He reviewed the husband’s income year
by year from 2005 through 2010, discussing derivation, characteristics, and
proposing annual incomes year by year for child support purposes.

[
472
]

He based his review on financial statements
prepared by an external accountant, who had been preparing the practice’s
statements for a number of years.  Mr Gobrin knew him to be a qualified,
reputable and reliable chartered accountant, who prepared the statements
according to accepted accounting practices.  Mr Gobrin therefore felt
comfortable with the underlying summaries to the statements and the way they
had been constructed.  However, if he had questions about something in the
statements, he testified that he drilled down to the source and reviewed it.
He was particularly careful to be assured of the accuracy of wages and benefits
paid to staff, including the husband.  The only time he could not rely on the
external accountant’s financial statement was in developing an analysis of the
first six months of the husband’s business results in 2010.  The year was not
complete at the time and Mr Gobrin was required to do an analysis of the period
for court purposes.  Still, he felt comfortable with the information he based
that analysis on because it had been prepared by a staff member who had been
doing the husband’s bookkeeping for many years and was very knowledgeable and
capable about it.  She posted and summarized the practice’s financial
information according to ledgers and processes required by the external
accountant. Mr Gobrin also observed that through his years of experience he
could often spot areas of concern in a statement where an item was
disproportionate to what it would normally be in a business of the kind. When
he noticed such areas, he would again go to the source information to
investigate on his own.

[
473
]

At first, the wife was happy with Mr Gobrin’s
analysis and work.  When he had finished his testimony in court, she thanked
him and remarked that she understood his analysis.  However, as the trial went
on she took the position that she did not trust the husband’s financial
information and she was concerned that he was hiding income or assets.
However, I was satisfied with Mr Gobrin’s approach.  I found his analysis
careful, thorough and forthright.  Audited financial information would have
been a prohibitively expensive proposition that the husband could not afford
and that the evidence did not justify.  The wife did not raise any questions
that would have justified closer examination.  Again, I am satisfied that Mr
Gobrin’s approach was reasonable in the circumstances and that it also produced
reasonably accurate results.  There was no reason to conclude otherwise.

[
474
]

The first task is to determine the amounts of
child support payable by the husband from 2008 until trial. That having been
achieved, the Order of April 16, 2009 may have to be changed, including to
account for arrears.

[
475
]

The starting point for determining the amount of
child support to be awarded under the
Divorce Act
is governed by
ss. 15

to
20
of the
Federal Child Support Guidelines
.  The first task is to
determine the payor spouse’s “annual income”.  Under s. 16 of the
Guidelines
,
“annual income” is the payor’s “Total income” as it appears in his T1 General
form income tax return as adjusted according to Schedule III of the
Guidelines
.
“Total Income” is the amount that appears at Line 150 of a taxpayer’s income
tax return.  It is also subject to considerations contained in ss. 17 to 20,
which give the court very limited discretion in narrow situations.  Overall,
courts have little discretion in quantifying a payor’s annual income and thus
the amount of child support payable.

[
476
]

The husband’s law practice had been incorporated
as Rapoport Professional Corporation (“RPC”) of which the husband was the sole
shareholder.  Mr. Gobrin described RPC as the husband’s “alter ego”.  RPC paid
the husband’s salary into a separate account in his name.  The husband never
drew funds directly from the corporation.  It was therefore fairly easy to
identify the husband’s income from RPC.  The corporation also maintained an
account in its financial ledger entitled “Expenses 5020” into which amounts
paid directly by the corporation for the husband’s benefit were recorded.  Some
of the wife’s support payments had come directly from the corporation and were
thus recorded in this account.  The amounts entered in RPC’s “5020” account had
been added to the husband’s income each year for income tax purposes and he had
paid tax on it.  Mr Gobrin was confident of this because he had examined it.
He also observed that the same staff person had made the entries each year and
that she understood the nature and purpose of the account.

[
477
]

RPC might also have a profit at the end of the
year.  Such profits that had not been paid out to the husband were reported in
RPC’s annual financial statements as “retained earnings”.  Mr Gobrin had
included RPC’s annual retained earnings in the husband’s income for each year that
they occurred, in order to calculate his annual income for child support
purposes.

[
478
]

The attribution of corporate profits (retained
earnings) in a corporation controlled by the payor is permitted under s. 18 of
the
Guidelines
where the court determines that the amount of the payor’s
annual income does not fairly reflect all the income available to him.  In
Brophy
v. Brophy
(2002),
2002 CanLII 76706 (ON SC)
, 32 R.F.L. (5th) 1 (Ont. S.C.), aff’d (2004),
2004 CanLII 25419 (ON CA)
, 45 R.F.L. (5th)
56 (Ont. C.A.), the court outlined factors to be addressed in determining
whether retained earnings ought to be included in annual income for
Guideline

purposes.  I conclude that Mr Gobrin was correct to include RPC’s retained
earnings in the husband’s annual income.  The husband was RPC’s only shareholder,
so there was no other shareholder who had a right to share the retained
earnings, and the husband ultimately exercised sole control of the corporation
and therefore its financial operations.  Also, there was no business or
historical reason put forward as to why profits had been retained. The money
was available to the husband if he had wanted it. It should be attributed to
him so that he could not shelter himself from child support obligations.

[
479
]

Mr Gobrin started with an analysis of the
husband’s financial situation for the first six months of 2010.  It had been
anticipated that the trial would occur before RPC’s tax year was complete and
its financial statements prepared.  During the first six months of 2010 RPC had
paid the husband $45,000 in income.  However, during the same period it had
incurred an operating loss of $28,175.  In most other years it had enjoyed a
profit.

[
480
]

As it turned out, the trial actually took place
after the company’s 2010 financial statements and tax returns were complete and
available.  These documents had been prepared by the husband’s usual accountant
according to accepted accounting practices. RPC had paid the husband $85,000
and the husband had also earned interest income of $1,878.67.  His total “Line
150” income was therefore $86,878.67 in 2010.  However, RPC still had an
operating loss of $16,283 at the end of its 2010 financial year.  The question
was whether that loss should be attributed to the husband’s income for that
year, just as the corporation’s retained earnings had in previous years.

[
481
]

Mr Gobrin testified that virtually all of RPC’s
income had come from client fees for legal services provided.  Therefore the
loss had been incurred in the course of RPC’s business and could not be charged
against anything else.  Also, the corporation and the husband were just as
closely involved in the year of loss as in earlier years of profits.  The
husband was RPC’s alter ego and sole controlling shareholder.  Mr Gobrin
therefore submitted that the loss should be attributed to the husband’s 2010
income just as profits had been attributed to him in previous years.  Mr Gobrin
acknowledged that Section 18 of the
Guidelines
did not make specific
mention of corporate losses.  However, he suggested that on the basis of the
reasoning used to impute retained earnings there was no reason not to attribute
operating losses by application of the same principles.

[
482
]

I agree with Mr Gobrin.  A fair calculation of a
payor’s annual income in circumstances such as this must take both corporate
income and loss into account.  The considerations addressed in
Brophy

are as applicable to RPC’s loss as to its profit.  Coats J. reached the same
conclusion in
Cunningham v. Montgomery
,
[2009] O.J. No. 1310 (S.C.), at
para. 101
.  I will therefore attribute the company’s loss to the husband in
calculating his annual income.

[
483
]

The income tax year of 2010 had one other
unusual aspect in calculating the husband’s annual income.  The husband’s 2006
income tax return had been audited and it was discovered that he had paid too
much tax that year because of benefits attributed to him in his “5020” account
that year (and on which he had accordingly paid income tax) but that had
actually been RPC’s expenses.  The husband therefore received an income tax
refund of $20,891 in the first six months of 2010.  This refund had no impact
on the husband’s 2010 income tax return and would not have been taken into
account in developing his Total Income at Line 150 of the return. The
Guidelines

do not address income tax refunds one way or the other, so I conclude it is not
a consideration.  In any event, if the husband was paying child support in 2006
when the income was attributed to him, the children would already have
benefited from it.  I conclude that the income tax refund should not be
included in the husband’s annual income for 2010.  Aston J. seems to have come
to the same conclusion in
Picard v. Picard
(2001),
2001 CanLII 28214 (ON SC)
, 18 R.F.L. (5th) 346
(Ont. S.C.) where he stated at para. 8 that “an income tax refund is not income
for the purposes of the Child Support Guidelines”.

[
484
]

I therefore conclude that the husband’s annual
income in 2010 for purposes of calculating child support was $49,705 [$86,879 (income)
– $16,283 (operating loss) + $20,891 (income tax refund))].

[
485
]

As Mr Gobrin testified, 2009 was the year that
the husband’s law practice went into steep decline.  Whereas RPC had received
$405,253 in income from fees in 2008, it received $226,780 from fees in 2009.  It
was also the year that the parties settled the dispute.  In order to pay the
wife her equalization (and also his own legal fees) the husband was required to
sell all his investments and collapse his RRSP’s.  Some of the investments were
also in RPC’s name and accounted for the company’s retained earnings over the
years.

[
486
]

In 2009, the husband’s Line 150 Total Income
consisted of employment income, interest income, taxable dividends, taxable
capital gains, and RRSP income.  Schedule III of the
Guidelines
requires
that taxable dividends and capital gains be adjusted to reflect the amount
actually received.  For income tax purposes, dividends are “grossed up” and
only half of capital gains are taxable, so that any amount appearing as a
capital gain in the lines of the tax return before Line 150 must be doubled.
Using September 16, 2006, as the date of separation, and therefore also the
date from which a capital gain or loss would be calculated, the husband had a
capital loss of $6,104.  Because only gains (not losses) go into the
development of Line 150, the loss had no effect and will have no bearing on the
calculation of annual income for child support.  The actual amount of taxable
dividends received was $1,088, and that is the amount that should be used in developing
the husband’s 2009 annual income.

[
487
]

The value of the collapsed RRSP income was
$300,733.  Mr Gobrin testified that most of these RRSP’s were in existence at
the date of separation, so they were included in the husband’s family property
and equalized.  He suggested that the court had discretion and submitted that it
should not be included (or at least part of it should not be included) in the
husband’s annual income because it had been included in his total income when
he acquired the RRSP in any year, and it would therefore have been included in
any base amount for the calculation of child support.  The deduction for the
year an RRSP was acquired was not taken into account in the tax form until
after Line 150.  If the husband had not had the benefit of the deduction when
he acquired it, he should not have to pay on it when he cashed it.  Also, he
suggested that the portion of the RRSP income that went into the wife’s
equalization should not be included in the husband’s annual income because it
would amount to making the husband pay twice – i.e. “double dipping”.

[
488
]

The issue was addressed in the context of child
support by Misener J. in
Mylrea v. Benoit
,
[2003] O.J. No. 2921(Ont. S.C.)
,
where he stated at para. 26:

...by virtue of section 16 of the Guidelines,
annual income is determined using the sources of income set out under the
heading "Total Income" in the T1 General form subject to the
adjustments directed by Schedule III. R.R.S.P. receipts are included as a
source of income in the tax form, and Schedule III makes no mention of any
adjustment. It seems clear therefore that what Mr Mylrea referred to, with some
justification, as "double dipping" is compelled by section 16,
whether or not it is fair to do so. Accordingly, even assuming that it would be
proper for me to vary paragraphs 3 and 8 at this stage - and again I do not
think it would - I am forbidden from doing so by the very terms of the
Legislation.

[
489
]

In
Stevens v. Boulerice
,
1999 CanLII 14995 (ON CTGD)
, [1999] O.J. No.
1568 (Ont. S.C.), Aitken J. also dealt with the issue in a father’s application
to vary child support.  The father had been including $5,000 of RRSP income in
his taxable income for some years.  He wanted to reduce his annual income for
child support purposes because this RRSP income had formed part of his
equalization obligation to his wife.  He argued that having to equalize the
RRSP’s then have it used as a basis for determining child support amounted to
“double dipping” for the mother.  Justice Aiken rejected the husband’s
submission in a reasoned statement at para. 9 of her decision:

I do not accept this argument
for two reasons. First s. 16 of the Guidelines requires withdrawals from
registered retirement savings plans to be included in income and Schedule III
to the Guidelines does not provide for any adjustment to this figure. Secondly,
the equalization process was between the two parents. This Application relates
to child support not spousal support. If Mr. Boulerice has income available to
him from any source, it must be taken into account in determining the level of
child support he is obliged to pay on behalf of his son. The additional child
support based on the registered retirement savings plan income is not being
paid to increase Ms. Stevens' lifestyle. It is being paid as part of Mr. Boulerice's
contribution to Justin's expenses. Consequently I will add an additional $5,000
to Mr. Boulerice's income for the purpose of applying the Guidelines.

[
490
]

Aitken J.’s conclusion has been followed in
Francis
v. Filion
,
[2003] O.J. No. 1138 (Ont. S.C.), at para. 42
, and in
Eskridge
v. Eskridge
,
[2008] O.J. No. 2367 (Ont. S.C.), at para. 21
.  I therefore
conclude that the husband’s 2009 RRSP income must be included in his annual
income for purposes of determining his obligation to pay child support.  The
Guidelines

require it be included and child support is for the benefit of the children,
not the wife, so that “double dipping” is not at play.  The
Guidelines

were intended to provide an objective manner of determining a parent’s income
for purposes of calculating the appropriate amount of child support payable,
and so that there would be consistency and uniformity across the country in the
making of such awards.  I therefore conclude that the husband’s $300,733 RRSP
income in 2009 should be included in his annual income for that year.

[
491
]

Mr Gobrin reviewed RPC’s 2009 financial
statement for the court.  This statement had been prepared by the corporation’s
chartered accountant according to accepted standards and practices.  Its income
from fees was $226,780 and the only other sources of income were “Expense
Recovery” of $676 and “Other” of $659.  However, the corporation had sold its
investments that year, resulting in a $100,310 loss.  In the result, RPC’s net
income for the year was $127,805.  The corporation’s 2009 operating expenses
were $341,139, resulting in a loss for the year of $213,334.  Because the
investment loss was of a non-recurring nature and not in the ordinary course of
RPC’s business, it had been added back into the $213,334 thus producing a net loss
for the year of $113,024 which should be attributed to the husband for reasons
already discussed.

[
492
]

The husband’s 2009 annual income under the
Guidelines

is therefore as follows:

Employment income                                          $110,000

Actual dividends received                                        $750

Interest Income                                         $1,721

Actual capital gains received                                        $0

RRSP income                                                    $300,733

RPC operating loss attributable
($113,024)

2009 Annual Income (Line 150)                       $300,180

[
493
]

Finally, Mr Gobrin reviewed the husband’s 2008
financial information.  Again, it was based on the husband’s 2008 income tax
return and RPC’s financial statement for that year, all prepared by the usual
chartered accountant according to accepted accounting practices and standards.
The husband had received employment income from RPC of $157,740.  He had also
received investment income of $4,808, partnership income of $368 and taxable
eligible dividends of $7,786.  The partnership income related to an investment
with a flow-through tax shelter arrangement that would not appear or be
reported in the income categories that resulted in Line 150 Total Income and
would therefore have no effect on child support.

[
494
]

As previously explained, the dividend income
must be adjusted to reflect the actual amount received, which was $5,370.  The
husband had also declared taxable capital gain income of $51,357, which as
explained earlier, had to be doubled to reflect the actual amount of capital
gain received – i.e. $102,712.  However, in realizing this capital gain he had
incurred brokerage and carrying charges of $8,283 which were deductible as part
of determining the actual amount of capital gain received.  These carrying
charges were not to be included in annual income according to Schedule III,
para. 8 of the
Guidelines
.  For the same reason discussed in respect of
RRSP income in 2009, the capital gain will not be adjusted to reflect
equalization of the investments to the wife.  The husband had also declared
“Other” income of $6,667, which was not explained.

[
495
]

RPC’s 2008 income totalled $410,744 (Fees
$405,253; Investment income $3,717; and, Expense recovery $1,774).  The
company’s expenses totalled $413,273, thus producing a net loss of $2,529,
which will be attributed to the husband for the reasons already discussed.
However, Mr Gobrin had discovered that RPC had wrongly paid expenses on the
husband’s behalf and claimed them as corporate business expenses.  They should
have been charged to the husband’s “2050” account so that they appeared as his
income upon which he paid tax.  These charges included professional fees (legal
and accounting) of $56,767 and other expenses in the amount $8,360, totalling
$65,127.  Because these expenses had already been paid on the husband’s behalf
before he had paid income tax on it, they had to be “grossed up” to reflect the
pre-tax value, which meant adding another $56,379 to the husband’s 2008
income.

[
496
]

Therefore, the husband’s 2008 annual income for
Guideline

purposes is as follows:

Investment income
$4,808

$5,370

$102,712

Brokerage and Carrying Charges
($8,283)

Grossed up “2050” For Income Tax                             $56,379

($2,529)

$387,991

[
497
]

The child support required in the April 16, 2009,
Order was based on the husband’s estimated 2008 annual income of $340,159,
which was $47,832 less than the final amount just determined.

[
498
]

In summary then, the husband’s annual income for
child support purposes with the requisite monthly payments required for two
children under the
Guidelines
is as follows:

Estimated                                    $340,159         $4,198

2008
Determined                                  $387,991         $4,753 per month

2009
Determined                                  $300,149         $3,734 per month

Determined                                   $49,705             $794 per month

3.

Child Support Order to be Made

[
499
]

There is no reason why the husband should not
pay
Guideline
child support based on these annual incomes.

[
500
]

The April 16, 2009, Order provided for payment
of the children’s special and extraordinary expenses in proportion to their
respective incomes.  From the evidence presented the husband paid almost all of
these expenses directly because the wife had no income except the support he paid
to her.  Because of this, there is no issue of arrears of special and
extraordinary child expenses.

[
501
]

At the time of trial the wife still had no
income.  The basic child and spousal support that had been ordered paid to her
went into substantial arrears, as has been discussed, and is still in arrears.
At the time of trial, her financial situation was desperate and precarious.  I
expect it will remain so until the arrears are paid and she manages to find
employment.  There is no point in making an order for payment of special and
extraordinary expenses at this time, either currently or retrospectively.  As
the wife has no income of her own at this time, there is no point to making
more than a nominal order for child support. The parties can address child
support in the future when it becomes necessary, but in any event, not before
July 1, 2012, at the earliest.  This will allow the parties time to re-organize
their affairs and address the arrears issue.  By June 1, 2012, the next
production of income disclosure should have occurred so that the parties can
sort out support adjustments if necessary.

[
502
]

Therefore, paras. 31, 32, 33, 34 and 35 of the
Order granted April 16, 2009, shall be rescinded and replaced by the following:

31.  The Applicant shall pay child support as follows:

(a) $4,753 per month commencing February 1, 2009, based on his 2008
annual income of $387,991;

(b)  $3,734 per month commencing July 1, 2010, based on his 2009 annual
income of $300,149;

(c) $794 per month commencing on July 1, 2011, until and including
December 1, 2011, based on his 2010 annual income of $49,705;

(d)  The Applicant shall be credited with all payments made on
account of support to the Family Responsibility Office, with payments being
first applied to child support and then spousal support, and any arrears of
child support outstanding shall be paid at the rate of $1,500 per month until
paid in full.

32.  The
Respondent shall pay child support of $1 per month commencing December 1, 2011,
based on her annual income of $0.

33.
Commencing on June 1, 2012, and on June 1 of each year, each party shall
provide disclosure of his or her income to the other party.  That disclosure
shall include all of the information necessary to calculate child support under
the
Federal Child Support Guidelines
.

34.  Child
support shall not be subject to review before July1, 2012.

35.
Rescinded.

4.  Calculation of Spousal Support

[
503
]

The April 16, 2009, Order required the husband
to pay spousal support of $7,250 per month commencing February 1, 2009, and
ending on March 31, 2015.  Although the underlying reasoning for the amount and
duration were not put in evidence at trial, it would appear that the parties
were generally following the Federal
Spousal Support Advisory Guidelines

(“
SSAG
”).  Under these
Guidelines
and using the usual computer
generated calculator, an individual earning an estimated annual income of
$340,159 with a five year marriage, shared custody of two children the ages of
Jacob and Levi, and a spouse with no income except the child tax credit, would
pay spousal support in the range of $6,078 to $8,839 (mid-range of $8,049) for
a period of two and a half to 15 years.  It should be noted that the duration
of the spousal support would be two and a half to five years where the husband
has sole custody of the children.  The amount of the spousal support ordered
($7,250 per month) was therefore $799 per month below the midpoint and the
ordered eight and a half year duration (i.e. from the date of separation) was
also a little below the midpoint.  However, the settled amount and duration of
spousal support were clearly in the range and closer to the mid-point than
either extreme.

[
504
]

While I am aware of the process and principles for
assessing the amount and duration of spousal support articulated in the leading
Supreme Court of Canada case of
Moge v. Moge
(1992),
1992 CanLII 25 (SCC)
, 3 S.C.R. 813, I do
not propose to embark on a detailed analysis outside of the application of the
SSAG

framework.  No reason was advanced to alter the duration of spousal support.  For
their own good reasons the parties settled on that term.  It does not seem
unfair given that by mutual agreement the wife had left the work force to
become a full time homemaker with the husband accepting the role of primary
breadwinner.  The wife is entering middle age and may require some retraining
and time to re-enter the workforce.  The parties have also lost time through
their bitter conflict.  The effect should be shared rather than placing it on
the wife’s shoulders as a result of the change in custody.  On the other hand,
the marriage was not a long one and while the wife gave up her employment there
was no evidence that she was not employable and could not find her way back
into the work place.

[
505
]

As I have observed, the parties seem to have
settled child and spousal support within the
Federal Child Support
Guidelines
and
SSAG
.  The Ontario Court of Appeal has recognized
SSAG

as a “useful tool” that is non-binding but akin to a “significant authority”: see

Fisher v. Fisher
(2008),
2008 ONCA 11 (CanLII)
, 88 O.R. (3d) 241 (C.A.).  The Appeal Court
suggested that in questions of spousal support
SSAG
is a good starting
point and that a trial judge should be careful to explain (with authorities) an
amount ordered outside the
SSAG
ranges.  Based on the original framework
for settlement, the conclusions of the Ontario Court of Appeal and the
circumstances of the case, I conclude that analyzing spousal support by
application of
SSAG
is a rational and just starting point in this case,
and also in the context of a variation application.

[
506
]

The April 16, 2009, Order did not provide for
the adjustment of the amount of spousal support when the husband’s actual 2008
annual income was determined.  Nor did it provide for adjustment based on
changes to the husband’s annual income in future years or increases in the cost
of living.  On the other hand, the Order did not specify that the amount (or
duration) of spousal support was not subject to variation, nor did it express
any intention or rationale for why it could not be varied (e.g. a specific
recognition of compensation).  The question then is whether the ordered amount
or duration of spousal support should be varied.

[
507
]

I conclude that the Order did not attempt to
foreclose variation or limit the court’s ordinary jurisdiction to vary
(assuming it could do so).  As I have found, the husband’s income has
diminished substantially in the past few years and his property was depleted by
necessity.  He has experienced significant financial change, which it is not
difficult to conclude meets the standard of a material change in circumstances
according to the principles of law previously discussed.  This material change
is enhanced by the fact that he will now have sole custody of the children, and
because the wife has no income of her own, he will also bear the sole financial
responsibility of supporting them and probably so for at least the next year or
two while the wife finds stable employment.

[
508
]

Before going further, I acknowledge that the
parties both provided the court with their current and budgeted incomes and
expenses, including as deposed in Statements of Financial Information.
However, as often happens in these cases, the expenses claimed were generally
well beyond actual incomes.  The wife’s situation was dire.  Her need is beyond
dispute and there was no question that she had little or no income.  At the
time of trial, she was eking out an existence on the sharply reduced support
payments the husband was giving her.  She was receiving help from her family
with groceries and smaller items.  She testified that she feared she was on the
verge of bankruptcy and losing her home.  I do not disagree.

[
509
]

I accept that the husband’s income plummeted
significantly, probably because of the economy and the changing face of family
law which is focused increasingly on mediation and with parties representing
themselves more and more.  While the Canadian economy has recovered or at least
stabilized considerably, it still faces great uncertainty.  I am not satisfied
that the market for legal services has recovered and there was no reliable
evidence to that effect.  The husband may also have priced himself out of the
market and become too narrow in his practice.  His income from the practice of
family law has diminished significantly, although his annual income in the
years in question sometimes appeared better than it was because of the effect
of collapsing RRSP’s and realizing gains from investments.  Most of the money
derived from these RRSP’s and investments was used to pay the wife’s
equalization payment and his own counsel.  The husband’s actual income (i.e.
his salary from RPC) from the practice of law has declined significantly from
the time of the separation, going from $157,740 in 2008, to $110,000 in 2009
and to $85,000 in 2010.

[
510
]

Still, the husband claimed expenses that were
well beyond his income and simply could not be sustained if his income was, as
I believe it to have been, accurately described by Mr Gobrin.  In a Statement
of Financial Information sworn March 8, 2011, and entered as Exhibit 12 at the
trial, the husband deposed to total a current annual income of $90,000 (all
from employment) and actual expenses of $204,110, which included support
payments totalling $4,000 monthly.   Of course it is absurd that income of
$90,000 can support expenses in excess of $204,000.  I realize that in 2009 he
borrowed $350,000 from his mother, although he had paid most of it back by the
end of the year.  However, in April 2009, he also purchased a 1500 to 2000
square foot two storey home in a new subdivision for $308,000.  The home
carried a $283,000 mortgage with monthly payments of $1,817.  He had to have
convinced the bank that he had the means to pay the mortgage in the face of his
practice’s decline and the April 16, 2009, Order for support.

[
511
]

Even more puzzling is the husband’s life-style,
which does not square with his law practice’s financial decline.  He owns three
cars (two are sports cars), and pays the nanny $1,400 per month plus room and
board.  In 2010 he also travelled extensively, including to Prague
Czechoslovakia, Kelowna B.C., Ecuador (via Miami Florida) and Paris France.  I
suspect he is receiving financial assistance from his mother.  In any event,
his declared income and expenses do not add up.  Consequently, I can place
little credence in his Statement of Financial Information and the personal
expenses set out there.  This is another reason to be guided by the
SSAG
.
It will result in the wife being treated fairly by an objective measure that is
consistently applied throughout Canada and will give general effect to the
principles articulated in
Moge
.  I have confidence in the documentation
of the husband’s income as presented by Mr Gobrin.  A payor’s income is the
major component of the
SSAG
calculation.  The husband will simply have
to make his expenses comply with his income.

[
512
]

SSAG
is not
mandatory.  It is only a guide, yet a good one and a good place to start in
normal circumstances.  It requires the determination of the payor’s annual
income as calculated in the
Federal Child Support Guidelines
, and once
this is calculated, the application of a formula to the amount will produce a
recommended range of spousal support which the court must then settle upon. It
is therefore necessary to revisit the annual income calculations determined
above in connection with child support.

[
513
]

As discussed in calculating child support, the
husband’s 2010 annual income consisted of employment and interest income, which
was then reduced by attribution of RPC’s loss for the year, resulting annual
income of $49,705.  This is also his annual income for purposes of calculating
spousal support in that year.

[
514
]

The components of the husband’s 2009 annual
income for child support purposes will also be the same for spousal support,
except for one item.  The $300,733 in RRSP that the husband cashed had been
equalized with the wife.  Accepting the case law cited, I included it in annual
income for purposes of calculating child support and for the reasons given. However,
in the context of spousal support, the situation is different.  Having previously
been equalized, the RRSP’s had already benefited the wife.  If the RRSP’s were
added into the husband’s annual income for spousal support, the wife would be paid
again to some extent – i.e. there would be “double dipping”.  I therefore
conclude that it would not be fair to include it in the husband’s annual
income.  It is in fact a non-recurring capital loss within the scope of s. 17
of the
Guidelines
, which gives the court discretion.  Coats J. accepted
this approach in
Cunningham v. Montgomery,
at paras. 85 and 101.  I will
reduce the husband’s earlier calculated 2009 annual income of $300,149 by the
amount of $300,733 resulting in his having no annual income that year for
spousal support purposes.

[
515
]

Only one adjustment must be made to the actual
2008 annual income calculated for
Guideline
child support.  Most of the
securities sold to produce the actual capital gain of $102,712 had been equalized
with the wife.  The entire capital gain was included in the husband’s 2008
annual income for child support purposes because it had not benefited the
children.  However, I conclude that there should be an adjustment for purposes
of calculating spousal support, just as was done with the RRSP income in 2009
and for the same reasons.  I accept Mr Gobrin’s testimony that the adjusted
capital gain is $66,710.  That amount will be included in the husband’s 2008
annual income for spousal support purposes instead of the amount included in
the child support calculation.  As a result, the husband’s 2008 annual income
for purposes of calculating child support under the
SSAG
will be $351,989.

[
516
]

The husband’s annual income for the years under
consideration and the resulting
SSAG
spousal support ranges are is as
follows (assuming shared custody of children the ages of Jacob and Levi, and attributing
the child tax credits to the wife during the years of shared custody):

2008 Agreed                $340,159 (estimated)            $6,078 to
$8,839 (mid $8,049)

2008 Actual                 $351,989                              $6,292
to $9,171 (mid $8,359)

2009 Actual                 $ nil
$ nil

2010 Actual                 $49,705
$788 to $1,093 (mid $963)

[
517
]

Because of the husband’s declining income since
2008 and the unusual items that impacted the calculation of his annual income
in those years, there is a significant fluctuation in the spousal support
payable over those years.  This fluctuation makes it particularly difficult to
calculate a fair level of current support.  I am not concerned as much with the
effect of the fluctuation in previous years because I expect that most of the
spousal support in those years will be arrears, especially if arrears of child
support must be paid first, as I have ordered.  Payment of previous years’
spousal support is more a matter of enforcement than of current sustaining
income, so there is justice in precision.  However, s. 17 of the
Federal
Child Support Guidelines
provides as follows:

17 (1)      If the court is of the opinion
that the determination of a spouse’s annual income under section 16 would not
be the fairest determination of that income, the court may have regard to the
spouse’s income over the last three years to determine an amount that is fair
and reasonable in light of any pattern of income, fluctuation in income or
receipt of a non-recurring amount during those years.

[
518
]

I note that the husband’s average annual income
for 2008, 2009, and 2010 (for purposes of
SSAG
) is $133,898.  With the
litigation out of the way and the husband being able to refocus on his work, I
expect that he will find a way to rejuvenate his practice and increase his
income.  I doubt very much that he will have another year with no income or
that he will repeat his 2010 income level.  The unusual set-offs and additions
of the previous years are also unlikely to repeat themselves because the
husband’s and RPC’s assets and retained earnings have been depleted.  The three
year average amount of $133,898 is a fair amount to impute to him for purposes of
calculating current spousal support and I will do so.  Based on an annual
income of $133,898,
with the children being in his sole custody
and the
wife having no income, the monthly spousal support payable under
SSAG
would
be in the range of $584 to $779 (mid-range of $682 per month).

[
519
]

Another possibility would be to average the
actual annual income (i.e. as per paras. 498 and 516) for the past three years
both for child and spousal support purposes and order the mandated
Federal Child
Support Guidelines
and
SSAG
amounts for each of 2009, 2010 and 2011
when shared custody prevailed. In that scenario, the average annual income for
child support purposes would be $245,948 resulting in
Guideline
monthly
child support of $3,105.  The average annual income of $133,898 for spousal
support purposes (
assuming shared custody of children the ages of Jacob and
Levi
and the wife having no income except the child tax credits) would
result in monthly spousal support in the range of $2,147 to $3,258 ($2,846
midpoint).  When one calculates the total child and mid-point spousal support
payable during the shared custody regime based on actual annual income and the
averaged annual income, the wife would receive almost $8,500 more over the
entire period under the actual annual income approach than under the averaged
approach.  I do not see why she should not be paid based on the actual annual
income approach.  She has endured considerable hardship while the husband has
apparently maintained a comfortable lifestyle in a new home with a nanny and
travel abroad.  The wife will need the arrears of support to stabilize her
financial affairs, to provide suitable accommodation for the children during
access and to get herself re-oriented to the workplace (including the
possibility of retraining). I have already decided that child support should be
varied to reflect the husband’s actual annual incomes as found in 2008, 2009,
and 2010 (para. 502).  I will do the same in respect of spousal support and in
that regard see no reason why the mid-point should not be used.

[
520
]

Accordingly, it is ordered that para. 35 of the
April 16, 2009, Order be rescinded and replaced with the following:

35.  The Applicant shall pay the Respondent spousal support monthly
as follows:

(a)  $8,248 commencing February 1, 2009, based on annual income of
$340,159;

(b)   $0 commencing January 1, 2010, based on annual income of $0;

(c)  $963 commencing January 1, 2011, until December 31, 2011, based
on annual income of $49,705;

(d) $682 commencing January 1, 2012, based on annual income of
$133,989 (the average annual income for 2008, 2009, and 2010);

(e)  Arrears of spousal support shall be paid at the rate of $1,500
per month until paid in full.

IV         Contempt Issue

[
521
]

The husband brought a motion for contempt against
the wife.  It was agreed that it be rolled into the trial and dealt with as
part of the larger proceedings.  The husband alleged that he and the wife had
agreed he would receive certain chattels from the home, including a side table
from an older bedroom set; a dresser, table and chairs from the loft of the
matrimonial home; and a picture of the Chicago skyline and other art work.
Para. 49 of the April 16, 2009, Order had provided for an equal division of
household contents with the exception of items each brought into the marriage,
which would remain the property of the party bringing those items in.  If they
could not agree on a division, they could have it decided by the court or a
named arbitrator.

[
522
]

There does not seem to be disagreement that an
agreement was reached on the division of the contents after the husband walked
through the home.  He asked for far less than half and it appears that he
received many of the items he wanted.  The difficulty was that the items were
not listed and initialled by the parties.  When the husband complained that he
had not received all the items he wanted, the wife’s lawyer wrote him on April
17, 2009, saying that he had received everything he wanted and more.

[
523
]

At trial, the wife suggested that when the
matrimonial home was sold (as ordered), the items of furniture sought by the
husband were left in it.  She stated that it was not her responsibility to
deliver them to the husband and that he ought to have arranged it himself.  She
also denied there that had been any agreement with respect to art.  She
testified that she had sold the “Chicago” picture when the husband failed to
pay her the required amount of support and she needed money to get by.  Of
course, the husband disagreed.

[
524
]

The problem is that there is no reliable proof
of agreement that the disputed items were to go to the husband.  Also, it may
well be that the items of furniture were left at the home and the husband
failed to pick them up, as the wife said.  It is all too uncertain and vague,
based on the scant but conflicting evidence received.  The husband’s motion for
contempt is therefore denied.

Summary of Order to Be Made and Costs

[
525
]

For all of these reasons, an order will issue as
particularized in paras. 464, 502, and 520 above.

[
526
]

If costs are an issue, submissions may be made
in writing.  The husband’s written submissions must be served and filed within
15 days of the release of these Reasons, and with the wife to respond within 15
days of the husband’s written submissions having been served upon her.  The
husband may file and serve a written reply to the wife’s submissions and that
reply shall be served and filed within 10 days of his having been served with
the wife’s written reply.  The husband’s initial written submission for costs
and the wife’s written reply shall each be no longer than ten typed pages of 8”
x 11” paper with one inch margins and size 12 font, plus copies of invoices or
statements of account if appropriate.  The husband’s final written reply shall
be no longer than five typed pages.  If no submission is made for costs by the
husband, the wife may make her own written submission within 20 days of the
release of these Reasons and the husband shall reply in writing within 15 days
thereafter, all written submissions to be typed on paper with margins and font
as directed above.  The failure of a party to make a written submission for
costs as provided above will result in an order being made that there shall be
no costs.
